2.content: Play the game's own clips, write animations as keys in Lua for anything, and add particles, lights, trails, shakes and sounds.

5.content: Reaching: a hand or a foot goes somewhere

6.content: Look at it before you use it

16.content:
Three names work together here. `game.Animations` moves things: bones of a character or a creature, or a thing
as a whole. `game.Effects` adds what is seen around it, and `game.Sounds` what is heard. None of them needs the
Unreal editor or a pak.

17.content: `game.Animations:Define(name, spec)` makes an animation. It is plain Lua until it plays.

18.content: A **track** says what moves. It is named by a bone, or `Self` for the thing as a whole.

19.content: A track is a list of **keys**: a time in seconds, then what is added at that time.

20.content:
A turn is about the character's own directions, whichever way the bone points: `Yaw` about up (positive
turns right), `Pitch` about the character's right (negative leans forward), `Roll` about forward.

21.content:
What a key adds is an offset: `Pitch`, `Yaw`, `Roll` in degrees, `X`, `Y`, `Z`, and `Scale`. A key of `{}`
means "as the game has it". So an animation that starts and ends with `{}` blends in and out by itself.

22.content:
Between two keys the values are eased. `ease` is `"smooth"` when omitted. The others are `"linear"`,
`"in"`, `"out"` and `"snap"`. A key can name its own as its third entry.

28.content: Tracks for the player's body in third person, when they should differ from `tracks`.

30.content: Where a hand or a foot goes. See below.

32.content: `"hand"` or `"shoulder"`: what a reach key is measured from.

34.content: How long it runs. The time of the last key when omitted.

36.content: `true` starts it again when it ends.

38.content: How keys are eased when a key does not say.

40.content: `{ { seconds, function } }`: functions that run when the animation passes a time.

41.content:
A bone is added to, not replaced: the game goes on animating, and your offsets come on top. So a swing you
write works while the character walks, and a creature keeps breathing under it.

42.content: These names fit the player's arms in first person and the body in third:

43.content:
`RightClavicle`, `RightShoulder`, `RightElbow`, `RightWrist`, `RightHand`, and the same with `Left`. On the
body there are also `Head`, `Neck`, `Chest`, `Spine`, `Waist`, `Hips`, `RightThigh`, `LeftThigh`, `RightKnee`,
`LeftKnee`, `RightFoot` and `LeftFoot`.

44.content:
Any other bone goes by the name its skeleton gives it. `game.Animations:GetBones(target)` lists them, and a
name the skeleton does not have raises an error that suggests the nearest.

45.content:
Turning a shoulder and an elbow by hand until the hand is where you want it is slow work. A **reach** says
where the end of a limb goes, and Wax bends the two bones above it to get it there. The limbs are `RightHand`,
`LeftHand`, `RightFoot` and `LeftFoot`. `X` is forward, `Y` to the right and `Z` up, as the character stands.

46.content: `reach_from = "hand"`, when omitted: a key adds to where the hand is in the game's own pose.

47.content:
`reach_from = "shoulder"`: a key says where the hand is, measured from the shoulder (for a foot, from the
hip). The reach comes in from the game's pose over the first moments and goes back at the end, so the keys
need no `{}` at the ends. An arm is about 60 long and a leg about 90. A place further off is reached as far
as the limb goes.

48.content:
To turn the hand as well, give the limb a table: `RightHand = { turn = true, keys = { ... } }`. With
`"shoulder"`, the `Pitch`, `Yaw` and `Roll` of a key are then how the thing in the hand is turned, as the
character stands: all three 0 points it the way the character faces.

49.content: The elbow or the knee stays on the side it is on in the game's pose.

50.content:
One limb can differ from the rest: `LeftHand = { from = "hand", keys = { ... } }` adds to the game's pose
while the other limbs of the animation are placed from the shoulder.

51.content: `reach_blend` is how long a reach from the shoulder takes to come in and to go back: `0.2`, or `{ 0.1, 0.4 }`.

52.content:
When these were tried on the player's body, the hand, the foot and the turn of the held thing each came out
where they were asked for, to the unit and to the degree.

53.content:
A model view can play your animation on a mesh in a window, where you can turn it and see it
from every side. `view:Play(animation, options)` takes the same options as `animation:Play`.

54.content:
`facing = 0` says the mesh faces along its own X, as the player's body does. Left out, a look faces the way
the game's creatures do.

55.content: `rate = 0.2` plays it in slow motion, which is the easy way to see where a limb goes.

56.content:
`view:Attach(shape, { socket = "R_prop_00", at = , turn = , material = })` puts a shape of your own in the
model's hand, so a tool is seen through the swing. With no turn, find out which way it points first.

57.content: `view = "third"` in the options plays the tracks under `third`, as the player's body does.

58.content:
A hand that follows a path while the rest stands still looks like a puppet. When a swing for the player's body
was first made here that way, it was plainly wrong. What made it read as a swing:

59.content: **Key poses, not a path.** A wind-up, the cut, the follow-through and a settle, each a whole pose.

60.content:
**The body leads.** Hips, waist and chest turn through the cut, each a little more than the one below. The
head turns the other way, so the eyes stay on what is hit.

61.content: **The other arm moves against it**, and a step or a sinking of the hips goes with a heavy blow.

62.content: **Uneven timing.** Slow into the wind-up (`"out"`), fast through the cut (`"in"`), slow to settle.

63.content:
**The tool leads with its edge.** Give the hand a turn at every key, so the blade is ahead of the handle the
whole way.

64.content: Hold one pose at a time in a model view, look from the front, the side and above, and only then join them.

65.content: `animation:Play(target, options)` plays it and gives you the play.

69.content: The arms in first person and the body in third. It follows when the player changes view.

72.content: A thing of a blueprint, or a part

73.content: The thing as a whole, by its `Self` track.

77.content: How fast it runs. `1` when omitted.

81.content: How much of the movement is added. `0.5` is half.

83.content: `true` leaves a thing where its `Self` track put it.

85.content: A function that runs when it has run to its end.

87.content: `"first"` or `"third"`: on the player, the one view it shows in.

89.content:
The game gives no way to set a bone of a mesh it animates. So while an animation plays, Wax shows a copy of
the mesh that it can pose: the copy takes the game's own pose every frame, your keys are added, and the real
mesh is hidden. What hangs on the mesh, such as a held tool or clothing, is moved over to the copy and back.
When nothing has played for ten seconds the copy is taken away. While nothing plays, it costs nothing.

90.content: `game.Animations:Play(target, clip, options)` plays one of the game's montages or sequences.

91.content:
The player's arms and body are two skeletons with clips of their own, so give `first` and `third`. For a
creature give one path.

92.content: Options: `rate`, `blend` (seconds in and out), `start`, and for a single sequence `slot` and `loops`.

93.content: `part` plays one named part of a montage, such as `"Action_0"`, or `{ first = name, third = name }`.

94.content:
With both `first` and `third`, the body's clip is paced to last as long as the arms'. `match = false`
lets each run at its own length.

95.content: `game.Animations:Find("1st sledge montage")` gives the paths that hold every word. The game has 4,091.

96.content: A clip only moves a skeleton it was made for.

97.content:
Everything here hangs on something: `on` is a character, a creature, a thing or a part, and `game.Me` when
omitted. `socket` names a bone or socket of it, and `at` is measured from there.

101.content: Starts one of the game's particle effects. `seconds` is how long it stays, `3` when omitted, `false` for until `Stop`. `set` gives parameters of the effect.

105.content: A glowing ribbon behind an edge that moves: `from` and `to` are the ends of the edge, `seconds` how long the ribbon is in time, `life` how long it runs.

107.content: Shakes the player's view with one of the game's camera shakes.

109.content: Paths of the game's 554 particle effects. `FindShakes` does the same for its 78 shakes.

110.content:
What `Particles`, `Light` and `Trail` give has `Stop()` and `IsAlive()`. Particles have `Set(name, value)`,
a light `SetColor` and `SetIntensity`.

111.content: Everything your mod started is taken away when the mod unloads.

112.content: At most 64 effects are alive at once for all mods. A new one past that takes the oldest away.

113.content:
A trail is laid on a curve through the places the edge was at, so a fast swing leaves an arc, not corners. It
keeps the edge's outer end (`to`) and closes in on it toward its old end, which gives a crescent.

117.content: Starts this many seconds from now. A trail that also runs during the wind-up doubles back on itself. `life` counts from the start.

119.content: Small glowing bits that come off the edge while it moves, drift, rise and shrink: how many a second, or `{ rate, size, life, speed, rise }`. A trail has 60 at a time at most.

121.content: Makes it a streak this wide along the middle of the edge, always turned to face the view. Without it a cut that comes straight at the view shows the ribbon from its side, as a line.

123.content: `true` keeps the trail with the view, as the arms of first person are, instead of leaving it behind in the world. For something held in first person.

125.content: A material of your own from `game.Assets:Material` in place of the plain glowing one.

126.content:
The game draws what is held in first person bent toward the screen, and it does that in the item's material
(the number `PaniniScale`, 1 in first person and 0 in third). A trail with the plain glowing material is drawn
where the blade really is, which is a little off where the blade shows. So give it a material of the game's
item kind with that number set, and `with_view = true`:

127.content:
`MI_ORB_Light` is one of the game's item materials that glow. The plain item material
(`/Game/ASS/MAT/MA_ITM`) takes the same textures and stays dark whatever `Emissive Intensity` says.
At an intensity of 14 orange turns yellow; 2 to 4 keeps the colour of the picture.

128.content: With nothing else it is heard everywhere. With `on` it comes from that thing: `{ on = creature }`.

129.content: `game.Sounds:Find("whoosh bear")` gives the paths that hold every word. The game has 5,515 sounds.

130.content: Only the game's own sounds can be played. A sound file of your own is not possible yet.

131.content: A sound cannot be stopped once it plays.

132.content:
All of it was run on the host of a prospect: a sound, a shake, sparks and a light on the player's hand, a clip
of the game, an animation of keys on the arms and on the body with the clothing following, and a spawned cube
turning with a trail behind it. These have not been looked at yet:

133.content: An animation of keys on a creature.

134.content: A reach on the arms seen in first person. On the body it was measured.

135.content: Particle effects of the older kind (`ParticleSystem`), and `Set` on any effect.

136.content: A sound that comes from a thing.

137.content: What other players of a session see. Expect them to see none of it: it is made on your PC.

138.content:
Every function is listed in the Animations reference and the
Effects reference.

140.content: game.Assets loads the game's meshes, textures and materials by path, makes materials of your own, and builds shapes from numbers.

148.content:
An **asset** is a file of the game: a mesh, a texture, a material, a blueprint's class. `game.Assets` loads
one by its path and keeps it in memory for your mod.

149.content:
Assets are what Blueprints are built from: the mesh a part shows and the material it is
drawn with.

150.content:
A path is written `"/Game/Folder/Name"` or `"/Game/Folder/Name.Name"`. The form the Unreal editor copies,
`Texture2D'/Game/Folder/Name.Name'`, works too. A blueprint's class is `"/Game/Folder/BP_Thing.BP_Thing_C"`.
Letter case does not matter.

154.content: Loads an asset and gives its Instance. Gives `nil` and the reason when there is no such asset.

156.content: `true` while the asset is in memory. It loads nothing.

158.content: Lets go of something your mod asked for, before the mod unloads.

159.content: When the path is wrong, the reason names the nearest names in that folder where it can.

160.content: Asked again, the same Instance comes back at once.

161.content:
After a map change an Instance from before answers with an error. Call `Load` again, which costs little
because the asset is still kept.

162.content:
To find paths, look in the game's files with a tool such as FModel, or read them from the
game's tables: an item's `Icon` is a path.

163.content:
A first load stops the game until it is done. An item picture took 0.2 to 1 ms and a mesh 5 ms. Load when
your mod starts or a window opens, not in the middle of a fight.

164.content:
The game frees an asset that nothing uses within minutes, and using it after that crashes. So Wax holds on to
everything `Load`, `Texture` and `Material` give your mod, and lets go of it all when the mod unloads. You
have nothing to do.

165.content: `game.Assets:Texture(file)` reads a `.png` or `.jpg` from your mod's folder and gives it as a texture.

166.content:
The file is named from your mod's folder. A path that leaves the folder with `..` raises an error, and so
does a file that is not there or is no picture.

167.content: Asked again, the same texture comes back and no file is read.

168.content: A changed file is read again after your mod reloads.

169.content: Such a texture goes onto a material, as below. Wax has no control yet that shows one in a window.

170.content:
`game.Assets:Material(parent, options)` makes a new material from one of the game's, with your colours,
numbers and textures set on it.

174.content: Colour parameters. A colour is a name such as `"Red"`, `"#rrggbb"`, or `{ R = 1, G = 0.5, B = 0 }`.

178.content: Texture parameters: a texture from `Load` or `Texture`, or the path of one.

179.content:
The parameter names belong to the material you start from. `EmissiveMeshMaterial` has `Color`. Another
material has other names. A name the material does not have changes nothing, and no error says so.

180.content: Every call makes a new material, so make it once and keep it.

181.content: A material does not outlive the map. Make it again after `game.MapChanged`.

182.content: A material that `Material` made cannot be the parent of another. Start from the one it was made from.

183.content:
`game.Assets:Mesh(shape)` describes a shape: a box, or your own corners and triangles. It is plain Lua until
you put it on a part with `mesh:Apply`.

184.content: 100 is one metre, measured from the part's own place.

185.content:
Triangles name three corners each, counted from 1. A triangle is seen from the side on which its corners
run counter-clockwise.

186.content: `collision = true` makes things stop at the shape. A character stood on such a slab when it was tried.

187.content: A mistake in the shape raises an error that names the entry.

188.content:
`mesh:Apply(part, options)` puts the shape on a part of the class `ProceduralMeshComponent`. The easiest way
to get such a part is a blueprint whose part has the shape as its
`mesh`. Putting a box on took 0.2 ms. Do it once, not every frame.

189.content:
Save a model as Wavefront `.obj` from any 3D program, put the file in your mod's folder, and `game.Assets:Model`
reads it. No Unreal editor and no pak are needed. It gives the same kind of shape as `game.Assets:Mesh`, so it
goes on a part the same way.

193.content: How much larger the model is made. `100` when omitted, which fits a model made in metres.

195.content: Which way is up in the file: `"y"` when omitted, as most programs save it, or `"z"`.

197.content: `true` turns every triangle round, for a model that shows inside out.

199.content: `true` makes things stop at the shape.

200.content:
The file holds the shape only. Give the part a material for its look, and a picture for that material with
`game.Assets:Texture`.

201.content:
A model can have up to 65,000 vertices and the file up to 16 MB. A larger one belongs in a mod's
game content.

202.content:
In VS Code, **Add 3D Model** on a mod copies the file into the mod's `models` folder and gives you the line
that loads it.

203.content: Nothing here runs between your calls, so it costs nothing a frame.

204.content: To spawn things from assets, see Blueprints.

205.content: Sounds, and packed files of a mod's own, are not in this version.

206.content: Every function is listed in the Assets reference.

208.content: Describe a thing in Lua, with parts, meshes, materials and functions, and spawn it into the world.

213.content: Functions that run for a thing

216.content:
A **blueprint** describes a kind of thing: which parts it has, what they show, and which of your functions
run for it. `blueprint:Spawn` then puts one into the world. No file is made: a thing is an actor of a class
the game already has, put together from your description.

217.content: A thing is made of **parts**. A part is a component of the game with what it shows and where it sits.

221.content: What it shows: the path of a mesh of the game, or a shape from `game.Assets:Mesh`.

223.content: The component class, such as `"PointLightComponent"`. Left out, it follows from the mesh.

225.content: The material of its first slot: a path, a material, or a table that says what to make.

227.content: Where it sits, measured from the thing: `{ 0, 0, 100 }` is one metre up.

229.content: How it is turned, in degrees: `{ Yaw = 45 }`.

231.content: Its size against the size its mesh has by itself. One number, or one for each direction.

233.content: `"none"`: things pass through. `"solid"`: things stop at it, which is what a mesh part does when nothing is said. `"touch"`: things pass through and your `touched` function hears of them.

235.content: Properties of the component, by name, written before the game starts using it.

237.content: `true` for the part the others hang on. It stands where the thing is spawned.

238.content: Give the parts by name, as above, or as a list in which each has a `name`. A blueprint can have 64.

239.content: With parts given by name, say which one is the `root` when more than one has a place.

240.content:
Paths and option names are checked when you call `Define`. A wrong path or a misspelt option raises an
error there, with the nearest right name, and not at the first spawn.

241.content: Give `material` a table and the blueprint makes the material itself from one of the game's:

242.content:
It is made once, shared by every thing of the blueprint, and made again after a map change. The names under
`colors`, `numbers` and `textures` belong to the material you start from. See
Assets.

243.content: A part can show a shape made of numbers in place of a mesh of the game:

244.content:
This has not been tried in the game yet. It runs in Wax's tests outside the game. What was seen in the game
is the call the blueprint makes for such a part, `mesh:Apply`, on a
part that a script made itself.

245.content: `blueprint:Spawn(position, rotation, data)` puts one in the world and gives you the **thing**.

246.content: `position` is `{ X = , Y = , Z = }` or `{ x, y, z }`. `rotation` is a turn in degrees and may be left out.

247.content: `data` is a table of your own that the thing keeps as `thing.Data`.

248.content: A mistake while the thing is put together raises an error and leaves nothing standing.

252.content: Your own table for this thing.

254.content: Where it is. Assign a position to move it there at once.

256.content: How it is turned, in degrees. Assign a turn to set it.

258.content: `true` until the thing is gone. Reading it never raises an error.

260.content: The Instance of its actor, for functions that take an Instance.

264.content: The Instance of one of its parts.

266.content: Makes one more part on it.

268.content: The box all its parts fit in.

270.content: Takes it out of the world with all its parts.

271.content:
A thing also has everything its actor has: `thing.Name`, `thing:IsA("Actor")`, and the actor's own
properties and functions.

272.content:
`blueprint:GetThings()` lists the things of a blueprint that are in the world, and `blueprint:Count()`
counts them. `game.Blueprints:GetThings()` lists the things of every blueprint.

276.content: Once, when the thing is in the world with its parts.

278.content: Every frame, with the seconds since it last ran for that thing.

280.content: At its own pace: the seconds between two runs, then the function.

282.content: When an actor starts to overlap a part with `collision = "touch"`.

284.content: Once, a frame after the thing has gone. Only `Data`, `Blueprint` and `Alive` can be read then.

285.content: All `stepped` and `every` functions together get 2 ms of a frame. What is left over waits a frame.

286.content: The time is real time, so `stepped` also runs while the game is paused.

287.content: `ended` does not run when the blueprint is removed or your mod unloads.

288.content:
The game does not save things. They are gone after a map change, after leaving the prospect and after
a restart. Spawn them again, for example on `game.MapChanged`. The blueprint itself stays through a map
change.

289.content: When your mod unloads or reloads, its things are destroyed and its blueprints forgotten.

290.content: Defining a name again replaces the blueprint, and the things of the old one are destroyed.

291.content:
The crate above was spawned on the host of a prospect: three crates, each turning from Lua, with their lamps
lit. Defining took 1 to 2 ms, a spawn about half a millisecond. These have not been looked at yet:

292.content: Whether the other players of a session see a thing.

293.content:
A base class other than `"Actor"`. `base` takes another class by name, or a blueprint class of the
game by its path, and then the thing is that actor. Only `"Actor"` has been seen working.

294.content: `touched` and `collision = "touch"`, and moving a thing by assigning `thing.Position`.

295.content: Part classes other than a mesh part, a shape part and a point light.

296.content:
While no blueprint is defined, this costs nothing. With things in the world and no functions given, a frame
costs one question to the game at most.

297.content: Every function is listed in the Blueprints reference.

299.content: game.Me gives your character's health, food, level and place by name, tells you when they change, and lets you change them.

305.content: `game.Me` is your own character. You read its numbers by name, and it has signals that fire when they change.

306.content:
`game.Character` is `nil` at the main menu and is a new object after every map change. `game.Me` is not an
object of the game. It finds your character each time you use it, so you can keep it and connect to its
signals once.

313.content: Calling a function or assigning a field

314.content: An error that says there is no character.

315.content:
`game.Me.Character` is the character itself, as an Instance, or `nil`. Use it where a
function wants an Instance.

316.content: Every field asks the game when you read it.

320.content: Health now, and when it is full.

322.content: Stamina now, and when it is full.

330.content: Armour now, and the most it can be.

334.content: The level, and all the experience earned.

336.content: What is carried and what can be carried, in kilograms.

338.content: Where it is, as `{ X = , Y = , Z = }`. 100 is one metre.

340.content: Which way the body is turned, in degrees.

342.content: How fast it moves now, and its top walking speed.

344.content: The biome it stands in, such as `"Conifer"`.

346.content: The temperature around it and of its body.

352.content: The name the player gave the character, as the character screen shows it.

353.content:
A field is `nil` when the character has no such value. `game.Me:DistanceTo(target)` gives the metres to an
Instance or a position.

354.content:
What the character carries is on Items and inventories. Its other numbers, and the effects
that are on it, are on Stats and modifiers.

359.content: The number is not what it was.

360.content: The new value and the one before.

362.content: The number is not what it was.

363.content: The new value and the one before.

366.content: The new weight and the one before.

369.content: The new level and the one before.

374.content: The character stands in another biome.

375.content: The new biome and the one before.

377.content: An effect came onto the character or left it.

380.content: The character was hit, or is dead.

386.content: The character is alive after it was dead.

389.content: A character appeared where there was none, or the one that was there is gone.

391.content:
Most of these are fed by looking at the character a few times a second, and only while something is
connected. So a signal you do not use costs nothing, and a value that changes and changes back between two
looks is not told. With twelve signals connected, Wax used about 0.02 ms more a frame.

392.content: The signals stay connected through a respawn and a map change.

393.content:
The same fields are on every character, not only yours: another player's, and nearly every creature.
`Food`, `Water`, `Oxygen`, the weight and the inventories are on players' characters only.

394.content:
An Instance of a character has `Damaged` and `Died` too. The other signals in the table above belong to
`game.Me`. To follow another value of any object, see Watching a value.

395.content: Each of these is the game's own call.

399.content: Sets the health. Never more than `MaxHealth`. Below 1 raises an error: use `Kill`.

403.content: Sets the food. `Water` and `Oxygen` work the same way. Players' characters only.

405.content: Gives health back. Without an amount, all of it. It does not bring a dead character back.

407.content: Kills a creature at once. On a player's character it raises an error in this version.

409.content: Moves the character at once. `place` is a position, an Instance or `game.Me`.

411.content: The same, by assigning. `{ X = , Y = , Z = }`, an Instance and `game.Me` work too.

413.content: Turns it. What you leave out stays as it is.

414.content: `Teleport` puts the character exactly where you say. Above the ground, it falls and can take damage.

415.content: No other field can be assigned.

416.content: What a mod changed stays changed when the mod unloads.

417.content:
Giving and taking items is on Items and inventories. Putting an effect on a
character is on Stats and modifiers.

418.content: Every field and function is listed in the Characters reference.

420.content: Find the animals and enemies in the world by kind, and hear when one appears, dies or leaves.

425.content: What the game's data says about a kind

427.content: Now and later in one call

432.content:
`game.Creatures` is a list of every animal and enemy in the world. Wax keeps it up to date while you play, so
asking for it costs almost nothing.

433.content: A kind is named the way the game names it. These all work:

441.content: The name the game shows players.

443.content: A class name, for every mount.

444.content:
Letter case, spaces and underscores do not matter, so `"cave worm"` and `"CaveWorm"` are the same.
A name Wax does not know raises an error that suggests the nearest one:

445.content:
`game.Creatures:GetKinds()` lists every kind in your version of the game, with how many of each are in the
world now. `game.Creatures:GetLiveKinds()` gives only the names of the kinds that are here.

450.content: Only creatures this many metres away or nearer. The result is sorted nearest first.

452.content: Where to measure from: an Instance or `{ X = , Y = , Z = }`. Your character when left out.

454.content: `true` also returns bodies that have not been cleared away yet.

456.content: Sorts nearest first without a distance limit.

457.content: Distances are in metres. Positions are the engine's own, where 100 is one metre.

459.content:
A creature has fields of its own, so you can read one value without `Describe`. Each asks the game when you
read it.

463.content: Its kind, such as `"Wolf"`, the version of its kind, such as `"Conifer_Wolf"`, and the name the game shows.

465.content: The name of the boss or alpha it is, such as `"AlphaWolf_Boss"`. `nil` for an ordinary creature.

467.content: Whom it treats as an enemy: `"Default"`, `"Friendly"`, `"Tame"`, `"HostileToPlayers"`, `"HostileToAll"`, or the name of one of the game's teams.

469.content: What it is doing now, as the game calls it: `"Wander"`, `"FindFood"`.

471.content: The actor it is after right now, or `nil`.

477.content: Whether it has been tamed, and whether the game's data has a taming rule for it.

480.content:
A creature is a character too. It also has `Health`, `MaxHealth`, `Level`, `Alive`, `Position` and the other
fields listed on Your character, and stats and
modifiers.

481.content:
A few bosses are built differently in the game: their class is `IcarusPawn`, which is not a character. On
those, `Epic`, `Behaviour`, `Action`, `Target`, `Stance` and `IsFrozen` read `nil`, and they have none of the
character fields.

482.content: `GetInfo` reads the game's tables for one kind or variant. The creature does not have to be in the world.

486.content: The kind's name, the name the game shows, and the game's own tag for it.

490.content: The variant the fields below are about.

492.content: The team it starts on, which decides whom it attacks.

496.content: The words the game's data describes it with, such as `"Passive"`.

498.content: The item its dead body is, and what the body gives.

500.content: The taming rule that names it: how long a taming takes, the food and shelter it wants, and what the animal becomes. `nil` when none does.

502.content: What the data says about the tamed animal: its orders and the saddles that fit. `nil` when there is none.

503.content:
Give a variant such as `"Conifer_Wolf"` or a creature for that variant. Give a kind such as `"Wolf"` for the
variant named like the kind, or else its first one.

504.content:
The first call reads three of the game's tables, which took between 1 and 15 ms. Later calls are quick.
Call it when a window opens, not in the middle of a fight.

505.content:
`game.Creatures:GetTamed()` lists the tamed animals in the world: mounts, pets and livestock, whoever they
belong to. It takes a kind and the same options as `GetAll`. No tamed animal was in the world when this was
tested, so it has only been seen to answer an empty list.

509.content: A creature appeared. It fires for creatures that appear from now on.

511.content: A creature was killed. Its body stays for a few seconds.

513.content: A creature left the world. `info.Reason` is `"Destroyed"` or `"Unloaded"`.

515.content: The map changed. It fires once, in place of one `Removed` for each creature.

516.content: After `Removed`, the creature can no longer be used. You can still compare it with one you kept.

517.content:
From Wax 0.3.0 there is also `game.Creatures.Damaged`, and `Died` says what killed the
creature. Both are on Events of the game.

518.content:
`Observe` calls your function for every matching creature that is here now and for each one that appears
later. If your function returns a function, that one runs when the creature is gone.

519.content: `Observe` returns a connection. Call `:Disconnect()` on it to stop. Everything is undone when your mod reloads.

520.content: `game.Players` has the same for the characters of the people in your session:

521.content:
`game.Creatures:Spawn(kind, place, options)` puts a new wild creature into the world with the game's own
spawn.

522.content:
`kind` is a variant, such as `"Conifer_Wolf"` or `"Deer"`, or a kind that has only one. A kind with several
raises an error that lists them.

523.content:
`place` is a position, an Instance or `game.Me`. Left out, the creature goes six metres in front of your
character.

524.content:
Wax asks the game for ground a creature can walk on within 5 metres of the place. Where there is none, it
raises an error and nothing is spawned.

525.content:
Inside a task, such as a button's function, `Spawn` waits until the game has given the
creature its level. Anywhere else it answers at once, and `Level` and `Health` are right a few frames later.

531.content: The middle level of the zone the place lies in.

533.content: Which variant, when `kind` names a kind that has several.

535.content: Which way it looks, as `{ Yaw = 90 }`.

536.content: In front of you it looks at you.

538.content: The team to put it on. See `Behaviour` below.

540.content: `false` takes the creature away again when your mod unloads.

542.content:
One spawn took 3 to 4 ms, and 18 ms once when the game had to load the kind first. A tamed animal cannot be
spawned in this version.

546.content: Sets its level, from 1 to 120. Its health is full afterwards, so set the level first and `Health` after it.

548.content: Holds it where it stands, and lets it go again.

550.content: Makes a hunter angry at a player's character. `target` is that character or `game.Me`.

552.content: Takes it out of the world, alive or dead, with nothing left behind.

554.content: Puts it on another team: `"Default"`, `"Friendly"`, `"Tame"`, `"HostileToPlayers"`, `"HostileToAll"`, or a team's own name.

556.content: What can be done to any character.

558.content:
These are for wild animals. On a tamed animal and on the few bosses of the class `IcarusPawn`, each raises
an error that says so.

559.content:
`Attack` works on animals the game gives aggression, the hunters. On a deer or a rabbit it raises an error.
Nothing calls an attack off again. `Remove` takes the animal away.

560.content:
A new `Behaviour` counts from the next time the animal notices somebody. An animal that is already
attacking goes on attacking after `"Friendly"`.

561.content: `Remove` happens a moment later, not in the same frame. `creature:IsValid()` says when it is gone.

562.content: Nothing is undone when your mod unloads, apart from a creature spawned with `keep = false`.

563.content: Whether the other players in your session see a spawned creature and its changes has not been looked at.

564.content:
When you join another player's game, your PC only knows the creatures near you. The list is shorter than the
host's, and `Removed` also fires when a creature moves out of range.

566.content: The window that comes with Wax: your mods, the log, a Lua command bar, performance, icons, an explorer of the running game and settings.

568.content: Put the mods in another order

572.content: Running Lua from outside the game

581.content: Wax comes with one window of its own, called **Wax**. Press **F8** and it is there. It has six pages.

582.content:
**F8** shows and hides this panel and nothing else. A mod's windows have a key of their own, which you
find on the mod's card of the Mods page. **Escape** hides everything that is up.

583.content:
The line along the bottom is always visible. It says how many mods loaded and whether there are errors. On
the right it shows the frame rate and the time Wax uses per frame.

584.content: Every mod in the mods folder has a card here.

588.content: `loaded`, `switched off` or `failed`. A failed mod shows its error in red underneath.

590.content: How long the mod took to start.

592.content: Switches the mod off and on. Wax remembers the choice.

594.content: Only on a mod that came from the catalogue. On, a newer version of that mod is put in by itself. Off, the card shows an **Update to** button when one is out.

596.content: Only on a mod that has a window. The key that shows and hides that mod's windows.

598.content: Starts the mod again from the top.

600.content: At the left of the card's name. Hold them and drag the card to another place in the list. Mods load in this order.

602.content: Removes the mod, after asking. Its folder is renamed, not erased. Get mods says how to bring it back.

603.content:
In the picture the card of Entity ESP is open and the card under it is closed. That card is Prospector's Codex,
under its earlier name, Recipe Browser. A card starts closed,
unless its mod is new, has a problem or has an update to put in. Click its name to open or close it. A name too long for the card is cut short with three dots. Rest the mouse on it to read all of
it.

604.content:
Hold the six dots of a card and move the mouse up or down. The card follows the mouse and the other cards
make room. Let go and the card stays there, and Wax remembers the order.

605.content: The card stays inside the list while you hold it.

606.content: Held near the top or the bottom of a long list, the list scrolls.

607.content: An open card folds to its name while you hold it, and opens again where you put it down.

608.content: **Escape** puts the card back where it was. So does letting go outside the list.

609.content:
A mod that needs another mod still loads after it. If you put it before that mod, the card goes back and a
notification says why.

610.content: With a search typed, you move the cards that show.

611.content: The search box filters the list. Type part of a name, or one of these words: `loaded`, `off`, `failed`, `new`.

612.content:
A mod Wax has not seen before is listed as **new** and switched off. Flip **Enabled** to load it. This is so
whether the mod was added while the game ran or while it was closed.

613.content:
**Look for updates** and **Check now**, above the cards, are for mods that came from the catalogue, and so is
the **Auto Update** switch on such a mod's card. Get mods says what they do.

614.content:
Every mod that has a window has an **Show / hide** on its card. Press that key in the game to show the mod's
windows, and press it again to hide them. The Wax panel and the windows of other mods stay as they are, so
several can be up at once. The mouse is free while anything is up.

615.content:
A mod can ask for a key. For a mod that asks for none, Wax picks the first of F6, F9, F10, F11, F5, F4, F3
and F2 that no window and no hotkey uses, and a notification tells you once which it is.

616.content: If a mod later makes a hotkey on a key that Wax picked, Wax picks another one and tells you.

617.content:
To change it, click the key on the card and press the new one. A key can be held with Ctrl, Shift or Alt.
Wax remembers your choice.

618.content:
A key that the Wax panel, another mod's windows or another mod's hotkey already uses is given all the same.
A notification says who else has it, and the card shows the clash until one of the two is changed.

619.content: The log shows what Wax and your mods printed. The newest line is at the bottom.

620.content: The **Errors**, **Warnings** and **Prints** switches choose which lines show.

621.content: The search box keeps only lines that contain your text.

622.content: **Follow** keeps the newest line in view. Switch it off to read older lines.

623.content: Drag across lines to select them. **Ctrl+C** copies. **Ctrl+A** selects everything.

624.content: The **copy** button copies every line that is showing.

625.content: The **clear** button empties the view. The lines are hidden, not deleted.

626.content: Each line starts with who wrote it, in square brackets. Lines from your mod start with your mod's id.

627.content: The box at the bottom of the Log page runs Lua in the game. Type a line and press **Enter**.

628.content: If you type something that has a value, the log shows the value after an `=` sign.

630.content: This one needs a character, so run it in a prospect. It lists the parts your character is made of.

631.content: What else the command bar does:

632.content: **Tab** completes a name. Type `game.Ch` and a grey `aracter` appears. Press **Tab** to take it. Press **Tab** again for the next name that fits.

633.content: After a dot, **Tab** lists what is there. Type `game.` and press **Tab**. The log lists the names you can use.

634.content: The history button brings back the last command. Click again for the one before.

635.content: The run button does the same as **Enter**.

636.content: A command can wait. `task.wait(2) print("later")` works.

637.content: The command bar has every name a mod has (`game`, `ui`, `task` and so on), plus three extras:

641.content: The globals of the mod with the id `Hello`.

645.content: Removes everything your commands made, such as windows and signal connections.

646.content: `require` does not work in the command bar. Reach a loaded mod through `mods` or `exports` instead.

647.content:
The command bar is inside the game, so it always works. A line you type there runs with the same rights as a
mod.

648.content:
A tool outside the game, such as the play button of the VS Code extension, can only run Lua
in the game in developer mode. A normal install does not take Lua from outside.
The bridge and developer mode says how to switch it on and
what that allows.

649.content: This page shows how much of each frame Wax uses.

655.content: The time Wax and all mods use in each frame.

657.content: That time, split between the parts of Wax. The waiting and repeating code of your mods is counted under **Tasks**.

658.content: The numbers are measured again every half second.

659.content:
This page shows every icon you can use. Type in the box to search. Click an icon and a notification shows its
name. Use that name anywhere an icon is accepted. See Icons.

660.content: This page shows what is in the game while it runs, and lets you change it.

661.content:
It has two sides. The left side lists what is in the game, and the right side shows what you picked. Both
are laid out alike, from the top down: a heading with its buttons, one small line, a search box, two
dropdowns side by side, one more row, and then the list.

665.content: The button closes every row that is open.

669.content: Finds something by its name or its class. With several words, all of them must match. The cross in the box empties it.

671.content: Picks what is listed: actors, creatures, players, items, buildings, components or everything.

673.content: Sorts the list: by name, by class, nearest first or newest first.

675.content: Keeps only what is within a distance of you, from 25 to 500 metres. **Any distance from you** shows everything.

677.content: The first rows are the parts of `game`: `Character`, `LocalPlayer`, `GameState`, `GameMode`, `GameInstance`, `Viewport` and `Engine`. Under **World** are the actors of the current world.

678.content:
A row with a small arrow has things inside it. Click the arrow to open the row. Click the row itself to pick
it.

679.content: Until you pick something, the right side explains the page in four short lines.

682.content: The name of what you picked

683.content: The button with the curved arrow goes back to what you had picked before. The copy button copies the Lua that reaches the object.

687.content: Finds a member by its name or its type.

691.content: Sorts the list: **By name** or **Changed first**.

693.content: Belongs to the member you pick in the table. It is described below.

695.content: One row for each member: its name, its value and its type. The first row is the object's class, and its arrow shows what the class inherits from.

696.content:
The values are read again while you look, and a value that changed is marked for a moment. That is how you
find the property that goes with something you do in the game. Choose **Changed** to see only those, or
**Changed first** to put them at the top.

698.content: A value in colour is another object. Click it to go to that object.

699.content: A true-or-false member has a switch at the end of its row.

700.content:
A vector, a rotator or a colour opens when you click it, and each part is a row of its own that you change
like a number. Its arrow closes it again.

701.content: A list opens with its arrow and shows what is in it. The places of a list are shown, not changed.

702.content: A value that could not be read says so, and Wax leaves it alone.

703.content: Click a member in the table. The value row, above the table, now shows its name.

704.content:
For a value you can type, such as a number or a text, the row has a box. Type the new value and press
**Enter**, or press the button with the tick.

705.content: For anything else the row says in a few words why there is no box.

706.content: The `<>` button copies the Lua that reads the member and the Lua that sets it.

707.content:
Choose **Functions** to see the object's functions with their parameters. They are not called from this
page. The `<>` button copies the call.

708.content:
**Changes as Lua** appears under both sides after your first change. It lists everything you changed here as
lines of Lua that do the same. **Copy** takes them for a mod, and **Clear** empties the list.

709.content:
In a narrow window one side shows at a time, and a **List** button at the top of the right side takes you
back.

710.content: Not every value is meant to be changed. Try things on a character you can afford to lose.

714.content: The key that shows and hides the Wax panel. Click it, then press a new key. It is **F8** until you change it. A mod's windows have their own key, on the mod's card of the Mods page.

716.content: The colours of every window. See Themes.

718.content: The highlight colour. `From the theme` uses the theme's own.

720.content: Switches the small movements on and off.

722.content: Makes everything larger or smaller. The list holds the sizes that text can still be read at on your screen, so a small game window offers fewer of them.

723.content: These settings are remembered the next time you play.

724.content: A mod can add a page to the Wax panel. Use it for tools you need while testing.

725.content: The page goes away when your mod reloads, and comes back when `init.lua` runs again.

726.content: Write `ui.Debug.Page` with a dot, not a colon.

730.content: Adds a page and returns it. Add controls to it as you would to a window.

732.content: Shows the Wax panel and frees the mouse. Your own windows stay as they are.

734.content: The panel's window, or `nil` while the panel is not running.

736.content: The Wax for Icarus extension for VS Code, and what you can do without it.

741.content: A mod is made of plain text files, so any text editor works.

742.content: For Visual Studio Code there is an extension called **Wax for Icarus**.

746.content: A command that makes the folder and the first files of a mod.

748.content: Type `ui.` and pick from a list of everything `ui` offers. Each entry has a short description. Mistakes are marked as you type.

750.content: Type `game.Character.` and pick from what a player character has. `game:Find("IcarusPlayerState")` gives an object whose members the editor knows.

752.content: Sends the open file, or the lines you selected, to the running game.

754.content: Shows the game's log in the Output panel.

756.content: Lists your mod's errors in the Problems panel, each with its file and line.

758.content: Lists every mod with its state. Its buttons reload a mod, switch it off or on, and open it.

759.content:
Four of those parts talk to the running game: **Run in game**, the log, Problems and the Mods view. They
work by sending Lua to the game, and the game only takes Lua from outside in developer mode. In a normal
install they stay empty.

760.content:
New Mod, completion, error checking and the game's classes need no developer mode. Neither does
hot reload.

761.content: To switch developer mode on, make an empty text file named `dev.txt` in Wax's folder, beside `Scripts`:

762.content: Then start the game, or start it again if it was running. To switch it off, delete the file.

763.content:
Read The bridge and developer mode first. With that file
in place, any program that runs as you can run code inside the game, and Wax no longer updates itself in the
game.

764.content: Install Wax into the game first. See Installing.

765.content:
The extension is a `.vsix` file on the same
release page as Wax.

767.content: In VS Code, open the Extensions view and click the `...` menu.

768.content: Choose **Install from VSIX...** and pick the file.

769.content:
The extension may not be on the VS Code Marketplace yet. To check, search the Extensions view for
"Wax for Icarus". Its id is `RobertCincotta.wax-icarus`.

770.content: You don't need it to write mods.

771.content: Saving a file reloads your mod. That is hot reload, and it works with any editor.

772.content: The log is on the **Log** page of the Wax panel, inside the game.

773.content: The command bar on that page completes names when you press **Tab**.

774.content: Every function is described in the reference.

776.content: Hear when a character is hit or dies, and when items come into an inventory or leave it.

784.content:
For a few things the game itself tells Wax the moment they happen: a hit, a death, and an item that comes or
goes. Wax hands them to you as signals.

788.content: Your own character. They stay connected through a respawn and a map change.

790.content: One character you have as an Instance: a player's or a creature's.

794.content: Every creature. Before Wax 0.3.0 it came without `Killer`, `Instigator` and `Damage`.

796.content: Everything your character carries, over all its inventories.

799.content: Your function gets the character, the damage of the hit, and a table with what the game knows of it.

803.content: The character's health after the hit.

805.content: What the game took off its health.

807.content: The actor the game names as what did it. For hunger and for a fall that is the character itself.

809.content: The controller the game names as who did it. For hunger and for a fall there is none.

814.content: Health that goes down with no hit is not damage. Assigning `character.Health` as the host does not fire it.

815.content: The handlers of one signal share one `info` table. Copy what you want to keep.

816.content: `Died` fires once when the character is dead.

820.content: The `Causer` of the hit that left it no health.

825.content:
All three are `nil` when the character died with no hit that Wax heard. A creature killed with `Kill()` is
such a death. For `game.Creatures.Died`, `info` also has `Kind`, `Variant`, `ClassName` and `Name`, as
before.

826.content:
A character that lives again and dies again is told again. When a character leaves the world, the handlers
you connected to that Instance are disconnected.

831.content: There is more of an item than a frame before.

832.content: The item's name, how many more, and a stack it went onto.

834.content: There is less of an item than a frame before.

835.content: The item's name, how many fewer, and a stack it came out of.

837.content: A slot holds something else than a frame before.

838.content: What it holds now and what it held, with `nil` for nothing.

839.content:
A stack that only moves from one slot or inventory of your character to another is not added and not
removed. It is a change of both slots.

840.content: A tool that wore is a change. A spoil timer that only counts down is not.

841.content:
The item's name is spelled as the game spells it, which is not always the same letter case. Compare names
without it, or ask `Count` or `Has`.

842.content: A stack is the same table that inventories give.

843.content:
Your function never runs inside the game's own call. Wax notes what it heard and tells you from its frame
loop, in the same frame or the next. So your function can wait, show a window or call the game, like any
other task.

844.content: Nothing until the first handler connects. Wax starts listening to the game's function then.

845.content:
While connected, each time the game calls that function costs a little: about 0.1 ms for a hit, and 0.02
to 0.06 ms for an item. The game reports a spoiling stack about once a second.

846.content: The first handler on `game.Me.ItemAdded`, `ItemRemoved` or `ItemChanged` reads all six inventories once.

847.content:
All of this was seen on the host of a session, on a player's character: damage from a fall, and items given
and taken. A poisoned deer fired `Damaged` for each tick of the poison. These have not been seen:

848.content: Any of it as a guest in someone else's game.

849.content: A player's death. `game.Me.Died` has only run in tests outside the game.

850.content:
A creature killed by a player's hit, so what `Killer` names then has not been looked at. Poison named the
animal itself.

851.content:
The item signals of a chest or a bench. There, an inventory you keep asking about is still kept up to date
by looking, as Items and inventories says.

852.content:
The few bosses of the class `IcarusPawn` are not told by `game.Creatures.Damaged`. Their death is told, with
no killer.

853.content:
Wax has no function for listening to other functions of the game. To follow a value, see
Watching a value.

854.content:
The signals are listed in the Characters reference and the
Items and inventories reference.

856.content: Make a mod with a window, a switch, a button and an overlay.

861.content: Change it while the game runs

866.content:
On this page you make the window below. You also make an overlay, a small panel that stays on screen while
you play.

867.content: Open the `Wax\mods\` folder (see Installing). Make a new folder in it called `MyFirstMod`.

868.content: In that folder, make a text file called `init.lua`. Paste this in and save it.

869.content:
Start ICARUS, or switch to it if it is running. Press **F8** and open the **Mods** page. Your mod is listed
there as new, and switched off. Flip its **Enabled** switch.

870.content: A small panel appears in the top left corner of the screen. That is the overlay.

871.content:
Wax never starts a mod it has not seen before. You switch it on once. After that it stays the way you left
it, and it loads by itself when the game starts.

872.content:
Every mod that has a window gets a key of its own. A notification tells you which one Wax picked for your
mod, for example **F6**. It is also on the mod's card, as **Show / hide**.

873.content: Press that key. Your window comes up.

874.content: Flip the switch. The overlay hides and comes back.

875.content: Click **Say hi**. A green message shows in a corner of the screen.

876.content: Press the key again to hide your window. **Escape** closes everything that is up.

877.content: Leave the game running. In `init.lua`, change `"Say hi"` to `"Wave"` and save the file.

878.content: The button in the game now says **Wave**. Saving the file reloaded your mod.

882.content: Makes a panel that stays on screen while you play. It never takes the mouse.

884.content: Adds a name with a value beside it.

886.content: The name of the map you are on.

888.content: Makes a window in the menu.

892.content: Adds a switch. The function runs each time you flip it. `on` is `true` or `false`.

894.content: Adds a button. The function runs each time you click it.

896.content: Shows a short message in a corner of the screen.

897.content: This step is optional. Add a second file next to `init.lua`, called `mod.lua`:

898.content: The Mods page now shows that name and version. Without this file it shows the folder name.

899.content: To see what an error looks like, delete a closing bracket in `init.lua` and save.

900.content: A red message tells you what is wrong, and on which line.

901.content: The **Log** page of the Wax panel shows the same error.

902.content: The Mods page marks the mod as failed.

903.content: Fix the mistake and save again. The mod loads.
