909.content: Bring models, textures, materials and blueprints made in the Unreal editor into a mod, and change them while the game runs.

911.content: What a mod with content looks like

913.content: Changing content while the game runs

917.content: Or let it build by itself

920.content:
A mod can bring **game content** of its own: meshes, textures, materials, sounds and blueprints made in the
Unreal editor. They travel in one file in the mod's folder, `content/<Id>.pak`. Wax checks that file, hands it to
the running game and your Lua then loads from it by name. The game is not restarted, and no file of the game is
replaced.

921.content: Most mods do not. A mod is Lua, and Lua alone does all of this in the running game, with nothing to build:

922.content: read and change the game's tables: items, recipes, creatures, the store

923.content: read and change what is in the world: your character, its stats, its inventory, the time

925.content: show a picture from a `.png` or `.jpg` in the mod's folder, and a 3D model from an `.obj` file (Assets)

926.content:
A pak is for what Lua cannot make from a file: a blueprint with logic of its own, a material built in the
editor, an animated or very large model, a sound set. Those are made in the Unreal editor, version 4.27, which is
a separate download of about 19 GB from Epic Games. ICARUS itself does not come with it: a game holds the part of
Unreal that plays content, not the editor that makes it.

927.content: So the order to try things in is: Lua first, a file in the mod's folder second, a pak last.

928.content:
The pak is named after the mod's id. Everything in it lives under `/Game/Mods/MyMod/` in the game, and nowhere
else: a mod's content can add files there and cannot replace anything the game or another mod has.

929.content: `mod.Content` is `nil` for a mod without a pak.

939.content: An asset by its name, such as `"T_Icon"` or `"Meshes/Rock"`, as game.Assets loads it

941.content: The class of a blueprint, such as `"BP_Lantern"`

943.content: The game's path of an asset: `/Game/Mods/MyMod/T_Icon.T_Icon`

945.content: The game's path of a blueprint's class, which `base` of game.Blueprints takes

947.content: `true` when the pak holds an asset of that name

948.content: What `Load` and `LoadClass` give is kept for your mod and let go of when the mod unloads.

949.content:
When the pak changes and the mod reloads, Wax hands the newer pak to the game and asks it to let go of the
older one. Assets that nothing uses any more are then read from the newer pak, so the change shows without a
restart.

950.content:
An asset the game still uses at that moment keeps its older look: a thing in the world that was spawned from a
blueprint, for example. `content.State` is then `"restart"` and `content.Reason` names those assets. Remove what
you spawned in `mod.OnUnload`, and the next reload takes the newer copy.

951.content:
The **Mods** page of the Wax panel shows the state on the mod's card, and its **Reload**
button takes up a changed pak. The **Log** page has a **Game content** switch that shows or hides these lines.
In the command bar, `content.List()` lists the mods with content and `content.Reload("MyMod")` reloads one.

952.content:
Assets are made in the Unreal editor, version 4.27, the version the game is built with. The Wax source folder
has a project for it and the tools that turn its assets into a pak the game can read.

953.content:
That makes `unreal/Icarus/Content/Mods/MyMod`, which the game sees as `/Game/Mods/MyMod`. Open the project with
`scripts\Open-UnrealProject.ps1` and save your assets in that folder.

954.content:
The assets are cooked and checked: every game file they refer to has to exist in the game, because the game stops
on one that does not. The pak is then put in the mod, and a running game reloads the mod and takes the pak.

955.content: While this runs, saving an asset in the editor builds the content again and the game takes it.

956.content:
In VS Code the same is **Wax: Build Game Content** and **Wax: Open the Unreal Project**, and the setting
**Wax: Content: Auto Build** builds whenever an asset is saved. Both are also buttons on the **Game content** line
under a mod in the Wax view.

957.content:
The first time, the extension asks where the Unreal editor is. **Wax: Choose the Unreal Editor Folder** points it
at an Unreal Engine 4.27 you already have, and **Wax: Install the Unreal Editor** downloads it into the Wax folder
with your Epic Games account. The setting **Wax: Unreal Path** holds the choice. A build takes a few minutes, most of it the
editor starting.

958.content: Wax refuses a pak that could stop the game, and says why on the mod's card:

959.content: pak version 11, not compressed and not encrypted

960.content: its mount point is `../../../Icarus/Content/Mods/<Id>/`, with the mod's own id

961.content: its index and every file in it lie inside the file and match their checksums

962.content:
The build above makes such a pak. The mod catalogue does not take a mod with a pak yet, so share such a mod as
a folder for now. Content is cooked for one build of the game. After a game update
build it again, so that it is checked against the new game.

963.content:
Checking and handing over a small pak takes a few milliseconds, once, when the mod loads. Loading a blueprint's
class from it took about one millisecond. A pak the game already has is not handed over again.

965.content: How Wax keeps up with each new build of ICARUS, and where the classes of the game can be read.

969.content:
ICARUS is updated most weeks. Each update can add classes, rename a variable or change a table. A server reads every
new build of the game by itself and writes down what is in it, so the Explorer and the editor's
completion follow the game without anyone doing it by hand.

970.content: The server asks Steam every ten minutes which build of the dedicated server is out.

971.content:
For a new build it downloads the game's program, its debug file and its content files. A DLC arrives the same
way, as more content files.

972.content:
It reads every class the program declares and every blueprint class in the content, each with its parent, its
variables and its functions. The game is never started.

973.content:
It writes the result to the Icarus SDK repository and sends the
new list of classes to the Explorer on this site.

974.content: A whole run takes about half an hour.

975.content: The Icarus SDK repository holds, for the newest build:

979.content: Every class and struct as a C++ header to read: what it derives from, each variable with its place, each function with its parameters

981.content: The same classes as definitions for the Lua language server

983.content: The whole model as one JSON file, for tools

985.content: What each update changed: classes, members and table rows

987.content: The scripts that make all of it

988.content:
The dedicated server is read because Steam gives it to anyone. Its code is the game's own. A few classes that only
the game's client has are missing.

990.content: Start at game and reach the world, the player and every object in it.

998.content: You reach everything in the game from one name: `game`.

999.content: Open the **Log** page of the Wax panel to see what it printed.

1004.content: The current world. Its children are the actors in it.

1010.content: The character you control. `nil` at the main menu.

1013.content: The players in the session. See below.

1015.content: The state of the session, shared with every player.

1018.content: The rules of the session. `nil` when you are a client in someone else's game.

1021.content: The object the game keeps from when it starts until it closes.

1027.content: The game's view on the screen.

1030.content: The name of the current world, as text.

1032.content: `true` while you are in a prospect.

1034.content: A signal that fires when the world changes.

1035.content:
Most of these are **Instances**: objects of the game that you can read, change and call. The next page,
Instances, shows how.

1036.content:
Each one is of a different class, so each has different properties and functions. A player controller has
`PlayerCameraManager`, and a game state has `PlayerArray`. Click a class in the table to see everything it
has in the Explorer. The object you get in the game can be of a class built on the one named here.
It then has everything listed, and more.

1037.content: `game` is read-only. If you misspell a name, you get an error that suggests the right one.

1038.content: `game.Character` is `nil` when you have no character, for example at the main menu. Check before you use it.

1039.content: Entering or leaving a prospect changes the world. `game.MapChanged` fires with the new map's name.

1040.content:
An Instance you got before the map changed is gone afterwards. Using it raises an error that tells you to
get it again. Ask `game` for a new one each time you need it. Don't keep an old one for long.

1044.content: A list with one Instance per player in the session (their player state). It works for the host and for clients.

1046.content: A list of the characters those players control right now.

1052.content: The first live object of a class, or `nil`.

1054.content: A list of every live object of a class.

1056.content: One of the game's function libraries. See below.

1058.content: Every Instance you marked with that tag.

1060.content: The top of the tree: world, game instance, game state and so on.

1063.content:
`game:FindAll` looks at every object in the game. Call it once and keep the answer for a while. Never call
it many times a second.

1064.content:
Some functions belong to no object in the world. The game keeps them in libraries, such as
`KismetMathLibrary`, `KismetSystemLibrary` and `GameplayStatics`. `game:Library` gives you one, and you call
its functions with a colon.

1065.content: Many of these functions ask for a `WorldContextObject` first. Pass `game.World`.

1066.content:
The Explorer lists every library and what its functions take. A wrong name raises an error that
suggests the right one.

1067.content:
An actor is one thing placed in the world, such as a character or a tree. The children of `game.World` are
the actors. This counts them by class and prints the five most common ones.

1068.content: Every function is listed in the game reference.

1070.content: Find a mod on the Mods page and add it to your game with the button, or by hand.

1081.content:
The Mods page lists the mods made for Wax. You can search it, filter it by category and tag, and open
a mod to read what it does. Each card shows the mod's version and when it was last updated.

1082.content:
A mod is code that runs in your game. Once it is switched on it can do what any program on your PC can do.
A mod is code says what is checked for you and what is not.

1083.content: Press **Add to game** on a mod. Your browser asks if it may open Wax. Say yes.

1084.content:
A window of Wax opens on your PC. It shows the mod's name, version and author and asks whether to add it.
Nothing has been downloaded yet. If you say no, nothing happens.

1085.content:
Wax downloads the mod from the catalogue, checks its signature and puts it in your game's mods folder. The
mod is **switched off**. Open the Wax menu (F8), go to **Mods** and flip its **Enabled** switch.

1086.content: If ICARUS is running, a notice in the game tells you the mod was added.

1087.content:
If ICARUS is not running, the mod is on the Mods page the next time you start the game, still switched
off.

1088.content:
A mod you already had keeps the state it had. The copy from before is kept, as described under
Manage your mods.

1089.content:
The button works on a PC where you said yes when `Install Wax.cmd` asked about it. If nothing happens when you
press it, use the download below. The registry key says how to switch the
button on later, and how to switch it off.

1090.content: The Wax menu has a **Browse** page that shows the same catalogue inside the game.

1091.content: Search by a name, an author or a tag, pick a category or a tag, and sort by what is new, liked or downloaded most.

1092.content:
Each mod is a card with its picture behind it, its downloads and votes, and a small mark that says how it stands:
**In your mods**, **Update ready**, or nothing when you do not have it.

1093.content:
Press a card to open the mod's own page, with its pictures, what it says about itself and its numbers.
**All mods**, or **Browse** in the list of pages, goes back.

1094.content:
The thumbs on a card and on a mod's page are buttons: press one to like or dislike the mod, and press it again to
take your vote back. It is the same vote as on this site, one for each mod, so a like here and a like there count once.

1095.content:
**Add to game**, on the mod's page, asks first, then downloads the mod and checks it against the owner's signature. It arrives
switched off, as with the button on this site. Switch it on on the **Mods** page.

1096.content: **Update to** puts in a newer version of a mod you have.

1097.content:
The catalogue is asked when you open the page, and again while it stays open. The list of the last time shows
at once. With **Look for updates** switched off on the Mods page, nothing is asked.

1098.content: Press **Download zip** on a mod. Extract the zip into the mods folder of Wax:

1099.content: The zip holds one folder, named after the mod. That folder goes straight into `mods`.

1100.content:
The mod shows up on the **Mods** page of the Wax menu, switched off. Switch it on there. It is the same
whether you put the folder in while the game ran or while it was closed.

1101.content:
Nothing checks a zip you put in by hand. Check a download by hand
says how to check it yourself.

1102.content: Open the Wax menu (F8) and go to **Mods**. Each mod has a card:

1106.content: Switches the mod on or off. It stays that way after you restart the game.

1108.content: On a mod you added from the catalogue: whether a newer version is put in by itself. See Updates.

1110.content: On a mod that has a window: the key that shows and hides its windows. Click it and press another key to change it.

1114.content: At the left of the card's name. Hold them and drag the card up or down to move the mod in the list. Mods load in this order.

1116.content: Removes the mod. Wax asks first.

1117.content:
A removed mod is not erased. Its folder is renamed so that it starts with `.removed-`, and Wax leaves folders
with such names alone. To get the mod back, rename the folder to the mod's name again.

1118.content:
Mods you add with the **Add to game** button keep themselves up to date. About 20 seconds after the game starts, and every six hours after that, Wax asks the catalogue whether a
newer version is out. If one is, Wax downloads it and checks it: the list of its files must carry the
signature of Wax's author, and every file must match that list. Only then is the mod replaced. A notification
tells you, for example "Prospector's Codex was updated to 1.0.1."

1119.content: The mod's settings stay, and so does whether it is switched on or off.

1120.content:
The version before is kept in the mods folder under a `.removed-` name. To go back, take the newer folder out
and rename the kept one to the mod's name.

1121.content:
A mod you wrote or copied into the mods folder yourself is never changed, even when the catalogue has a mod with
the same name. Wax only updates a folder that holds a `wax.origin` file, which **Add to game** writes.

1122.content: A version that needs a newer Wax than yours is left out until you update Wax.

1123.content:
Every mod that came from the catalogue has its own **Auto Update** switch. Open the Wax menu (F8), go to
**Mods** and open the mod's card to find it. It is on until you switch it off.

1124.content:
With a mod's switch off, Wax only shows that a newer version of that mod is out: its card has an
**Update to** button, and the mod is updated when you press it. Your other mods go on updating themselves.

1125.content: **Check now**, above the cards, asks the catalogue at once.

1126.content:
**Look for updates**, above the cards, is the switch for all of it. Off, the catalogue is not asked at all,
and no mod is updated.

1127.content:
A mod's **Auto Update** switch is about that mod only. Updates of Wax itself have a setting of their own:
Switching it off says how to change it.

1128.content:
Wax 0.2.0 and 0.2.1 have one **Auto Update** switch for all mods, above the cards, and no **Look for
updates** switch. Wax 0.3.0 gives each mod its own. If you had switched the old one off, every
mod's switch starts off.

1129.content:
Wax asks one address, `wax-icarus.duckdns.org`. It sends the name and version of the mod it fetches and its own
version. What Wax asks the network for has every request.

1130.content:
This needs Wax 0.2.0 or newer, and a mod added with a Wax older than that has to be added once more. A mod you
installed from a zip is updated by extracting the new zip over the old folder.

1131.content:
Every mod has two buttons with a thumb, one up and one down, on its card in the list and on its own page. Press
one to vote. Press it again to take your vote back, or press the other one to change it.

1132.content: You need no account. A vote is counted once for each internet address.

1133.content: The number beside each thumb is how many votes it has.

1134.content: Choose **Most liked** in the sort list to put the mods with the most votes up, less the votes down, first.

1135.content: To put a mod of your own on the Mods page, see Publish a mod.

1137.content: Every control you can put in a window, with a picture and an example for each.

1165.content: A **control** is one thing in a window: a line of text, a button, a switch, a slider.

1166.content:
You add a control by calling a function on a **container**. A window is a container. So is a page, a
section, a row and an overlay. They all have the same functions.

1167.content:
Every example with the file name `init.lua` above it is a whole file. Paste it, save, and press the key of
your mod's windows. It is on the mod's card of the Mods page, as **Show / hide**.

1168.content: Most controls take a function that runs when the user changes them.

1169.content:
Every control also has a `Changed` signal. It does the same thing, and you can connect to it
later or more than once.

1170.content: Your function may call `task.wait`. It runs as a task.

1171.content: Changing a control from code with `Set` does not run your function. Only a change by the user does.

1175.content: Shows or hides the control. A hidden control takes no room.

1177.content: `false` greys the control out and stops it reacting.

1180.content:
`container:Label(text, options)` adds text. Long text wraps to the width of the container. In a
row a label is one line: see Text that has to fit.

1184.content: `true` uses the theme's dimmer text colour.

1186.content: A colour of your own. Make one with `ui.Color("#RRGGBB")`, or take one from `ui.Theme()`.

1190.content: The weight of the game's interface font, such as `"Book"`, `"Medium"` or `"Bold"`.

1192.content: `"ui"` for the game's interface font (the usual one), `"mono"` for a fixed-width font, or `"plain"`.

1199.content: `container:Heading(text)` adds a bold title line for a group of controls. `heading:Set(value)` replaces the text.

1200.content:
`container:Title(text, description)` adds a title for a whole page: large text, an optional line of
explanation, and a rule under it.

1202.content: `container:Spacer(height)` adds an empty gap. Leave the height out to get the theme's normal gap.

1203.content: `container:Button(caption, on_click, options)` adds a button. `on_click` runs on each click.

1204.content: Pass `nil` as the caption and give an `icon` to get a small icon button.

1208.content: `true` draws the button in the accent colour. Use it for the main action.

1210.content: An icon shown before the caption.

1212.content: `true` turns the icon round once on every click. It shows that the click started something.

1214.content: A button with a caption fills the width. `false` makes it only as wide as its caption. An icon button is small. `true` makes it fill the width.

1216.content: For an icon button: the side of the square it is drawn as, such as `24` for a line that is lower than a button. Left out, it is as tall as the other buttons. New in Wax 0.3.0.

1218.content: Help shown beside the mouse once it has rested on the button. Give one to every button that is only an icon.

1222.content: Shows another icon. The button must have been made with one.

1226.content: Replaces the caption. The button must have been made with one.

1228.content: Changes the help shown while the mouse rests on the button. `nil` takes it away.

1232.content: The button is clicked. `button.Changed` is the same signal.

1233.content:
`container:Icon(name, options)` adds an icon on its own. Find names on the **Icons** page of the
Wax panel.

1244.content:
`container:Toggle(caption, initial, on_change)` adds a switch. `initial` is `true` for on. `on_change` gets
`true` or `false`.

1250.content: Turns the switch on or off.

1257.content:
A switch can be given another caption later, and be set without its sliding animation. Both are for a row
that is reused to show something else:

1258.content:
`container:Slider(caption, options, on_change)` adds a slider with a number beside it. The user can drag the
handle, or click the number and type a value.

1272.content: Values snap to steps of this size, counted from `min`.

1275.content: How the number is written, as a `string.format` pattern.

1276.content: `"%.2f"`, or `"%d"` with a step of 1 or more.

1278.content: `true` puts the caption above the track, `false` beside it.

1279.content: Beside it when there is room, above when there is not.

1281.content: `false` reports the value once, when the mouse lets go. Use it when a change is slow to apply.

1288.content: Moves the slider. The value is snapped and kept inside the range.

1293.content: The value changes while dragging, or a number is typed.

1296.content: The user lets go of the handle.

1298.content:
`container:Input(caption, options, on_commit)` adds a text box. `on_commit` runs when the user presses
**Enter**, or clicks somewhere else. Pass `nil` as the caption for a box without one.

1304.content: Grey text shown while the box is empty.

1306.content: `true` puts the caption above the box, `false` beside it. Left out, it goes beside the box when there is room, above when there is not.

1308.content: `true` uses a fixed-width font. Good for code.

1312.content: The text in the box right now.

1316.content: Puts the typing cursor in the box, so the user can type without clicking it.

1318.content: `true` while the typing cursor is in the box.

1320.content: Shows grey text after what is typed, such as the rest of a suggested word. Only a box made with `mono = true` shows it.

1325.content: The user finishes typing: Enter, or the box loses the cursor.

1328.content: Enter is pressed. It fires even when the text is the same as last time.

1331.content: The text changes while typing. Every letter.

1333.content: A search box uses `Typed`, so the list updates with every letter:

1334.content: `container:Dropdown(caption, choices, selected, on_change)` adds a list the user picks one choice from.

1336.content: `selected` is the one chosen at the start. Left out, it is the first.

1337.content: `on_change` gets the choice the user picked.

1338.content:
The list opens in place, under its header. The chosen row is highlighted. Only one list is open in a
window at a time. A long list scrolls.

1351.content:
A colour the user can change. The row shows the colour and its code. A click opens a panel under it with a box
of shades, a bar of hues, and the code as text.

1352.content: The value is a string such as `"#ff7a00"`.

1353.content: Drag in the box to pick a shade, and along the bar to pick a hue.

1354.content: Type or paste a code into the text box and press Enter. The button beside it copies the code.

1355.content: A click anywhere else closes the panel.

1361.content: Sets the colour. It does not call your function.

1363.content: Fires with every change, also while the mouse is held down.

1365.content: Fires once when the user lets go. Use it for saving.

1366.content:
`container:Keybind(caption, key, on_change)` adds a key the user can change. The user clicks the button,
then presses a key. **Escape** cancels.

1367.content:
`on_change` gets the name of the new key, such as `"M"` or `"F5"`. That name is what
`ui.Hotkey` takes, so the two work together.

1371.content: The key's name, or `nil` when none is set.

1378.content: The user picks a new key.

1380.content:
`container:Progress(caption, value, options)` adds a bar. `value` goes from 0 (empty) to 1 (full). The
percentage is written beside the caption.

1385.content: The colour of the filled part.

1394.content: Changes the colour of the filled part.

1395.content: `container:Field(name, value, options)` adds a name with a value on the right. Use it to show facts.

1399.content: `true` shows the value in a small fixed-width font. Good for numbers that keep changing, because the text does not shift as they change.

1405.content: Changes the colour of the value.

1406.content: `container:Section(title, options)` adds a card with a title. The user clicks the title to open and close it.

1407.content: A section is a container. Add controls to the section, as you would to a window.

1413.content: `false` makes a plain titled group that is always open.

1415.content: `true` keeps the title on one line. A title too long for the card is cut short with three dots, and shown whole as a tip while the mouse rests on it. Without it a long title wraps. New in Wax 0.3.0.

1422.content: To hide, disable or remove the whole card, use `section.control`:

1423.content: `container:Row()` adds a row. Controls you add to the row sit side by side and share the width.

1424.content: A row is a container too. `row.control` is the row itself, for `SetVisible`, `SetEnabled` and `Destroy`.

1425.content:
`container:Flow(options)` adds an area where controls keep their own size. When a line is full, the next
control goes onto a new line.

1429.content: Makes it a grid instead. Every control gets the same width, at least this wide, and each line is full.

1430.content:
`container:Console(options)` adds a scrolling box of text lines, such as a log. The user can drag across
the lines to select them, and copy with **Ctrl+C**.

1431.content: Each line is a small table: the text, then an optional colour.

1439.content: How many lines are shown at most. Older lines drop off the top.

1446.content: Everything being shown, as one piece of text. Pass it to `ui.Copy` to put it on the clipboard.

1448.content: `true` scrolls to the newest line on every `SetLines`. It starts on.

1449.content: A console shows the list you give it. To add a line, keep the list, add to it and call `SetLines` again:

1450.content:
Text that has one line to itself does not spill out of its box. When it is too long, it is cut short with
three dots, and the whole text shows as a tip while the mouse rests on it. This happens by itself for:

1454.content: the title of a section made with `fit = true`.

1455.content: A label that is not in a row wraps onto more lines, as before.

1456.content: For text you place yourself, two functions measure it:

1460.content: How wide a line of text is drawn, in the units windows are sized in. It is right to within a few percent.

1462.content: The text if it fits in that width, else its start with three dots after it. A second value is `true` when it was cut.

puts a search box above it.

It does not look at whether the menu is open or a text box has the keyboard. `ui.IsTyping()` tells you the

Every call asks the game. So call it in a loop that runs while something is held, not in every frame of

Name the key in `mod.lua` as well (`keys = { "F6: Ping" }`), and it is on the card while your mod is still switched

1645.content: Show a creature of the game in 3D in a window, turning, walking, and turned by the player with the mouse.

1650.content: A young animal beside its parent

1653.content:
`container:Model(options)` adds a box that shows a creature in 3D. `game.Creatures:GetModel(name)` gives what
the box needs for one creature. The creature does not have to be in the world.

1654.content: The model turns slowly by itself until the player touches it.

1655.content:
Drag turns it. The model follows the mouse: dragged to the right its near side goes right, and dragged
down it is seen more from above.

1656.content:
The wheel moves the camera nearer and further while the mouse is over the view. The page does not
scroll then.

1657.content: Two presses in a row put the view back, and so does the small button in the corner.

1658.content:
`game.Creatures:GetModel(name)` takes a variant, such as `"Bear"` or `"Conifer_Wolf"`, or a kind, such as
`"Wolf"`. It gives the creature's mesh, its fur, its other pieces and its animations, read from the game's
own files when Wax was made.

1659.content:
It gives `nil` and the reason when Wax has no model for the creature. A creature added by a game update
after your Wax was made is one of those.

1660.content: A name that is no creature raises an error.

1661.content: Give the result to `Model` or to `Show` as it is.

1662.content:
A few creatures do not show well in this version. The bee draws nothing, some large ones are cut by the box
where the view starts, and a few are too dark or too bright. Pieces that sit on another skeleton, such as an
ice mammoth's armour, are left out.

1663.content: `Model` takes the options of a look, and these:

1668.content: The side of a square view.

1670.content: The size of a view that is not square.

1671.content: 240 wide, and as tall as it is wide.

1673.content: Where the view sits in its line: `"left"`, `"center"` or `"right"`.

1676.content: A colour behind the model, or `true` for the theme's card colour.

1679.content: Degrees a second it turns by itself. `false` for none.

1685.content: `false`: the wheel is left to the page.

1688.content: `false` leaves out the small button that puts the view back.

1691.content: How bright the lights are, from 0 to 4.

1694.content: Where the view starts: degrees round the model, degrees above it, and how far away.

1699.content: A view made without a mesh shows nothing until you call `Show`.

1703.content: Shows another model in the same box. The view goes back to where it starts.

1707.content: Changes what plays: `"walk"`, `"idle"`, or `false` to stand still.

1709.content: Where the camera is: yaw, pitch and distance.

1711.content: Puts the camera somewhere. What is left out stays. The slow turn stops.

1713.content: Puts the view back where it started, and starts the slow turn again.

1715.content: `true` once the model is in the picture.

1719.content: The model is in the picture.

1721.content: The mesh could not be loaded, or the game could not make the view. Your function gets the reason.

1723.content: The player let go after a drag, turned the wheel or put the view back. Your function gets yaw, pitch and distance.

1725.content: The player pressed the view and let go without turning it.

1726.content:
Every model is fitted to its box, so a cub would look as large as a bear. Give a look `against` another one
and it is drawn as much smaller as it is in the game.

1727.content: It never fills less than four tenths of the box.

1728.content:
A look is a table, and you can write one yourself for any skeletal mesh of the game: `mesh` is its path, and
`materials`, `parts`, `walk` and `idle` are optional. A mesh that is not a skeletal mesh fires `Failed`.

1729.content: Finding the paths is on Assets.

1730.content:
The first time a creature shows, the game loads its mesh, which holds the game up once: 10 ms for a bear
and up to about 100 ms for the largest when it was measured.

1731.content: A view that shows is drawn again every frame. One view 256 wide cost about half a millisecond a frame.

1732.content: Nothing is drawn while the view is not on screen: a closed menu, another page, or scrolled out of sight.

1733.content:
Five views in one window were seen working. It works in a window and in a
panel.

1740.content: Where they appear, and how many

1742.content:
A **notification** is a short message in a corner of the screen. It shows while you play and goes away by
itself. It never takes the mouse.

1743.content: `ui.Notify(text, options)` shows a notification. You can leave out any option.

1748.content: A bold line above the text.

1751.content: `"info"`, `"good"`, `"warn"` or `"bad"`. It sets the colour and the icon.

1754.content: An icon of your choice, in place of the kind's own.

1757.content: How long it stays. `0` keeps it until it is closed.

1760.content: A number from 0 to 1. It shows a progress line, and the notification stays until it is closed.

1762.content: Write `ui.Notify` with a dot, not a colon.

1763.content:
If you show a message that is already on screen, Wax does not add a copy. The one that is showing starts
its time again and shows a count: `x2`, `x3`.

1764.content: Click a few times in a row. You get one notification with a counter.

1765.content:
`ui.Notify` gives the notification back. You can change it while it is on screen. Use that to show the
progress of a job.

1771.content: Replaces the title. It does nothing on a notification made without a title.

1773.content: Shows how far a job is, from 0 to 1. The notification then stays until it is closed.

1776.content: Notifications start in the bottom right corner, and at most five show at once.

1780.content: Moves notifications to `"top-left"`, `"top-right"`, `"bottom-left"` or `"bottom-right"`. The ones showing are closed.

1782.content: Sets how many show at once. At least 1.

1787.content: The corner and the limit are the same for every mod, so change them only if the player asks.

1788.content:
When there are too many, the oldest one that is only counting down is closed first. A notification that
shows the progress of a job stays in view.

1789.content:
When a mod has an error, Wax shows it as a red notification by itself. See
Printing and the log.

1802.content:
An **overlay** is a panel pinned to the screen. It stays up while you play, and it never takes the mouse.
Clicks go through it. Use it for things you only read, such as your position or a health bar.

1803.content:
An overlay is a container, like a window. Add controls to it the same way. Nobody can click an overlay, so
use controls that show things: `Label`, `Heading`, `Field`, `Progress`, `Icon`, `Separator`.

1804.content: The example above shows values that never change. Use a task to update them.

1805.content:
Walk around and the position changes. For a bar that shows a real value, see
Example: player stats.

1806.content: `ui.Overlay` takes one table. Every entry is optional.

1811.content: Where on the screen the panel is pinned.

1814.content: How far in from that edge of the screen.

1823.content: `false` leaves out the dark panel, so only the controls are drawn over the game.

1825.content: There are nine anchors. Each name says where on the screen it is:

1833.content: Pins it somewhere else. Leave `x` and `y` out to keep their values.

1835.content: Removes the overlay and everything on it.

1836.content:
Open the menu with **F8**. Every overlay gets an outline, and you can drag it to another place. Wax
remembers where you left it.

1837.content:
Some players do not want a panel on screen all the time. Add a switch for the overlay to a window, and save
the choice.

1838.content:
A **panel** is an overlay whose controls take the mouse. `ui.Panel` makes one. It has no title bar and the
player does not drag it. Use it for something that stands beside the game's own screens, such as a list of
items next to the inventory.

1839.content: A panel takes the options of an overlay, and these:

1844.content: When it shows. `"cursor"`: while the Wax menu is open or one of the game's own screens has the mouse. `"menu"`: only with the Wax menu. `"always"`: whenever it is switched on.

1847.content: The space between its edge and its controls.

1853.content: Draws everything in it this much larger. `1.25` is a quarter larger. Text stays sharp.

1856.content: How solid its background is, from 0 to 1.

1862.content: A function that runs when the panel is pressed where it has no control.

1865.content: A function that says where the panel goes on a screen of a given size. See below.

1866.content: The panel stays where its anchor puts it.

1867.content:
While the mouse is over a panel, the mouse wheel belongs to the panel and the game does not see it.
`panel.Scrolled` fires with `1` when the wheel is turned down and `-1` when it is turned up.

1868.content:
`ui.Open({ windows = false })` frees the mouse without bringing a window up. A mod that only has panels uses
it to show them with its own key.

1869.content:
Give a panel a `place` function and it follows the game's window. The function gets the width and the height
of the screen and returns a table with any of `x`, `y`, `width`, `height` and `zoom`. Wax asks it when the
panel is made, and again in the same frame whenever the game's window changes size. The panel that exists is
moved and sized. Nothing is built again.

1870.content: `panel.Resized` fires with the panel's new width and height when the answer gave it another size.

1871.content:
The size a `place` function gets is the screen in the units the game lays its own menus out in. The panel's
`zoom` is used as it is. So such a panel keeps its size beside the game's menus whatever interface size the
player chose.

1872.content:
`slots:SetLayout(columns, size)` changes how many cells stand in a row and how large a cell is. The cells
that exist are kept, and missing ones are made over the next frames.

1873.content:
`container:Slots(options)` adds a block of square cells that each show a picture, as an inventory does. It
works in a panel and in a window. Each cell shows a **look**: a table with a picture or an icon, and what
you want back when the cell is clicked.

1874.content:
`ui.Hovered()` gives the value of the slot under the mouse, or nothing. The
reference lists everything a look can hold and every signal of a block.

1875.content:
`ui.FitGame` draws the game's own menus smaller, which leaves room beside them for panels. `ui.GameScreen()`
says which of the game's screens is showing, and `ui.GameScreenChanged` fires when that changes. Listen to the
signal, and do not ask every frame.

1876.content: Every function is listed in the ui reference.

1878.content: A line of text that stays over a creature, a player or anything else in the world.

1879.content: What a tag can sit on

1883.content: Example: name and level over every wolf

1885.content:
A tag is a line of text that sits over something in the world and follows it. It shows while you play, not
only when the menu is open.

1889.content: Follows it: a creature, a player's character, an item, something built.

1891.content: Follows the actor, at the place of that part.

1893.content: Stays on that spot in the world.

1899.content: The text colour. White when left out.

1903.content: The tag only shows when the thing is this many metres away or nearer. 100 when left out.

1905.content: How far above the thing's middle the tag sits, in centimetres. Wax works it out when left out.

1906.content: A tag removes itself when the thing it is on leaves the world, and when your mod reloads.

1907.content:
When several things stand close together, their tags would cover each other. Wax piles them up, with the tag
of the nearest thing lowest. A tag with no room left is hidden until there is room.

1908.content:
Each tag that is on screen is placed again every frame. A few dozen tags are fine. For hundreds, give them
a smaller `within`.

1920.content:
A **theme** is the set of colours every window, overlay and notification uses. One theme applies to all mods
at once.

1921.content: The player chooses the theme, on the **Settings** page of the Wax panel. The same page has:

1922.content: The accent colour: From the theme, Blue, Green, Teal, Amber, Orange, Red, Pink or Purple.

When you colour something yourself, take the colour from the theme. Then it still looks right when the
player picks another theme.

`ui.Theme()` gives the theme in use. Pass its colours on as they are. They keep following the theme, even
after it changes.

1943.content: Errors and danger. Red in most themes.

1948.content: A second value from 0 to 1 makes it see-through. 0 is invisible and 1 is solid.

1949.content:
Pick a theme from the list. Everything on screen changes to the new colours. No window is rebuilt, and no
mod is reloaded.

`ui.AddTheme` adds a named theme. Give it the colours you want to change. Everything you leave out comes
from Midnight.

`ui.AddSettings(container)` adds the menu's own settings to a container of yours: menu key, theme, accent,

1994.content: A window is a box in the menu that holds your controls.

1995.content:
Switch the mod on, then press the key of your mod's windows to see it. Wax tells you once which key that is,
and it is on the mod's card of the Mods page as **Show / hide**. The title bar has a button to roll the window
up, and a cross to close it. The user can drag the window by its title bar and resize it by any edge or
corner. The bottom right corner shows a grip.

1996.content: Everything you add with `window:Something(...)` is a control. The Controls page lists them all.

1997.content: `ui.Window` takes one table. Every entry is optional.

2002.content: The text in the title bar.

2005.content: An icon shown before the title.

2014.content: Where the window first appears, counted from the top left of the screen.

2015.content: A little below and to the right of the window before it.

2020.content: `false` makes a window the user cannot resize. It has no grip, its edges and corners do nothing, and it is always the size you give it. `window:SetSize` still works.

2023.content: The key that shows and hides your mod's windows, such as `"F6"` or `"Ctrl+K"`. The first window your mod makes decides. The user can pick another on the mod's card.

2024.content: Wax gives your mod a key.

2026.content: `false` makes the window hidden. Show it later with `window:Show()`.

2029.content: `"side"` or `"top"` gives the window pages. See below.

2032.content: The width of the page list of a `"side"` window.

2035.content: `false` stops Wax remembering where the user put the window.

2037.content:
Wax remembers a window's place and size by its title. Two windows of one mod with the same title would share
one place.

2041.content: Shows the window, in front of the others.

2043.content: Hides it. With the last window of your mod hidden, your mod is no longer up, and the menu closes once nobody's windows are.

2051.content: Moves it. It always stays on the screen.

2053.content: Resizes it. A window does not go below its smallest size.

2055.content: Rolls it up to its title bar. `false` rolls it back down.

2059.content: Removes the window and everything on it.

2067.content: Another page is chosen. Your function gets the page's name.

2068.content: A window is removed when your mod reloads. `init.lua` then makes it again.

2069.content: `ui.Windows()` gives a list of every window in the menu.

2070.content:
The player resizes a window by dragging any of its four edges or four corners. You do nothing for it:
every window has it.

2071.content:
The mouse pointer changes over an edge or a corner, and that piece of the window's outline lights up. It
is brighter while it is held. The bottom right corner also shows a grip.

2072.content: The edge across from the one that is dragged stays where it is.

2073.content: Resizing stops at the window's smallest size and at the edges of the screen.

2074.content: A window rolled up to its title bar cannot be resized.

2075.content: Wax remembers the size, as it remembers the place.

2076.content:
The smallest size is 240 by 140 for a plain window. A window with side pages is never narrower than 420, and
one with tabs along the top never lower than 200 or narrower than its tabs need.

2077.content:
`resizable = false` makes a window that is always the size you give it. It has no grip, its edges and
corners do nothing, and a size remembered from before is not used. `window:SetSize` still works.

2078.content:
Lay your controls out so that they work at any size the player picks. Controls fill the width they are
given, a Row shares it, and a page scrolls when the window is too low for it.

2079.content:
All windows of your mod come up together, with one key, and go away with it. Other mods' windows and the Wax
panel stay as they are. Ask for the key with the `key` option of your first window. Without it Wax gives your
mod a free key and tells the player once.

2080.content:
The player can change the key on your mod's card of the Mods page. The menu says how
to read and set it from code.

2081.content:
Give a window `nav = "side"` and it gets a list of pages on the left. `window:Page` adds a page. Add
controls to the page, not to the window.

2082.content:
The first page you add is the one that shows first. The user can drag the line beside the list to make the
list wider.

2083.content:
With `nav = "top"` the pages become tabs. The tabs are all the same width, and the window cannot be made
narrower than its tabs need.

2087.content: An icon shown before the page's name.

2089.content: `true` lists the page at the foot of a side list. Good for a settings page.

2091.content: `false` makes a page that does not scroll. A Grid or Console on it then fills the space that is left.

2095.content: Adds a page and gives it back.

2097.content: Switches to the page with that name.

2099.content: Removes a page and everything on it.

2101.content: Sets the width of the side list.

2102.content: If you add a control straight to a window that has pages, Wax puts it on a first page called **Main**.

2103.content:
A page has a signal called `NearEnd`. It fires when the user scrolls close to the bottom. Use it to add
more as the user scrolls.

2104.content:
`NearEnd` also fires a few times a second while the page is not full yet. So do nothing when there is no more
to add, as the first line of `add_more` does.

2105.content: For very long lists, use a Grid instead.

2106.content: `window:StatusBar()` adds a line along the bottom of a window. Use it to say what your mod is doing.

2110.content: Shows a message. `kind` sets the colour: `"info"`, `"good"`, `"warn"` or `"bad"`. `icon` adds an icon.

2112.content: Shows a message with a spinning circle, until the next `Set`.

2114.content: Shows a thin line across the bar, from 0 to 1. `nil` hides it.

2116.content: Shows text at the right-hand end.

2118.content: Empties the message and hides the line.

2122.content: Save a file and your mod reloads in the running game.

2130.content: Save a `.lua` file of your mod. A moment later, Wax reloads that mod. The game keeps running.

2131.content: No other program has to run for this. Wax watches your mod's files from inside the game.

2132.content: Wax removes everything the mod made: windows, overlays, hotkeys, tasks and signal connections.

2133.content: Wax runs `init.lua` again, from the top.

2134.content: After a reload your mod is in the same state as after a new start. Local variables start again too.

2135.content: Mods that depend on the reloaded mod reload after it.

2136.content: Use `persist` for values that should live through a reload.

2137.content: Save the file a few times. The number goes up each time.

2138.content:
`persist("state", { loads = 0 })` gives back the same table on every reload. The second value is only used
the first time. Change what is inside the table. Don't replace the table.

2139.content:
`persist` forgets everything when the game closes. To keep settings between game sessions, use
`storage`.

2140.content: There are two ways a save can go wrong.

2141.content:
**The file does not compile.** This happens when you save in the middle of a line, or when your editor saves
by itself while you type. Wax leaves the mod as it is: the version from before that save keeps running. The
mod's card on the Mods page says which line is wrong. It is not counted as an error.

2142.content: **The file compiles but fails when it runs.** The mod does not load.

2143.content: A red notification shows the error.

2144.content: The Mods page marks the mod as failed and shows the error under its name.

2145.content:
Either way, fix the file and save. Wax tries again by itself. Once the mod loads, its old errors are cleared
from the panel.

2146.content:
Wax remembers which mods you have seen. A mod folder it has not seen before is listed **switched off**. Open
the **Mods** page and flip its **Enabled** switch to load it.

2147.content:
This is so whether the folder was added while the game ran or while it was closed. A mod is code, and nothing
that lands in the mods folder should run before you have had a look at it.

2148.content: A mod you switched on stays on. It loads by itself the next time the game starts.

2149.content:
When a folder is added while the game is running, a notification tells you. Wax looks for new mod folders
when you open the menu. While the Mods page is showing it looks again every couple of seconds. The refresh
button beside the search box makes it look at once.

2150.content: Each mod on the Mods page has a **Reload** button. Use it to start the mod again without changing a file.

2151.content:
Flip a mod's **Enabled** switch off. The mod unloads and everything it made is removed. It stays off the
next time you start the game, until you switch it on again.

2152.content: Build your interface at the top level of `init.lua`. Then it is rebuilt on every reload.

2153.content: Don't keep game objects in `persist`. They can be gone by the time you use them, for example after a map change. Get them again from `game`.

2154.content: Remove a mod's folder to remove the mod. Wax unloads it the next time it looks.

2156.content: Wax is a Lua scripting framework for ICARUS. It runs your mods inside the game.

2161.content: Wax lets you write mods for ICARUS in Lua.

2162.content: A mod is a folder with one file in it, called `init.lua`. Wax runs that file inside the game.

2163.content:
The download is on the Installing page.
Security says what Wax puts on your PC and what a mod can do.

2164.content: This is a whole mod. It makes a window with one button.

2165.content:
Switch the mod on once, on the Mods page of the Wax menu. Wax gives the mod a key and tells you which. Press
that key in the game and the window is there. Click the button and a message shows in a corner of the screen.

2166.content: Read and change the game's objects. Start at `game` and go to the world, the player and every other object. See The game tree.

2167.content: Make an interface with windows, buttons, switches, sliders, lists, overlays and notifications. See Controls.

2168.content: Run code over time. Wait, repeat and delay without freezing the game. See Tasks.

2169.content: Run a function when something happens, such as a map change or a flipped switch. See Signals.

2170.content: Keep settings between game sessions. See Saving settings.

2171.content: When you save a file, the mod reloads in the running game. You don't restart anything. See Hot reload.

2172.content: A key shows and hides your mod's windows and frees the mouse. See The menu.

2173.content: A panel in the game lists your mods, shows the log and runs a line of Lua. See The Wax panel.

2174.content: Wax catches an error in your mod. The error shows as a notification and in the log, with the line it happened on.

2175.content: Everything your mod makes is removed when the mod reloads. You don't write clean-up code.

2201.content: Switching a mod off, or removing it

2202.content:
ICARUS on Steam, on Windows. You install nothing else. UE4SS, the script loader Wax runs on, is in the
download.

2203.content:
Download the zip from the latest release.
Extract the whole zip before you run anything in it.

2204.content: The same page has the VS Code extension as a `.vsix` file. The editor page says what it is for.

2205.content:
It also has a `.manifest` file and a `.manifest.sig` file, with the same version in the name as the zip.
They are the signed list of the release's files. You don't need them to install.
Check a download by hand says how to use them.

2211.content: Looks for a newer Wax and installs it.

2215.content: The script those three files run. It is plain text, so you can read what it does.

2217.content: The steps on this page, as a text file.

2219.content: The licences of UE4SS and of the Lucide icons.

2221.content: The files that go into the game folder.

2230.content: Your mods. It is empty after a new install.

2231.content: Security says what each part does on your PC and how to remove it.

2232.content: Close ICARUS first. Then install in one of two ways.

2233.content:
Double-click `Install Wax.cmd`. It finds the game through Steam and copies the files. If it can't find the
game, it asks you for the folder.

2234.content: Windows may ask you to confirm first, because the file came from the internet.

2235.content:
The installer asks one question: whether the **Add to game** button of the Mods page may open Wax
on this PC.

2236.content:
Type `y` and press **Enter** for yes. Windows then hands links that start with `wax://` to Wax. That takes
one entry in your own part of the registry.

2237.content: Press **Enter** alone for no. Everything else works without it. You download a mod as a zip.

2238.content:
Such a link can be on any web page, not only on the Wax site. So Wax shows you the mod and asks before it
downloads anything, and a mod it adds stays switched off until you switch it on.
The registry key says what the entry holds, how to remove it and how to
make it later.

2239.content:
The installer also closes Wax's folder to the other Windows accounts on the PC. Your account and
administrators can change it, and other accounts can only read it.
Who can change Wax's folder has the reason.

2240.content:
Run the installer from the Windows account you play on. Under another account Wax could not save its
settings.

2241.content: Copy everything inside the `game` folder into this folder of the game:

2242.content:
To find it, right-click ICARUS in Steam and choose **Manage**, then **Browse local files**. Open `Icarus`,
then `Binaries`, then `Win64`.

2243.content: When you are done, `dwmapi.dll` and the `ue4ss` folder sit next to `Icarus-Win64-Shipping.exe`.

2244.content: Copying by hand sets up no button and changes no permissions.

2245.content:
Wax is tested on the UE4SS build in the zip, so the installer puts that build in. If it finds a different
one, it first copies the old files to a folder inside `Win64`. The folder's name is `ue4ss-backup-` followed
by the date and time. Your other UE4SS mods in `ue4ss\Mods` are left alone.

2246.content:
UE4SS comes with a few small mods of its own. Three of them open the game's developer console and its cheat
commands (`CheatManagerEnablerMod`, `ConsoleCommandsMod`, `ConsoleEnablerMod`), and the others load blueprint
mods, add keys for UE4SS's own tools, or are examples. Wax needs none of them, so none of them is in the
download: the only thing in `ue4ss\Mods` is Wax.

2247.content:
Earlier versions of Wax installed them. If you install over one of those and never changed
`ue4ss\Mods\mods.txt`, the installer removes them and says so.

2248.content:
If you changed that file, the installer keeps it and the mods, and tells you which of the three above are
switched on in it.

2249.content: If you want one of them, get it from UE4SS's own release and list it in `mods.txt` as that release does.

2250.content: Start ICARUS the way you always do. Nothing else has to run next to it.

2251.content:
The menu opens and you see the Wax panel. Its **Mods** page lists every mod Wax found. After a new install
it is empty: the **Browse** page beside it has mods to add.

2252.content: The bottom of the panel says how many mods loaded, and whether there were errors.

2253.content: Wax sits in the UE4SS mods folder inside the game:

2254.content: Two folders in there matter to you:

2258.content: Your mods. One folder for each mod.

2260.content: Settings that Wax and your mods save. You never need to edit these by hand.

2261.content: Each mod is a folder inside `Wax\mods\`. The folder holds a file called `init.lua`.

2262.content:
The folder name is the mod's id. Use only letters, digits, `_` and `-` in it. A folder with another kind of
name is skipped, and the log says so.

2263.content:
A mod that Wax has not seen before is listed switched off. Open the **Mods** page of the Wax menu and flip
its **Enabled** switch. This is so whether the folder was put there while the game ran or while it was
closed.

2265.content: Double-click `Update Wax.cmd`. It asks GitHub for the newest release of Wax. If that is newer than yours:

2266.content: It downloads the release's list of files and checks that the list carries the signature of Wax's author.

2267.content: It downloads the zip and compares it with the list.

2269.content:
If any of that fails it changes nothing, and tells you to get Wax from the site instead.
What is signed has the key and its fingerprint.

2270.content:
Use the `Update Wax.cmd` of version 0.2.1 or newer. The one that came with Wax 0.2.0 and older installs what
it downloads without that check, so delete the folders of those older downloads.

2271.content: You can also download the newest zip and run its `Install Wax.cmd`. Installing over an old copy updates Wax.

2272.content:
Both ways keep your mods (`Wax\mods`), your settings (`Wax\saved`) and your UE4SS settings. They also leave
the **Add to game** button the way you set it.

2273.content:
Download the newest zip and copy the contents of `game` into `Win64` again. Say yes when Windows asks to
replace files.

2274.content:
Your own mods and your settings are not in the zip, so they stay. The UE4SS settings files `UE4SS-settings.ini`
and `mods.txt` are replaced by the copies from the zip.

2275.content:
While the game runs, Wax asks the catalogue whether a newer Wax is out. When one is, Wax downloads it,
checks it against the same signature and puts it in the next time the game starts. If the new version does
not start, the version before is put back.

2276.content: Some versions need the installer. Wax then shows a notification that asks you to run `Update Wax.cmd`.

2277.content:
What Wax asks the network for says what is sent and how to
switch this off.

2279.content:
Double-click `Uninstall Wax.cmd`. It removes Wax and the registry entry of the **Add to game** button. It
asks before it removes your mods and settings, and before it removes UE4SS. Press **Enter** at a question to
keep them.

2281.content: Your mods and settings are in it. Copy `mods` and `saved` somewhere else first if you want to keep them.

2282.content: To remove UE4SS too, delete `dwmapi.dll` and the `ue4ss` folder from `Win64`.

2283.content:
If you said yes to the **Add to game** button, remove its registry entry as well. Open a Command Prompt and
type:

2284.content: To switch a mod off, use its **Enabled** switch on the Mods page. It stays off the next time you play.

2285.content: To remove a mod, delete its folder from `Wax\mods\`.

2288.content: Read, change and call any object of the game.

2291.content: Find out what an object has

2296.content: Check what kind of object it is

2297.content: Check that it is still there

2300.content:
An **Instance** is one object of the game: your character, a tree, a component, the world itself.
`game.Character` gives you an Instance. So does `game.World`, and so does every entry of a list such as
`game.World:GetChildren()`.

2306.content: The name of the object's class.

2308.content: The engine's full name for the object.

2310.content: The Instance it sits under. The same as `GetParent()`.

2312.content: The UE4SS object itself, with no safety checks. For experts.

2313.content:
Every other name is one of the object's own properties or functions. These are the ones the game gave it.
Which ones it has depends on its class. Your character is an `IcarusPlayerCharacter`. That class is built on
`IcarusCharacter`, which is built on `Character`, then `Pawn`, then `Actor`. The character has what all of
those have, and so does everything else built on `Actor`.

2314.content: Read a property with a dot: `state.Health`.

2315.content: Change a property by assigning to it: `state.Health = 100`.

2316.content: Call a function with a colon: `character:K2_GetActorLocation()`.

2317.content: If the name does not exist, you get an error. The error suggests the closest name that does exist.

2319.content:
The Explorer on this site lists every class of the game, what it is built on, and each property
and function with its types.

2320.content:
The **Explorer** page of the Wax panel shows the objects in your running game
with their values.

2321.content: In VS Code, the extension completes the members of a class as you type.

2322.content: In a mod, `GetMembers()` lists every property and function name of an object.

2323.content:
The command bar of the Wax panel is faster. Type `game.Character.` and press
**Tab**. Type a few letters and **Tab** completes the name.

2324.content:
When you set a property or call a function, Wax checks the value first. A value of the wrong kind raises a
normal Lua error. It does not crash the game.

2325.content: Writing a property changes the value the game holds. The game may change it again on its next update.

2326.content:
Every actor, and every part of one that has a place, has `Position` and `Rotation`. Read them, or assign to
move the thing at once.

2327.content: A class of the game that has a member of its own by one of these names keeps it.

2332.content: A name or a piece of text

2334.content: A number or a true/false value

2338.content: A structure, such as a position

2339.content: The structure itself. Read its parts by name: `.X`, `.Y`, `.Z`.

2340.content: Three functions do the same as the dot and the colon, with the name given as text.

2342.content: The name is in a variable.

2343.content:
The object has a property whose name Wax also uses, such as `Name` or `Parent`. `instance.Name` gives Wax's
value. `instance:Get("Name")` gives the object's own.

2344.content: `IsA(class_name)` is `true` when the object's class is that class, or is built on it.

2345.content: `GetClassChain()` lists the class names from the object's own class up to `Object`.

2346.content:
The game makes and destroys objects all the time. `IsValid()` is `false` once the object is destroyed, or the
map changes.

2353.content: Its components, and the actors attached to it.

2356.content: This prints the parts your character is made of:

2357.content: The output looks like this. Each line shows the class, then the name.

2361.content: The Instance this one sits under.

2363.content: A list of the Instances directly under this one.

2365.content: The first child with that `Name`, or `nil`.

2367.content: The same, but it looks at every level below.

2369.content: The first child of exactly that class, or `nil`.

2371.content: The first child of that class, or of a class built on it.

2373.content: Everything below, nearest first. It stops at `limit`, which is 5000 when left out.

2374.content:
`instance.Raw` is the UE4SS object behind an Instance. Nothing is checked when you use it, and a mistake can
crash the game. Most mods never need it.

2375.content: If you have a UE4SS object and want the safe version, `game.wrap(object)` gives you its Instance.

2376.content: Every function is listed in the game reference.

2378.content: Look up what an item is, count what a character carries, and give or take items.

2381.content: Search by the name players see

2387.content:
There are two things here. `game.Items` knows what each kind of item is. An **inventory** knows what is in
it: a character's backpack, its hotbar, and so on.

2388.content:
An item is named by its row in the game's table `D_ItemsStatic`, such as `"Wood"` or `"Stone_Pickaxe"`.
Letter case, spaces, underscores and hyphens do not matter, so `"stone pickaxe"` is the same item. A name the
game does not have raises an error that suggests the nearest ones.

2392.content: The item's name, spelled as the game spells it.

2394.content: The name the game shows players.

2400.content: How many fit in one stack.

2402.content: Its durability when new. `nil` for an item with none.

2404.content: The path of its picture in the game's files.

2410.content: `true` when the game has an item of this name.

2414.content: The names that contain the text.

2416.content: Reads the name the game shows for every item, so that `Find` matches those too.

2417.content: The first `Get` of an item reads a few rows of the game's tables. After that it costs nothing.

2418.content:
`Find` goes by item names until `Load` has run. After it, `"iron"` also finds `Metal_Ore`, which the game
shows as Iron Ore. `Load` only works inside a task. It reads a little each frame and took
about half a second when it was measured.

2419.content: `Find` goes through every item. Call it when the player types something, not every frame.

2420.content: A player's character has six inventories:

2430.content: The envirosuit, its upgrades and the vision slot.

2431.content: One is `nil` when the character has no such inventory. The character in the station has no backpack.

2432.content: These work on a player's character, and on `game.Me`, over all six:

2436.content: How many of an item it carries.

2438.content: `true` when it carries at least that many. One when `count` is left out.

2440.content: Every stack it carries. Each says in `Inventory` which one it is in.

2441.content:
`character.HeldItem` is the stack in the hotbar slot that is in hand, and `character.HotbarSlot` is that
slot's number.

2442.content: Each inventory has the same three functions for itself, and a few more:

2446.content: How many slots it has, and how many hold something.

2448.content: What everything in it weighs, in kilograms.

2450.content: What kind the game says it is, such as `"Backpack"` or `"Quickbar"`.

2452.content: Every stack, in the order of its slots.

2454.content: What one slot holds, or `nil`. Slots are counted from 1.

2456.content: As for a character, for this inventory alone.

2461.content:
A stack is a plain table: `Item`, `Count`, `Slot`, `Durability`, and `Properties` with every number the game
keeps for it. Changing the table changes nothing in the game.

2462.content:
Other things that hold items have inventories of the game's class `Inventory` too, and the same functions
work on them. Reading them was tried on a drop ship and a gravestone. Giving, taking and the signals were not
tried there.

2463.content: Wax keeps a copy of an inventory you ask about, so asking often costs little.

2464.content:
For the inventories of your own character on the host, the game tells Wax of every slot it changes, and the
copy follows at once.

2465.content:
Anywhere else Wax looks at most four times a second. A new stack shows about a quarter of a second
later, and a change that leaves the weight as it was, such as durability, within two seconds.

2466.content:
`inventory:Refresh()` reads it all now. A whole backpack took about a millisecond, so use it when something
has to be exact at once, not every frame.

2467.content: `Count` looks at the inventory's own slots. It does not look inside a bag that lies in a slot.

2471.content: Puts items into the backpack. Gives back how many went in, and why not all of them when fewer did.

2473.content: Takes items out of the backpack first, then the hotbar. Gives back how many were taken.

2477.content: The same for one inventory. The last stack of the item goes first.

2478.content: Items go onto the stacks of that item first, then into empty slots.

2479.content: What does not fit is not given. Nothing is dropped on the ground and nothing goes to the hotbar.

2480.content: A tool comes new, with its full durability.

2481.content: What is taken is gone, not dropped. What a character wears is left alone.

2482.content: `Count`, `Has` and `List` follow in the same frame. The weight follows a moment later.

2483.content: Both were tried on a player's backpack. One call took 0.6 to 2.3 ms.

2484.content: What a mod gave stays when the mod unloads.

2485.content: `inventory:Resize(slots)` gives an inventory that many slots.

2486.content: Slots are added and taken at the end of the inventory.

2487.content:
A slot that holds something is never taken, nor any slot before it. The inventory then keeps as many slots
as it needs, and the second value says so: `"slot 31 holds something, so 31 slots stay"`.

2488.content: `Size`, `List` and the others follow in the same frame.

2489.content:
It lasts as long as the inventory does. One the game makes anew, as after a map change, has the number of
its row in `D_InventoryInfo` again. Change `StartingSlots` there with `game.Data` to cover
those.

2490.content: The new size stays when your mod unloads. Put it back in `mod.OnUnload`.

2491.content: It was tried on the station's loadout, from 15 slots to 50 and back.

2492.content: Signals for items that come and go are on Events of the game.

2493.content: Every field and function is listed in the Items and inventories reference.

2495.content: See what your mod is doing with print and log.

2498.content: When your mod has an error

2500.content: To see what your code does, print it.

2501.content:
Open the **Log** page of the Wax panel. Each line starts with your mod's id in square
brackets:

2502.content: `print` takes any number of values and puts a tab between them.

2503.content: `print` is for normal messages. `log` lets you say how serious a message is.

2508.content: Normal messages. `print` writes at this level too.

2511.content: Something looks wrong, but the mod carries on.

2515.content: Red. Shown with the **Errors** switch. Also pops up as a notification.

2517.content: Details you only want while looking for a bug.

2520.content: Very fine detail. Dropped by default.

2523.content: The first value is a pattern, as in Lua's `string.format`. `%s` stands for any value and `%d` for a whole number. The values after it fill those places.

2524.content: When the same message is logged several times in a row, the log shows it once, with a count at the end:

2525.content: You don't need to catch errors yourself. Wax catches them.

2526.content: The error goes to the log, in red, with the file and line it came from.

2527.content: A red notification shows the first line of the error.

2528.content: Only the code that failed stops: that click, that task. The rest of your mod keeps running.

2529.content: The one exception is an error while `init.lua` itself is running. Then the mod does not load until you fix it.

2530.content:
Click **Break something**. A red message appears and the log shows the line number. Then click **Still works**.
Its message shows, because the error stopped only the first click.

2531.content:
If the log says `switched off after 5 consecutive errors`, a function kept failing every time it ran, and
Wax stopped calling it. Fix the error and save the file.

2532.content:
Everything in the log is also written to the game's `UE4SS.log` file, so you can read it after the game has
closed.

2533.content: Every function is listed in the mods reference.

2535.content: Each mod's windows come up with that mod's own key, and the mouse is free while any are up.

2539.content: Things that are not part of the menu

2544.content: Windows made by mods are shown in **the menu**. The menu is open while anybody's windows are up.

2545.content: **F8** shows and hides the Wax panel.

2546.content:
Every mod that has a window has a key of its own. That key shows and hides that mod's windows, and nobody
else's.

2547.content: So you can have the Wax panel up, or one mod's windows, or several at once.

2743.content: Call a mount that is yours and can be ridden at once, give a creature another body, and make a mount strike.

2749.content:
Three things for mods that deal with animals you ride: a mount made in one call, a creature that wears another
model, and a mount that attacks when you tell it to. Together they are what a mod needs to add a mount of its own
to the game.

2750.content:
`game.Creatures:SpawnMount(kind, place, options)` puts a tamed animal into the world.
`kind` is the animal's set-up row, such as `"Mount_Moa"` or `"Mount_Horse"`, or a kind such as `"Moa"`.

2751.content: It does what the game does when a taming ends, and then the two things a player would do by hand:

2752.content: The animal is made with the game's own spawn, a few metres in front of you or at the place you give.

2753.content: It gets its name and you become its owner.

2754.content:
A saddle goes into its saddle slot. That is what makes the game give a mount its seat. Without a saddle the
game does not offer to ride it.

2755.content:
After that it is an ordinary mount of the game: the game's own prompt to ride it works, it follows you, and it is
saved with the prospect.

2761.content: The saddle item it wears. `"Saddle_Standard"` when left out, `false` for none.

2763.content: `false` leaves it with no owner, to be claimed in the game.

2765.content: Which way it looks, as `{ Yaw = 90 }`. Toward you when left out.

2766.content:
Inside a task the call answers once the saddle is on. When the saddle did not go on, the mount still comes back,
with the reason as a second value. Outside a task it answers at once and finishes a moment later.

2767.content:
Where the game knows no ground to walk on, as on a platform a mod built high in the air, the mount is made on the
ground below and brought up to the place.

2768.content:
`creature:SetModel(model)` gives a creature another skeletal mesh to wear, with its materials. The creature goes
on walking, running and being ridden as before.

2772.content: The skeletal mesh: from `game.Assets:Load`, from `mod.Content:Load`, or a path.

2774.content: Materials by slot, 1 first. A slot you leave out shows what the mesh itself names.

2776.content: `false` hides the creature's coat of fur or feathers. The game grows it on a body of its own and would draw it over the new one.

2778.content: `false` hides the saddle the game shows on a mount, for a model that has one of its own. The rider still sits on it.

2780.content:
**The mesh has to be on the creature's own skeleton.** A creature's animations belong to one skeleton. A mesh
built on another one would stand still, so `SetModel` refuses it and names both skeletons.

2781.content:
**Wax puts the model back.** The game writes a mount's own skin again now and then, a second after it appears
and whenever its looks are worked out again. Wax looks once a second and puts your model back on.

2782.content:
**It undoes itself.** When your mod unloads, or on `creature:ResetModel()`, the creature has its own body
again. `creature.HasModel` says whether it wears one.

2783.content:
`SetModel` works for a client as well as for the host. Each player sees it only in their own game, so everybody
who should see the model needs the mod.

2784.content:
`mount:Strike()` makes a mount attack. It is what the game does when the rider of a mount attacks:
the mount plays its own attack, pays the stamina for it, and hits what stands in front of it at the strike. The
game keeps that for mounts with the talent for it. `Strike` asks for no talent.

2785.content:
It answers `false` and the reason while the mount is in the middle of another move, and for a kind of mount the
game gives no attack.

2786.content:
The mesh for `SetModel` comes from a pak made with the Unreal editor (Game content of your own).
A model from a 3D program has no bones the game knows, so it has to be bound to the skeleton of the animal it
replaces. These are the steps the Strider, the example mount, was made with:

2787.content:
**Pick the animal.** Take one whose shape is close: two legs for two legs, four for four. Its skeleton decides
which bones your model can move, and its set-up row is what you pass to `SpawnMount`.

2788.content:
**Place the joints.** For each bone of that skeleton, mark where the same joint is in your model: hips, knees,
ankles, the line of the spine, the neck, the head. Lay them through the model as the animal stands in the
game, not as its skeleton lies at rest.

2789.content:
**Reshape to the bone lengths.** The game's animations carry the animal's own bone lengths. A leg that is
longer or shorter than the animal's gets pushed out at its joints. So stretch each part of the model evenly
between its two joints until the joints sit where the animal's are, and bind that shape.

2790.content:
**Bind and export.** Give every point of the model its bones, with a soft blend at each joint, and write an FBX
whose bones have the names and the turns of the game's skeleton.

2791.content:
**Import onto the game's skeleton.** In the Unreal project, import the FBX as a skeletal mesh and choose the
game's own skeleton asset for it. A copy of the skeleton in your mod's folder does not work: the creature's
animations only run on the one the game has.

2792.content:
**Use the game's creature material.** A material built in the stock editor draws grey in ICARUS. Make yours a
material instance of the game's creature material and set its three pictures: `Color`, `Normal` and `MRO`.

2793.content: **Cook and load.** Build the pak, then `mod.Content:Load` and `SetModel`.

2795.content: Load the mesh with `mod.Content:Load` before you show it by its path.

Parts of the model with no bone in the animal's skeleton stay stiff. A Moa has no wing bones, so wings on a
model bound to it do not flap.

The mount keeps the animal's own stats, sounds and talents. To change numbers, change the animal's rows
