In this version of Wax it checks the names of its options and then raises "a new category is not switched on in this version of Wax": a category's name is text and its picture a reference to an asset, and game.Data does not write those yet.

10083.content: Puts a described store into the game: rows for its new categories, its nodes, what they sell and what they hand over, each named "\<ModId>\_\<id>" and added by the mod they are named after. The description is checked as Check does it, and an error of Check is raised as an error here, with how many more there are. In this version of Wax a store that passes then ends in one of three errors and nothing is added: a node that needs `all` of several is refused, a store with a new category raises "a new category is not switched on in this version of Wax", and any other store raises "adding rows to the game's tables is not switched on in this version of Wax". Research is saved in the player's account under a node's row name for good. So an id, and with it the mod's folder name, never changes once players have the mod: a node under a new name is a new node, and what was researched under the old name no longer counts.

10089.content: Takes back everything the calling mod changed through Node and Category: every field goes back to what it would hold without this mod. What the mod changed through game.Data itself, and what other mods changed, stays. If the game does not take a field back, an error says so and that change stands, so Reset can be called again.

10090.content: **Returns** `integer` (`count`) How many changes were taken back.

10091.content: Shapes that place a category's nodes, and what does not fit the store's screen. A place is the middle of a node in the store's own units, on a canvas that begins at 0, 0 at the top left. The store pans sideways only, so a category can be as wide as it likes and its height has to fit the screen.

10092.content: Below, `layout` stands for one of these.

10093.content: Places for nodes in a shape, in the order the nodes were given, rounded to whole numbers. "line" puts them one after the other, "grid" in rows, "ring" and "arc" round a middle, "spiral" outwards from a middle, "path" evenly along a line through points, and "tree" by what each node needs: a node goes one step further than the furthest node it needs. A function is called with (index, id, count) for each node and returns its place as two numbers. The defaults keep to the screen's height where the count allows. Options you give are used as they are. A wrong shape or option raises an error that suggests the right name. A shape that would put a node further than 1000000 from 0 raises an error too. One call places up to 10000 nodes.

10098.content: `"line"` \| `"grid"` \| `"ring"` \| `"arc"` \| `"spiral"` \| `"tree"` \| `"path"` \| `fun(index: integer, id: any, count: integer): number, number`

10101.content: How many nodes, or a list of ids. For "tree" a list of `{ id = , needs = }`, where `needs` is one id, a list of ids, or a table with `any` and `all` as a described store has it. A node goes after every node it needs, whichever of these names it.

10105.content: What does not fit among places that share a category, as warnings: two nodes that lie on each other, two whose middles are closer than 300, a node whose middle is outside the heights 250 to 1450, and a node that reaches past the canvas's left or top. A place that is not two numbers, one further than 1000000 from 0, and a Size that is not a number raise an error that says which place it is.

10122.content: The node's row name, as the game spells it.

10123.content: Changes the node: its prices, what it needs, its place, its line style, its level. It is written before Set returns. Everything is checked first, and when something is wrong an error says what, with the nearest right name, and nothing is written: an option Set does not have, a currency or a node the game does not have, a price that is not a whole number from 0 to 2147483647, a place that is not two numbers, and needs that could never be met, such as the node itself or nodes that wait for each other in a circle. When the game's tables refuse one of the fields, what this call had already written is taken back and the error says why. Returns what Check would warn about now that the change is in, as warnings: a parent in another category, a node it lies on or too close to, a place outside the heights that fit the screen, a straight line that runs over a node, a price in more than two currencies. An empty list when there is nothing. The change belongs to the mod and goes back when the mod unloads or calls Reset. When two mods change one field, game.Data's rules decide which shows.

Switched off in this version of Wax: Hide raises an error that says so. A node in no tree is in no store, and it is not known what the game does with a player's research of such a node when it saves their account.

10133.content: Takes back what this mod changed of the node through its handle: its fields and the prices in its store item. What other mods changed stays.

10134.content: **Returns** `integer` (`count`) How many fields were taken back.

10135.content: One category of the store, to lay it out or to add nodes to it. It holds a name and nothing of the game.

10136.content: You get one from `game.Workshop:Category`, `game.Workshop:AddCategory`. Below, `storeCategory` stands for one of these.

10142.content: The category's row name, as the game spells it. For a category from AddCategory, the row name it will have.

10143.content: Gives every node of the category a place in a shape, as `Layout:Place` does, and writes the places that differ from where the nodes are. Joints are placed like any other node, and a "tree" goes by what each node needs inside the category. A function is called with (index, row name, count). A wrong shape or option raises an error that suggests the right name, and nothing is written. Returns what Check would warn about for the new places: nodes that lie on each other or too close, nodes outside the heights that fit the screen, straight lines that run over a node. The places are written all the same. Each place is a change of the calling mod, put back when it unloads. On the store's screen the nodes follow a few a frame. Every node that moves is written in the one call, so call it when the mod loads or when something is pressed, not every frame. For a category from AddCategory it sets the shape for the nodes that have no `at`, as `arrange` does in a described store.

10533.content: What Wax puts on your PC, what a mod can do, how downloads are checked, and what is not protected.

10535.content: What Wax puts on your PC

10541.content: What Wax asks the network for

10547.content:
This page is for a player who wants to know what they install, and for anyone who reviews Wax. It describes
Wax 0.2.1 and newer.

10548.content:
Wax loads mods, and a mod is code. A mod that is switched on can do what any program on your PC can do. Wax
does not fence it in.

10549.content: No mod starts without you. A mod Wax has not seen before stays switched off until you switch it on.

10550.content:
Every Wax release and every mod in the catalogue is signed with one key. Your PC checks the signature
before an update or a mod from the catalogue is put in.

10551.content: Wax does not start with Windows, has no accounts and sends nothing about you to anyone.

10552.content: The whole source is public at github.com/bostonstrong567/icarus-wax.

10553.content:
Almost everything is inside the game folder, `...\steamapps\common\Icarus\Icarus\Binaries\Win64\`. Two
things are not: a registry key that is only made when you say yes, and a small log file of the
**Add to game** button.

10558.content: UE4SS, the script loader Wax runs on, as its own project released it, without the mods it brings (its console and cheat mods among them). The game loads `dwmapi.dll` from its own folder when it starts, and that file starts UE4SS.

10559.content: `Uninstall Wax.cmd` asks whether to remove it. By hand: delete both.

10561.content: Wax: Lua files in `Scripts`, pictures in `assets`, tables in `data`, two helper files in `bin`, and `Wax-Import.ps1`, which handles the **Add to game** button.

10562.content: `Uninstall Wax.cmd`. By hand: delete the folder.

10564.content: Your mods. None comes with Wax.

10565.content: `Uninstall Wax.cmd` asks first. By hand: delete a mod's folder.

10567.content: The settings of Wax and of your mods.

10570.content: Working files: the log of this session and of the one before, downloads while they are checked, and your answer about the **Add to game** button.

10573.content: Tells Windows that links starting with `wax://` go to Wax. Made only when you say yes at install.

10574.content: `Uninstall Wax.cmd` removes it. By hand: the line below.

10576.content: What the **Add to game** button did: one line with the time, the mod and the outcome for each `wax://` link that was opened. It stays on your PC, and it starts again when it passes 256 KB.

10578.content: The two helper files are small programs written in C, and their source is in the repository:

10579.content:
`bin\waxco.dll` lets a Lua task call the game and gives Lua a precise clock. It opens no files and no
connections. Source: `waxco.c`.

10580.content:
`bin\waxnet.dll` downloads updates and checks signatures. What Wax asks the network for
says what it can reach. Source: `waxnet.c`.

10582.content:
Nothing starts with Windows. Wax adds no service, no scheduled task and no start-up entry. It runs inside
ICARUS and only while the game runs.

10583.content: Nothing reports on you. Wax has no accounts, shows no adverts and sends no usage data.

10584.content:
Nothing else is written outside the game folder, with one exception that does not stay. While
`Update Wax.cmd` checks a download, it keeps it in a folder in your temp folder, and deletes that folder
afterwards.

10585.content:
The installer runs with your own rights. If Windows does not let your account change the game folder, it
says so and stops. It never raises its own rights.

10586.content:
The key holds one command: Windows PowerShell, in a window you can see, runs `Wax-Import.ps1` from Wax's
folder with the link. `Install Wax.cmd` asks before it makes the key, and Enter alone means no.

10587.content: To look at it, open a Command Prompt and type:

10589.content: To make it later, open a Command Prompt in the folder you extracted the zip to and type:

10590.content: Without the key everything else works. You download a mod as a zip and put it in the mods folder.

10591.content:
Steam lets every Windows account on a PC change the files of its games. Wax runs the Lua code in its own
folder, so the installer closes that folder to the other accounts.

10592.content:
After an install or an update, `ue4ss\Mods\Wax` can be changed by the Windows account that ran the installer,
by administrators and by Windows itself. Other accounts can read it and no more. Your mods and settings are
inside it, so they are covered too.

10593.content: The rest of the game folder stays as Steam made it. See What is not protected.

10594.content: Copying Wax in by hand changes no permissions.

10595.content:
A mod is Lua that runs inside the game with your rights. It can read and write your files, start programs
and use the network, like any program you run. There is no sandbox.

10596.content: This is what stands between you and a bad mod:

10597.content:
**A person looks at the catalogue.** A mod gets onto the Mods page in one of two ways. Its author
submits it, automatic checks run, and a person reads the code before it is listed. Or the author of Wax
publishes a mod of his own. Every new version goes the same way. Publish a mod has
the rules.

10598.content:
**Every listed version is signed.** The signature is made on the owner's PC, not on the server. Someone who
took over the server, or the site's address, could not make your PC put in a mod.
What is signed has the details.

10599.content:
**The button asks first.** When a `wax://` link is opened, a window on your PC shows the mod's name,
version and author, and asks whether to add it. No is the answer if you press Enter. Such a link can be on
any web page, which is why the question is asked on your PC and not on the page. The link carries the mod's
id and nothing else. The mod itself always comes from the Wax catalogue.

10600.content:
**A new mod is switched off.** Wax remembers which mods you have seen. A mod it has not seen is listed as
new and switched off, however it got into the mods folder: with the button, from a zip, copied by hand or
put there by another program. That is so when the game starts as well as while it runs. The mod runs after
you flip its **Enabled** switch on the Mods page of the Wax menu.

10601.content:
**An update is checked like the first copy.** A mod from the catalogue is only replaced by files whose
signed list is good, and the version before is kept in the mods folder.

10602.content: What this does not give you:

10603.content:
A signature says the mod is the one that was listed. It does not say the mod is harmless. A person read it
once, and that is not a promise.

10604.content:
A mod you copy in by hand is checked by nobody. Take such a mod only from someone you trust, or read it
first. A mod is plain text: open the `.lua` files in its folder.

10605.content: There is one signing key. It is an ECDSA key on the curve P-256, used with SHA-256.

10606.content: The public half, as 128 hex digits:

10607.content: Its fingerprint is the SHA-256 of those 64 bytes:

10608.content: The same fingerprint is in `README.txt` in the download and in the README of the repository. Compare them.

10609.content: The private half is on the owner's PC and nowhere else. It is not on the server and not in the repository.

10610.content: The server stores signatures and hands them out. It cannot make one.

10611.content:
The public half is written into the three things that check a signature: `Wax-Setup.ps1`, `Wax-Import.ps1`
and `bin\waxnet.dll`. No setting, file or parameter changes the key or the address they use.

10612.content:
Four kinds of text are signed. Each starts with a word that says what it is, so a signature for one kind
cannot be passed off as another.

10618.content: `release <version>`, then one line `<sha256> <size> <file name>` for each file

10619.content: `Wax-<version>.manifest` and `Wax-<version>.manifest.sig`, beside the zip on the release page

10621.content: The zip of one version of a mod

10623.content: `signature` of that version in `/api/mods/<Id>`, and the `X-Wax-Signature` header of the download

10625.content: The files of one version of a mod

10626.content: `mod <Id> <version>`, then one line `<sha256> <size> <path>` for each file

10628.content: Wax in the game, before it replaces a mod

10632.content: Wax in the game, before it updates itself

10633.content:
The texts are UTF-8 and every line ends with a line feed. Checksums are SHA-256 in small hex letters, sizes
are bytes, and the file lines are sorted. A signature is 64 bytes, `r` then `s`, written as base64.

10634.content:
After the signature is found good, the download itself is compared with the text: every file must have the
size and the checksum the text gives.

10635.content: Nothing checks the first Wax you download, unless you do. This is how.

10636.content:
From the release page, download three files
into one folder: the zip, and the `.manifest` and `.manifest.sig` files with the same version in the name.
Open PowerShell in that folder and paste this.

10637.content: It prints four lines. The fingerprint must be the one on this page, and the other three must say `True`.

10638.content: Releases older than 0.2.1 have no such list.

10639.content:
To check the zip of a mod, download it with **Download zip** on the Mods page. Then paste these
lines into the same PowerShell window, with the name of your file in the first line:

10640.content: In the game, one file talks to the network: `bin\waxnet.dll`. These things are fixed in its code:

10641.content: It reaches one address, `wax-icarus.duckdns.org`, over HTTPS.

10642.content: It only fetches. Every request is a `GET` for something under `/api/`.

10643.content: It follows no redirect and keeps no cookies.

10648.content: 20 seconds after the game starts, then every six hours, when a mod from the catalogue is installed

10649.content: `/api/versions`, the newest version of every listed mod

10650.content: To see whether one of your mods has a newer version. Prospector's Codex comes from the catalogue, so this happens in a new install.

10651.content: When one of them has a newer version

10652.content: The list of that version's files, then each file

10654.content: When you open the Browse page of the Wax menu, and again while it stays open once the list is five minutes old

10656.content: To show the catalogue in the game

10658.content: `/api/votes/mine`, the mods your internet address has voted on

10659.content: To show your own likes and dislikes, also the ones you cast on this site

10660.content: When you open a mod on that page

10662.content: To show what the mod says about itself

10663.content: When you press like or dislike there

10664.content: A ticket for that one vote, then the vote

10665.content: To count your vote. The catalogue keeps one vote for each mod and internet address, whether it came from the game or from this site

10666.content: When you press Add on that page and say yes

10667.content: The list of that version's files, then each file

10668.content: To add the mod. It stays switched off until you switch it on

10669.content: 30 seconds after the game starts, then every six hours

10671.content: To see whether Wax has a newer version

10673.content: The list of that version's files and the list of yours, then the files of the parts that differ

10674.content: To update Wax. The new version is put in when the game next starts. If it does not start, the version before is put back.

10675.content: What is sent with a request:

10676.content: The path, which names the mod and the version that is fetched.

10677.content: `Wax/` and the version of Wax, as the name of the program that asks.

10678.content: Your internet address, as with every connection.

10679.content:
Nothing else is sent: nothing about your PC, your Steam account, your saves or what you do in the game. The
list of versions is the same for everyone, so asking for it does not say which mods you have.

10680.content:
**Updates of one mod.** Open the Wax menu (F8), go to **Mods**, open the mod's card and switch off its
**Auto Update**. Wax then does not replace that mod by itself. It still asks the catalogue which versions are
out, so that the card can offer an **Update to** button. Every mod that came from the catalogue has this switch
on its own card.

10681.content:
**Asking the catalogue at all.** Switch off **Look for updates**, above the cards. Wax then asks the catalogue
nothing: not about your mods and not about itself.

10682.content:
**Updates of Wax.** Wax has a setting of its own for this, apart from the switches of the mods. It is on until
you switch it off, and no control shows it yet. Type this line into the command bar of the **Log** page and
press **Enter**:

10683.content:
Wax then asks nothing about itself and puts in no new version of itself. It remembers this the next time you
play. The same line with `true` switches it on again. A mod's **Auto Update** switch does not change it.

10684.content:
**Everything.** Take `waxnet.dll` out of `ue4ss\Mods\Wax\bin`. Without that file Wax in the game cannot use
the network at all. It says once in the log that the helper is missing, and everything else works. Installing
or updating Wax with the installer puts the file back.

10685.content:
`Update Wax.cmd` asks GitHub for the newest release of Wax, and only when you run it. It downloads from
`https://github.com/bostonstrong567/icarus-wax/releases/download/` and from nowhere else.

10686.content:
`Wax-Import.ps1` runs when you open a `wax://` link. It asks the catalogue for the mod's name, version and
author, shows them to you, and downloads the mod after you say yes.

10687.content:
The site loads nothing from other addresses and sets no cookies. It keeps your own votes in your browser,
and the catalogue counts a vote once for each internet address.

10688.content:
Wax watches one folder of its own, `run\in`, for requests from tools on the same PC. That is how
`Wax-Import.ps1` tells a running game that a mod was added.

10689.content: In a normal install the game takes two commands this way and nothing else:

10695.content: Looks at the mods folder again. A mod it has not seen is listed switched off. It shows one notification, and the words of it come from the mod's own files in the game, not from the request.

10696.content: It does not run code that arrives in that folder.

10697.content:
**Developer mode** is for people who write mods. It is on while a file named `dev.txt` stands in Wax's
folder, beside `Scripts`:

10698.content: With that file there, two more things work:

10699.content:
The game runs Lua that a tool writes into `run\in`. The play button of the VS Code extension and the
command-line tools in the repository work this way.

10700.content: The game reads `run\mods.index.lua`, a list of mods that are kept in folders outside the game.

10701.content:
Know what you switch on. In developer mode any program that runs as you can run code inside the game by
writing one file. Leave it off unless you write mods. The download never contains `dev.txt`.

10702.content: A copy of Wax with `dev.txt` also does not update itself in the game. `Update Wax.cmd` still works.

10703.content:
To switch developer mode on, make an empty text file with that name in that folder. To switch it off, delete
the file. Start the game again after either.

10704.content:
**A program that already runs as you.** It can change the game's files, Wax's files and your mods, and it
could do the same harm without Wax. Signatures are checked when something is downloaded, not every time
the game starts.

10705.content:
**The game folder outside Wax's own folder.** `dwmapi.dll`, the rest of `ue4ss` and the game's own files
keep the permissions Steam gave them. On most PCs every Windows account can change them.

10706.content:
**Windows does not know the downloads.** The zip, the three `.cmd` files, the scripts and the two helper
files carry no Windows code-signing certificate. So Windows may warn you when you run `Install Wax.cmd`,
and it cannot tell you who made the files. The signature on this page is Wax's own. It tells Wax's tools
that an update or a mod is the one the owner released, and Windows knows nothing of it.

10707.content:
**Virus scanners may warn about UE4SS.** It loads into the game the way a cheat would. Wax adds no such
technique of its own.

10708.content:
**The three `.cmd` files set PowerShell's script rule aside** for the one run they start
(`-ExecutionPolicy Bypass`). Without it Windows refuses a script that came out of a downloaded zip. It
changes no setting on your PC.

10709.content:
**The site's address is a free dynamic-DNS name.** `wax-icarus.duckdns.org` belongs to the DuckDNS
service, not to Wax. Whoever controls that service, or the owner's account there, could point the name at
another server. That is why nothing relies on the address for what gets installed: a mod or an update
from another server would not carry the signature and would be refused. A false site could still show
wrong instructions or a wrong download link. Get Wax itself from the release page on GitHub, and check it
by hand if you want to be sure.

10710.content:
**One key.** Everything rests on the private key staying on the owner's PC. If it were stolen, a new key
would need a new release of Wax that you install by hand.

10711.content: **The first download.** Nothing on your PC can check it before Wax is there. The steps above are the way.

10712.content:
Send it in private at
github.com/bostonstrong567/icarus-wax/security/advisories/new.
Only the owner of Wax sees a report made there. You need a GitHub account.

10907.content:
The game calls the store on the station the **Workshop**. `game.Workshop` reads it and can change parts of
it.

10908.content: Nothing here buys, researches or makes anything for the player.

10909.content: A **category** is one screen of the store, such as the axes. Its `Id` is a name like `"Workshop_Axes"`.

10910.content:
A **node** is one thing on that screen that can be researched and then made. Its `Id` is a name like
`"Workshop_Axe_Printed"`.

10911.content:
A node has two prices: `Research`, paid once, and `Replicate`, paid for each one made. A price is a table
from a currency to an amount, such as `{ Credits = 100 }`.

10912.content: A node can come after other nodes. With several, one of them bought is enough.

10913.content: A **joint** is a node of no size that shows nothing and sells nothing. It only joins lines.

10917.content: Reads the whole store ahead of time, a little each frame. Only inside a task.

10919.content: The categories, in the game's order.

10921.content: The nodes of one category, or of every category when you name none.

10926.content:
Call `Load` first. Without it, the first `GetNodes` reads the whole store in one call, which holds the game
up. With it, the store was read over 8 frames.

10927.content: A node is a plain table. These are the fields you will use most:

10933.content: The name of what it sells and the path of its picture.

10935.content: The item that is handed over, as `game.Items` names it.

10941.content: The middle of the node on its category's screen, and how large it is.

`GetNodes` builds its list anew each time. Keep what it returns, and ask again when `game.Workshop.Changed`
fires with `"store"`.

10949.content: `"bought"`, `"available"` or `"locked"` for a node. What it costs is not part of the answer.

10951.content: How many of a currency the account holds. Without a name, a table of them all.

10952.content:
`game.Workshop.Changed` fires with `"player"` when the player's side changed, and with `"store"` when the

This node and this key are what was tried in the game: its research price was changed, and the store's screen

The change belongs to your mod. It goes back when your mod unloads, or with `suit:Reset()`.

The store's screen pans sideways only. A category can be as wide as you like, and its height has to fit the

A category of your own. `game.Workshop:AddCategory` raises an error that says so. A node in one of the

The game makes its store when the player arrives on the station and keeps the nodes it found then. When a

10990.content: game.Data reads the game's own tables of recipes, items and creatures as plain Lua, and changes them for as long as your mod is loaded.

10996.content: What cannot be changed in this version

10997.content: What the game makes of a change

10998.content:
Nearly everything the game knows about its items, recipes, creatures and talents is kept in **data tables**.
`game.Data` gives them to you as plain Lua values.

10999.content:
A table is named as the game names it, with or without the `D_` in front: `"ProcessorRecipes"`,
`"ItemsStatic"`, `"Itemable"`. Letter case does not matter, and a wrong name raises an error that suggests
the right one. `game.Data:GetTables()` lists them all.

11007.content: `true` when the game has a table of this name.

11011.content: The name of every row, in the game's order.

11013.content: `true` when it has a row of this name.

11017.content: The fields of a row as the game declares them, with what each holds.

11018.content: A row is a plain table, shaped like the game's own data files with every default filled in:

11020.content: A struct is a table and an array is a list.

11021.content: A name, a string and a text are Lua strings. Text is in the language the game is showing.

11022.content: A reference to an asset, such as an icon, is its path.

11023.content: A **row handle** points at a row of another table. It is a table with `RowName` and `DataTableName`.

11024.content: `game.Data:Resolve(handle)` gives the row a handle points at:

11025.content:
A row is shared by every mod that reads it. Writing into it changes nothing in the game and confuses the
others. To change the game, use `Set` or `Change`, below.

11026.content:
Reading takes time: about 20 whole recipes fit in a millisecond. Rows are read once and kept, so the second
time costs nothing.

11027.content:
Name the fields you want and only those are read. A field path is a field's name, with a dot for each step
into a struct or an array:

11028.content:
To read many rows, use `Load` inside a task. It reads for a millisecond a frame and pauses, so
the game keeps running:

11029.content: `table:Loaded(fields)` says how far a `Load` has come.

11030.content:
`game.Data.Changed` fires when what you read may no longer hold: the game made a table again, or a mod
changed rows of it. Your function gets the table's name, or `nil` when everything was dropped. Work out
again what you kept from that table.

11031.content:
Some fields are a **map**: a table from keys to values, such as the stats a piece of armour gives. Others
refer to a **curve**, such as a creature's health by level. Both are left out of a row unless you name them.

11032.content:
A curve comes as a table with `First`, `Last`, `Values` and `Keys`. `Values` holds the curve's value at
`First`, `First + 1` and so on. For a creature's growth a step is a level:

11033.content: A map is read whole. A path cannot go on into it.

11034.content:
A struct or a list that you read with a map or a curve inside it cannot be handed to `Set` as it is.
Take that key out first.

11035.content:
Some maps cannot be read, such as one whose values are lists. Naming one raises an error that says what
it is.

11036.content:
`Set` gives one field of a row a new value in the game. It is written before `Set` returns, so whatever the
game reads from the row next is the new value.

11037.content:
This is the write that `game.Recipes` makes for `SetWork`. In the game the Stone Axe's row
read 3500 after it, where it read 2500 before, and a Stone Axe whose work was raised this way took longer to
craft. The tables that were written in a running game are the recipes and the store's. `Set` takes any table,
but whether the game reads a changed field again differs from table to table, so look at the result in the
game when you change another one.

11038.content:
`Change` works from the value the field has. Your function gets a copy and returns the new one. For a struct
or a list it may change the copy and return nothing.

11039.content: For recipes there is a shorter way to do this: Recipes.

11040.content: What to know about a change:

11041.content:
A field is changed whole. `field` is a field of the row, such as `"Inputs"`, not a path into one. The
value has every part of it: a struct with each of its fields, a list with each of its entries.

11042.content:
Everything is checked first. The row, the field, the kind of every value, and that a row handle names a
row its table has. What is wrong raises an error that names the place, such as `Inputs[2] lacks Count`, and
nothing is written.

11043.content:
It belongs to your mod. When your mod unloads, the field goes back to what it was. When your mod
reloads and makes the same change again, nothing is written twice.

11044.content:
`Set` replaces, `Change` builds. When two mods `Set` one field, the mod that loads later wins. Two
`Change`s both hold: each builds on the other, in the order the mods load. So prefer `Change` for anything
another mod might also touch.

11045.content:
The function you give `Change` must return at once. Wax keeps it and runs it again when an earlier
mod's change comes or goes, so it should depend on nothing but the value it is given.

11049.content: Gives a field a new value.

11051.content: Several fields of one row. All are checked before any is written.

11053.content: Changes a field from the value it has.

11055.content: Takes your mod's changes back: of one field, of a row, or of the whole table when you name nothing.

11057.content: What mods changed and still stands, with what each field was and is.

11059.content: The fields where one mod's `Set` hides another mod's different value.

11060.content: `game.Data.Patched` fires for each field of a row that was written, with the table, the row and the field.

11061.content:
`table:Add(name, values, { like = row })` adds a row: a copy of the row named in `like`, with your values
written over it. This is how a mod makes an item of its own.

11062.content: The name begins with your mod's id and an underscore, so two mods never add the same row.

11063.content: It is there at once. When your mod unloads the row stays in the table, and a recipe row is switched off.

11064.content:
A whole item is a row in several tables that point at each other: `ItemsStatic`, `Itemable`, `ItemTemplate`,
and the ones for what it does, such as `ToolDamage` and `Durable`. A recipe that makes it is a row of
`ProcessorRecipes` whose output names your `ItemTemplate` row.

11065.content:
This was tried once: six rows for a new tool, which was then given, held and used. It has not been tried
across a save and a restart. An item of a row that is gone, because the mod is off, has not been looked at.

11066.content: Text, references to assets, maps and a few rarer kinds of field. `Set` raises an error that says which.

11067.content:
A list can be made longer or shorter only when it is a field of the row itself, has 4 entries or fewer
before and after, and its entries hold no strings, text or lists of their own. Any other list keeps its
length: its entries can be changed where they are.

11068.content: A row handle cannot be pointed at another table than the one it names now.

11069.content: A row of the game is never removed.

11070.content: A table's meta table can be read, not changed.

11071.content: A change that is refused raises an error that says so, and changes nothing.

11072.content:
The game reads its tables at different moments. Some things follow at once, such as what a recipe costs when
its making ends. Others the game worked out earlier and keeps, such as a screen that is already open. Try
your change in the game, and look at what it changed.

11073.content: Every function is listed in the Game tables reference.

11075.content: Put your own labels and values on any object, and find the objects again later.

11077.content: Example: mark what you have seen

11081.content:
Tags and attributes store something about an object on the object itself. Use them to remember which trees
you already counted, or how often you visited a place.

11082.content: A **tag** is a label. An object has it, or it does not.

11083.content: An **attribute** is a named value: a number, some text, `true` or `false`, or a table.

11084.content: Wax keeps both. The game does not know about them.

11088.content: Marks the Instance with a tag.

11092.content: `true` when the Instance carries the tag.

11094.content: The Instance's tags, as a sorted list.

11096.content: Every live Instance that carries the tag.

11097.content: This tags every player's character, then counts the tagged ones.

11098.content: Save the file a few times. The number goes up, because attributes live through a reload of your mod.

11102.content: Stores a value under a name. `nil` removes it.

11106.content: A copy of every attribute, as a table of name and value.

11108.content: A signal that fires when that attribute changes.

11109.content: The signal for one attribute fires with the new value and the one before.

11110.content:
Call `GetAttributeChangedSignal()` with no name to get a signal for every attribute. That signal fires with the
name, the new value and the one before.

11111.content: Setting an attribute to the value it already has does nothing, and the signal does not fire.

11112.content: They live through a reload of your mod.

11113.content: All mods share them. Another mod can read a tag you set. Pick names that are your own, such as `mymod.seen`.

11114.content: They are forgotten when the map changes, together with the objects they were on.

11115.content: They are not saved. After a restart of the game they are gone.

11116.content: To keep something between game sessions, use `storage`.

11118.content: Wait, repeat and delay without freezing the game.

11127.content:
`init.lua` runs once, from top to bottom, and the game waits while it runs. So a mod can't wait in a loop
there. The game would freeze.

11128.content: A **task** is code that can pause. While it pauses, the game carries on.

11129.content: `task.spawn` starts a task. Inside it, `task.wait` pauses for a number of seconds.

11130.content:
The task runs until its first `task.wait`. Then the rest of `init.lua` carries on, so the `print` happens
while the countdown is still running.

11131.content: Put a loop in a task, with a wait inside it.

11132.content:
A loop without a wait never lets the game run. Wax stops any Lua code that runs for more than five
seconds without pausing, and logs a `script timeout` error. The game still freezes for those five seconds.

11133.content: `task.delay` runs a function after some seconds. The rest of your code does not wait for it.

11134.content:
`task.spawn` and `task.delay` give back the task. Pass it to `task.cancel` to stop it. A stopped task does not
start again.

An error ends only the task it happens in. The error goes to the log and shows as a notification. Your other

Only one piece of Lua runs at a time. A task runs until it waits or finishes, and no other task interrupts it

11162.content: Read the game's clock, the weather on your character and the prospect you are in, and hear when a player joins or leaves.

11168.content:
Three names tell you about the session you are in: `game.Time`, `game.Weather` and `game.Prospect`. Each
field asks the game when you read it, and is `nil` while you are not in a prospect.

11172.content: The hour of the game's clock, from 0 to 23.

11176.content: The time as text, such as `"7:05"` or `"19:30"`.

11182.content: The speed the game's clock is set to. 1 as the game sets it.

11183.content:
The game's clock does not run evenly. It runs faster at night. So read `Hour`, and do not work the time out
from seconds.

11184.content:
`game.Time.HourChanged` fires with the new hour and the one before. It is looked at twice a second, and only
while something is connected.

11185.content: The clock can be moved forward to a time later the same day.

11186.content: `game.Time:Set(hour, minute)` gives back `true` when the clock says that time afterwards.

11187.content:
The game's clock only goes forward within a day. An earlier time raises an error that says what the clock
shows. Going on to the next day is not in this version.

11191.content: The weather event your character is in, such as `"T3_Conifer_Rain"`. `nil` in clear weather.

11193.content: How heavy it is: 0 for the lightest up to 6 for the heaviest. `nil` in clear weather.

11195.content: `true` while your character is in weather of tier 1 or more.

11197.content: Every weather event running on the map. Only the host has it.

11198.content: The names are rows of the game's table `D_WeatherEvents`.

11199.content:
`game.Weather.Changed` fires when the weather on your character is another event than before. Your function
gets the new event and the one before, with `nil` for clear weather. It is looked at once a second.

11200.content:
`game.Weather.Active` is a list with one entry for each biome an event runs in: `Event`, `Biome`, `Tier`
and `Since`. It reads each of them, so do not read it every frame. It is `nil` when you are a guest in
someone else's game.

11201.content: Wax reads the weather. Starting or stopping it is not in this version.

11205.content: The prospect's name in the game's data, such as `"Tier1_Forest_Recon_0"`.

11207.content: The mission's name in the game's data, or `nil` when the prospect has none.

11211.content: How long the prospect has run, in seconds.

11213.content: How long it lasts in all, in seconds.

11215.content: `Duration` less `Elapsed`. `nil` when the game gives the prospect no duration.

11217.content: The game's own marks for an open world and an outpost.

11219.content: The game's id and seed for this prospect.

11220.content: `game.Players` has two signals for the session:

11221.content: The players are looked at once a second, and only while something is connected to one of the two.

11222.content: `Joined` does not fire for the players who are there when you connect.

11223.content: After `Left`, the player's Instance can no longer be used. You can still compare it with one you kept.

11224.content: Neither fires for what a map change brings or takes away.

11225.content: A player from `game.Players:GetPlayers()` or from `Joined` has three fields:

11229.content: The player's name. `nil` while the game has not said.

11231.content: `true` for the player who hosts the session.

11233.content: The character the player controls right now, or `nil`.

11234.content:
These two signals have only been run with one player in the session. A second player joining has not been
seen yet.

11235.content: Every field is listed in the Time, weather and the prospect reference.

11237.content: Get a signal when a value of the game changes, run code at a steady pace, or run it every frame.

11243.content:
Most of what a mod wants to know is a value that changes now and then. There are three ways to follow one,
from the cheapest to the most exact.

11247.content: You want to hear when one value of an object changes.

11249.content: You want to do something at a steady pace, such as refresh a window.

11251.content: It has to happen every frame, such as moving something smoothly.

11252.content:
`GetPropertyChangedSignal` gives a signal for one value of an Instance.
It fires with the new value and the one before.

11253.content:
The value can be a property of the game that holds a number, `true` or `false`, text or an object. It can
also be a field Wax gives the class, such as a creature's `Behaviour`.

11254.content:
Wax reads the value ten times a second, and only while something is connected. A change that is undone
between two reads is not told.

11255.content: An object arrives as an Instance, or `nil` when the property holds none.

11256.content: A wrong name raises an error that suggests the right one.

11257.content: Give a second value for another pace, in seconds:

11258.content: The pace is rounded to the nearest 0.05 seconds and can be as long as an hour.

11259.content:
It works on an actor in the world, such as a character or a creature, and on a part of an actor that one
of the actor's properties holds. On anything else it raises an error that says why.

11260.content:
Vectors, rotations, lists and maps of the game cannot be watched. A field of Wax that gives a table, such
as `Position`, can: it is compared by what it holds.

11261.content:
When the object is gone, reading stops and every handler is disconnected. A task that waits on the signal
with `:Wait()` is then not woken.

11262.content:
An Instance does not outlive a map change, so connect again on the new object, as the example does with
`game.Me.Spawned`.

11263.content:
For your own character you seldom need this. `game.Me` has ready signals for its
health, food, level and the rest, and they stay connected through a respawn and a map change.

11264.content:
Six watched values cost about 0.02 ms a frame when it was measured, and 68 values on 17 creatures about
0.06 ms. Nothing is read while no handler is connected.

11265.content: `task.every` runs a function again and again.

11266.content:
The first run comes after that many seconds, and each next one that many seconds after the run before
has ended.

11267.content: It never runs more than once a frame.

11268.content: An error is reported and the runs go on. After five errors in a row they stop.

11269.content: It gives back the task. `task.cancel` stops it, and it stops by itself when your mod unloads.

11270.content: It does the same as a loop with `task.wait` inside a `task.spawn`, in one line. See Tasks.

11271.content: `game.Frame` fires once every frame, with the seconds since the frame before.

11275.content: Calls `fn(seconds)` every frame. Gives back a connection.

11277.content: The same, for the next frame only.

11279.content: Pauses the task it is called in until the next frame, and gives back the seconds.

11280.content: `seconds` is 0 on the first frame Wax runs.

11281.content:
Each call runs as a task and may wait. A handler that is still waiting is called again on the next frame
all the same.

11282.content: The handler is disconnected when your mod unloads.

11283.content:
What you do here is done 60 times a second or more. Read a value or two and set a control. Do not search
the world, read tables or build windows in it. For anything that can wait a quarter of a second, use
`task.every`.

orderedDocs: "hand" (when omitted): a reach key adds to where the limb's end is. "shoulder": a key says where it is, forward, right and up of the limb's root, and the reach comes in from the game's pose and goes back to it.

"none": things pass through the part. "solid": things stop at it, which is what a mesh part does when nothing is said. "touch": things pass through and the blueprint's touched function hears of them. A shape from `game.Assets:Mesh` only stops things when it was made with collision = true.
"ready": the content is there. "restart": it is there, and some assets still show an older copy until the game is restarted. "off": the game does not have it, and Reason says why.
"Red", "#rrggbb" or \{ R = , G = , B = }. Red when omitted.
"ui" (the game's own interface font) when omitted.
"Wax" for Wax's own panel, else the id of a mod.
**`make(cell)`** builds one cell. The grid calls it once for each cell it needs, not once for each item.
**`show(made, item, index)`** fills a cell with an item. The grid calls it whenever a cell has to show another item.

**A new mod is switched off.** Wax remembers which mods you have seen. A mod it has not seen is listed as
new and switched off, however it got into the mods folder: with the button, from a zip, copied by hand or
put there by another program. That is so when the game starts as well as while it runs. The mod runs after
you flip its **Enabled** switch on the Mods page of the Wax menu.

**A person looks at the catalogue.** A mod gets onto the Mods page in one of two ways. Its author
submits it, automatic checks run, and a person reads the code before it is listed. Or the author of Wax
publishes a mod of his own. Every new version goes the same way. Publish a mod has
the rules.

**A program that already runs as you.** It can change the game's files, Wax's files and your mods, and it
could do the same harm without Wax. Signatures are checked when something is downloaded, not every time
the game starts.

**Add to game**, on the mod's page, asks first, then downloads the mod and checks it against the owner's signature. It arrives
switched off, as with the button on this site. Switch it on on the **Mods** page.

**An update is checked like the first copy.** A mod from the catalogue is only replaced by files whose
signed list is good, and the version before is kept in the mods folder.

**Asking the catalogue at all.** Switch off **Look for updates**, above the cards. Wax then asks the catalogue
nothing: not about your mods and not about itself.

**Bind and export.** Give every point of the model its bones, with a soft blend at each joint, and write an FBX
whose bones have the names and the turns of the game's skeleton.

**Changes as Lua** appears under both sides after your first change. It lists everything you changed here as
lines of Lua that do the same. **Copy** takes them for a mod, and **Clear** empties the list.
**Check now**, above the cards, asks the catalogue at once.
**Cook and load.** Build the pak, then `mod.Content:Load` and `SetModel`.

**Developer mode** is for people who write mods. It is on while a file named `dev.txt` stands in Wax's
folder, beside `Scripts`:

**Escape** closes the menu: everything that is up goes away. If a dropdown list is open, Escape closes that
first.
**Escape** puts the card back where it was. So does letting go outside the list.

**Every listed version is signed.** The signature is made on the owner's PC, not on the server. Someone who
took over the server, or the site's address, could not make your PC put in a mod.
What is signed has the details.

**Everything.** Take `waxnet.dll` out of `ue4ss\Mods\Wax\bin`. Without that file Wax in the game cannot use
the network at all. It says once in the log that the helper is missing, and everything else works. Installing
or updating Wax with the installer puts the file back.
**F8** shows and hides the Wax panel.

**F8** shows and hides this panel and nothing else. A mod's windows have a key of their own, which you
find on the mod's card of the Mods page. **Escape** hides everything that is up.
**Follow** keeps the newest line in view. Switch it off to read older lines.

**Import onto the game's skeleton.** In the Unreal project, import the FBX as a skeletal mesh and choose the
game's own skeleton asset for it. A copy of the skeleton in your mod's folder does not work: the creature's
animations only run on the one the game has.

**It undoes itself.** When your mod unloads, or on `creature:ResetModel()`, the creature has its own body
again. `creature.HasModel` says whether it wears one.
**Key poses, not a path.** A wind-up, the cut, the follow-through and a settle, each a whole pose.

**Look for updates** and **Check now**, above the cards, are for mods that came from the catalogue, and so is
the **Auto Update** switch on such a mod's card. Get mods says what they do.

**Look for updates**, above the cards, is the switch for all of it. Off, the catalogue is not asked at all,
and no mod is updated.

**One key.** Everything rests on the private key staying on the owner's PC. If it were stolen, a new key
would need a new release of Wax that you install by hand.

**Pick the animal.** Take one whose shape is close: two legs for two legs, four for four. Its skeleton decides
which bones your model can move, and its set-up row is what you pass to `SpawnMount`.

**Place the joints.** For each bone of that skeleton, mark where the same joint is in your model: hips, knees,
ankles, the line of the spine, the neck, the head. Lay them through the model as the animal stands in the
game, not as its skeleton lies at rest.

**Reshape to the bone lengths.** The game's animations carry the animal's own bone lengths. A leg that is
longer or shorter than the animal's gets pushed out at its joints. So stretch each part of the model evenly
between its two joints until the joints sit where the animal's are, and bind that shape.

**Tab** completes a name. Type `game.Ch` and a grey `aracter` appears. Press **Tab** to take it. Press **Tab** again for the next name that fits.

**The body leads.** Hips, waist and chest turn through the cut, each a little more than the one below. The
head turns the other way, so the eyes stay on what is hit.

**The button asks first.** When a `wax://` link is opened, a window on your PC shows the mod's name,
version and author, and asks whether to add it. No is the answer if you press Enter. Such a link can be on
any web page, which is why the question is asked on your PC and not on the page. The link carries the mod's
id and nothing else. The mod itself always comes from the Wax catalogue.
**The file compiles but fails when it runs.** The mod does not load.

**The file does not compile.** This happens when you save in the middle of a line, or when your editor saves
by itself while you type. Wax leaves the mod as it is: the version from before that save keeps running. The
mod's card on the Mods page says which line is wrong. It is not counted as an error.
**The first download.** Nothing on your PC can check it before Wax is there. The steps above are the way.

**The game folder outside Wax's own folder.** `dwmapi.dll`, the rest of `ue4ss` and the game's own files
keep the permissions Steam gave them. On most PCs every Windows account can change them.

**The mesh has to be on the creature's own skeleton.** A creature's animations belong to one skeleton. A mesh
built on another one would stand still, so `SetModel` refuses it and names both skeletons.
**The other arm moves against it**, and a step or a sinking of the hips goes with a heavy blow.

**The site's address is a free dynamic-DNS name.** `wax-icarus.duckdns.org` belongs to the DuckDNS
service, not to Wax. Whoever controls that service, or the owner's account there, could point the name at
another server. That is why nothing relies on the address for what gets installed: a mod or an update
from another server would not carry the signature and would be refused. A false site could still show
wrong instructions or a wrong download link. Get Wax itself from the release page on GitHub, and check it
by hand if you want to be sure.

**The three `.cmd` files set PowerShell's script rule aside** for the one run they start
(`-ExecutionPolicy Bypass`). Without it Windows refuses a script that came out of a downloaded zip. It
changes no setting on your PC.

**The tool leads with its edge.** Give the hand a turn at every key, so the blade is ahead of the handle the
whole way.
**Uneven timing.** Slow into the wind-up (`"out"`), fast through the cut (`"in"`), slow to settle.
**Update to** puts in a newer version of a mod you have.

**Updates of one mod.** Open the Wax menu (F8), go to **Mods**, open the mod's card and switch off its
**Auto Update**. Wax then does not replace that mod by itself. It still asks the catalogue which versions are
out, so that the card can offer an **Update to** button. Every mod that came from the catalogue has this switch
on its own card.

**Updates of Wax.** Wax has a setting of its own for this, apart from the switches of the mods. It is on until
you switch it off, and no control shows it yet. Type this line into the command bar of the **Log** page and
press **Enter**:

**Use the game's creature material.** A material built in the stock editor draws grey in ICARUS. Make yours a
material instance of the game's creature material and set its three pictures: `Color`, `Normal` and `MRO`.

**Virus scanners may warn about UE4SS.** It loads into the game the way a cheat would. Wax adds no such
technique of its own.

**Wax puts the model back.** The game writes a mount's own skin again now and then, a second after it appears
and whenever its looks are worked out again. Wax looks once a second and puts your model back on.

**Windows does not know the downloads.** The zip, the three `.cmd` files, the scripts and the two helper
files carry no Windows code-signing certificate. So Windows may warn you when you run `Install Wax.cmd`,
and it cannot tell you who made the files. The signature on this page is Wax's own. It tells Wax's tools
that an update or a mod is the one the owner released, and Windows knows nothing of it.

`#list` is how many, `list[1]` the first. `list:Each(fn)` calls your function with each recipe, and

`ActorState` still works. `game.Me` is the shorter way to the numbers.

`AddModifier` has been tried on a player's character. The game's table marks some modifiers as not for
creatures.

`All`, `At`, `Making`, `Using` and `Find` give a list of recipes. The list has every changing function too,
and does it to each recipe.
`animation:Play(target, options)` plays it and gives you the play.

`Attack` works on animals the game gives aggression, the hunters. On a deer or a rabbit it raises an error.
Nothing calls an attack off again. `Remove` takes the animal away.

`bin\waxco.dll` lets a Lua task call the game and gives Lua a precise clock. It opens no files and no
connections. Source: `waxco.c`.

`bin\waxnet.dll` downloads updates and checks signatures. What Wax asks the network for
says what it can reach. Source: `waxnet.c`.

`blueprint:GetThings()` lists the things of a blueprint that are in the world, and `blueprint:Count()`
counts them. `game.Blueprints:GetThings()` lists the things of every blueprint.
`blueprint:Spawn(position, rotation, data)` puts one in the world and gives you the **thing**.
`boolean` (`cut`) True when the text did not fit.
`boolean` (`ok`) True when the recipe's node is researched now.
`boolean` (`started`) False when the mount is in the middle of another move, or the game gives its kind no attack.
`cell` is a container. Add one control to it, and no more.

`Change` works from the value the field has. Your function gets a copy and returns the new one. For a struct
or a list it may change the copy and return nothing.
`character:HasModifier("Berry")` is `true` while a modifier of that name is on the character.
`character.HealthRegen` and `character.StaminaRegen` are two stats with a field of their own.

`character.HeldItem` is the stack in the hotbar slot that is in hand, and `character.HotbarSlot` is that
slot's number.
`character.Stats` is a table of the stats the game lists on the character, as name and value.
`collision = true` makes things stop at the shape. A character stood on such a slab when it was tried.
`Connect` gives back a **connection**. Call `Disconnect` on it to stop.
`container:Button(caption, on_click, options)` adds a button. `on_click` runs on each click.

`container:Console(options)` adds a scrolling box of text lines, such as a log. The user can drag across
the lines to select them, and copy with **Ctrl+C**.
`container:Dropdown(caption, choices, selected, on_change)` adds a list the user picks one choice from.
`container:Field(name, value, options)` adds a name with a value on the right. Use it to show facts.

`container:Flow(options)` adds an area where controls keep their own size. When a line is full, the next
control goes onto a new line.
`container:Heading(text)` adds a bold title line for a group of controls. `heading:Set(value)` replaces the text.

`container:Icon(name, options)` adds an icon on its own. Find names on the **Icons** page of the
Wax panel.

`container:Input(caption, options, on_commit)` adds a text box. `on_commit` runs when the user presses
**Enter**, or clicks somewhere else. Pass `nil` as the caption for a box without one.

`container:Keybind(caption, key, on_change)` adds a key the user can change. The user clicks the button,
then presses a key. **Escape** cancels.

`container:Label(text, options)` adds text. Long text wraps to the width of the container. In a
row a label is one line: see Text that has to fit.

`container:Model(options)` adds a box that shows a creature in 3D. `game.Creatures:GetModel(name)` gives what
the box needs for one creature. The creature does not have to be in the world.

`container:Progress(caption, value, options)` adds a bar. `value` goes from 0 (empty) to 1 (full). The
percentage is written beside the caption.
`container:Row()` adds a row. Controls you add to the row sit side by side and share the width.
`container:Section(title, options)` adds a card with a title. The user clicks the title to open and close it.

`container:Slider(caption, options, on_change)` adds a slider with a number beside it. The user can drag the
handle, or click the number and type a value.

`container:Slots(options)` adds a block of square cells that each show a picture, as an inventory does. It
works in a panel and in a window. Each cell shows a **look**: a table with a picture or an icon, and what
you want back when the cell is clicked.
`container:Spacer(height)` adds an empty gap. Leave the height out to get the theme's normal gap.

`container:Title(text, description)` adds a title for a whole page: large text, an optional line of
explanation, and a rule under it.

`container:Toggle(caption, initial, on_change)` adds a switch. `initial` is `true` for on. `on_change` gets
`true` or `false`.
`Count` looks at the inventory's own slots. It does not look inside a bag that lies in a slot.
`Count`, `Has` and `List` follow in the same frame. The weight follows a moment later.

`creature:SetModel(model)` gives a creature another skeletal mesh to wear, with its materials. The creature goes
on walking, running and being ridden as before.

`Duration` less `Elapsed`. `nil` when the game gives the prospect no duration.

`false` leaves out the small button that puts the view back.

`false` makes a plain titled group that is always open.
`false` makes a window the user cannot resize. It has no grip, its edges and corners do nothing, and it is always the size you give it. `window:SetSize` still works.

`false` reports the value once, when the mouse lets go. Use it when a change is slow to apply.
`false` stops Wax remembering where the user put the window.
`false` takes the creature away again when your mod unloads.
`false`: the wheel is left to the page.
`Fill` is how strong the fill is, from 0 to 1. `Width` is the line width, from 1 to 4.

`Find` goes by item names until `Load` has run. After it, `"iron"` also finds `Metal_Ore`, which the game
shows as Iron Ore. `Load` only works inside a task. It reads a little each frame and took
about half a second when it was measured.
`Find` goes through every item. Call it when the player types something, not every frame.

`game:FindAll` looks at every object in the game. Call it once and keep the answer for a while. Never call
it many times a second.
`game.Animations:Define(name, spec)` makes an animation. It is plain Lua until it plays.
`game.Animations:Find("1st sledge montage")` gives the paths that hold every word. The game has 4,091.
`game.Animations:Play(target, clip, options)` plays one of the game's montages or sequences.

`game.Assets:Material(parent, options)` makes a new material from one of the game's, with your colours,
numbers and textures set on it.

`game.Assets:Mesh(shape)` describes a shape: a box, or your own corners and triangles. It is plain Lua until
you put it on a part with `mesh:Apply`.
`game.Assets:Texture(file)` reads a `.png` or `.jpg` from your mod's folder and gives it as a texture.

`game.Character` is `nil` at the main menu and is a new object after every map change. `game.Me` is not an
object of the game. It finds your character each time you use it, so you can keep it and connect to its
signals once.
`game.Character` is `nil` when you have no character, for example at the main menu. Check before you use it.

`game.Creatures:GetKinds()` lists every kind in your version of the game, with how many of each are in the
world now. `game.Creatures:GetLiveKinds()` gives only the names of the kinds that are here.

`game.Creatures:GetModel(name)` takes a variant, such as `"Bear"` or `"Conifer_Wolf"`, or a kind, such as
`"Wolf"`. It gives the creature's mesh, its fur, its other pieces and its animations, read from the game's
own files when Wax was made.

`game.Creatures:GetTamed()` lists the tamed animals in the world: mounts, pets and livestock, whoever they
belong to. It takes a kind and the same options as `GetAll`. No tamed animal was in the world when this was
tested, so it has only been seen to answer an empty list.

`game.Creatures:Spawn(kind, place, options)` puts a new wild creature into the world with the game's own
spawn.

`game.Creatures:SpawnMount(kind, place, options)` puts a tamed animal into the world.
`kind` is the animal's set-up row, such as `"Mount_Moa"` or `"Mount_Horse"`, or a kind such as `"Moa"`.

`game.Creatures` is a list of every animal and enemy in the world. Wax keeps it up to date while you play, so
asking for it costs almost nothing.

again what you kept from that table.
`game.Data.Patched` fires for each field of a row that was written, with the table, the row and the field.
`game.Frame` fires once every frame, with the seconds since the frame before.

`game.Highlight` draws an outline round a thing in the world. The outline follows the shape of the model and
shows through walls and trees. It can also fill the model with a colour.

`game.Me.Character` is the character itself, as an Instance, or `nil`. Use it where a
function wants an Instance.

`game.Me` is your character by name. It has the numbers as fields of their own, and
signals that fire when they change. So the overlay needs no loop, and no check for the main menu or a new
map: `game.Me` finds the character each time, and its signals stay connected.
`game.Me` is your own character. You read its numbers by name, and it has signals that fire when they change.

`game.Recipes` is for the game's crafting recipes. You find a recipe by name, read it, and change it with one
call.
`game.Sounds:Find("whoosh bear")` gives the paths that hold every word. The game has 5,515 sounds.
`game.Time:Set(hour, minute)` gives back `true` when the clock says that time afterwards.

`game.Time.HourChanged` fires with the new hour and the one before. It is looked at twice a second, and only
while something is connected.

`game.Weather.Active` is a list with one entry for each biome an event runs in: `Event`, `Biome`, `Tier`
and `Since`. It reads each of them, so do not read it every frame. It is `nil` when you are a guest in
someone else's game.

`game.Weather.Changed` fires when the weather on your character is another event than before. Your function
gets the new event and the one before, with `nil` for clear weather. It is looked at once a second.

`game.Workshop:Category(id):Arrange(shape, options)` gives every node of a category a place in a shape:
`"line"`, `"grid"`, `"ring"`, `"arc"`, `"spiral"`, `"tree"` or `"path"`.
`game.Workshop:Check(store)` returns what is wrong with a description without putting anything in.

sickles, after the Larkwell sickle:

`game.Workshop.Changed` fires with `"player"` when the player's side changed, and with `"store"` when the
store's tables may read differently. Each of these calls asks the game, so call them when something is shown
or pressed, not every frame.
`game` is read-only. If you misspell a name, you get an error that suggests the right one.
`GetClassChain()` lists the class names from the object's own class up to `Object`.
`GetInfo` reads the game's tables for one kind or variant. The creature does not have to be in the world.
`GetModifiers()` gives a list, the modifier put on first at the front. Each entry is a table:

fires with `"store"`.

`GetPropertyChangedSignal` gives a signal for one value of an Instance.
It fires with the new value and the one before.
`GetStat` gives the value of one stat. A stat is named as in the game's table `D_Stats`.
`hud:Progress` adds a bar. `hud:Field` adds a name with a value. Each one gives back a control with a `Set` function.
`in_menu = true` in the options lets it run while the menu is open as well.
`index` is its place in the list.
`init.lua` is the code that runs, as in every mod. This is all of Session Clock:

`init.lua` runs once, from top to bottom, and the game waits while it runs. So a mod can't wait in a loop
there. The game would freeze.

crash the game. Most mods never need it.

`IsA(class_name)` is `true` when the object's class is that class, or is built on it.
`item` is the entry of your list to show.
`Joined` does not fire for the players who are there when you connect.
`key` is what `ui.Window` uses when you give it no `key` of its own.
`key` is what `ui.Window` uses when you give it no `key` of its own.

`kind` is a variant, such as `"Conifer_Wolf"` or `"Deer"`, or a kind that has only one. A kind with several

`loaded`, `switched off` or `failed`. A failed mod shows its error in red underneath.

Call them when your mod loads, inside a task, not every frame. Inside a task they pause after

hip). The reach comes in from the game's pose over the first moments and goes back at the end, so the keys
need no `{}` at the ends. An arm is about 60 long and a leg about 90. A place further off is reached as far
as the limb goes.

another mod might also touch.

0 for a joint, which Check leaves out. 250 when omitted.
0..1. Shows progress in place of the countdown and keeps the notification until closed.
1 leaves the size as it is.
1 to 10 short words that players can filter the list by.
100 is one metre, measured from the part's own place.
1920 by 1080 pixels is a good size. The card shows the cover in that shape and cuts off what does not fit.

A **blueprint** describes a kind of thing: which parts it has, what they show, and which of your functions
run for it. `blueprint:Spawn` then puts one into the world. No file is made: a thing is an actor of a class
the game already has, put together from your description.
A **category** is one screen of the store, such as the axes. Its `Id` is a name like `"Workshop_Axes"`.
A **control** is one thing in a window: a line of text, a button, a switch, a slider.
A **grid** shows a list of items in cells of the same size. It is made for long lists.
A **hotkey** runs your function when the player presses a key.
A **joint** is a node of no size that shows nothing and sells nothing. It only joins lines.

A **node** is one thing on that screen that can be researched and then made. Its `Id` is a name like
`"Workshop_Axe_Printed"`.

A **notification** is a short message in a corner of the screen. It shows while you play and goes away by
itself. It never takes the mouse.

A **panel** is an overlay whose controls take the mouse. `ui.Panel` makes one. It has no title bar and the
player does not drag it. Use it for something that stands beside the game's own screens, such as a list of
items next to the inventory.
A **problem** stops the submission. Fix it in the repository and submit again.
A **row handle** points at a row of another table. It is a table with `RowName` and `DataTableName`.

A **signal** is an event you can listen to. You connect a function to it. Each time the event happens, your
function runs.
A **tag** is a label. An object has it, or it does not.
A **task** is code that can pause. While it pauses, the game carries on.

A **theme** is the set of colours every window, overlay and notification uses. One theme applies to all mods
at once.
A **track** says what moves. It is named by a bone, or `Self` for the thing as a whole.
A **warning** does not stop it. The reviewer sees it too.
A `?` after a name means you may leave it out.
a `docs` folder at the top of the repository

A base class other than `"Actor"`. `base` takes another class by name, or a blueprint class of the
game by its path, and then the thing is that actor. Only `"Actor"` has been seen working.

A bench is named by the item that is the bench, such as `"Crafting_Bench"`, or `"Hand"` for what a player
makes without one.
A bench screen that is open is not built again. The crafting tab is.

A block of square cells that each show a picture, a count and a mark. Switched off with SetEnabled(false), its cells take no click, are not under the mouse for `ui.Hovered`, and show the arrow in place of the hand.

A block of square cells that each show a picture, as an inventory does. It is described with panels:
Slots.
A bold line above the text.
A bold line above the text.
A bold line of text above a group of controls. It is smaller than a Title and has no rule under it.

A bone is added to, not replaced: the game goes on animating, and your offsets come on top. So a swing you
write works while the character walks, and a creature keeps breathing under it.
A bone or socket of what it comes from.
A bone or socket of what it hangs on, such as "bn_Prop_R_1" for the right hand of the player's arms.
A bone or socket of what it hangs on.

A box around the part's place in the stead of vertices and triangles: the length of its sides, or one length for each direction. It has 24 vertices, four a side, so each side is flat and takes a whole picture.
A box that shows a creature of the game in 3D. It has its own page: 3D models.
A box the user types text into, with or without a caption.
A button with a caption fills the width. `false` makes it only as wide as its caption. An icon button is small. `true` makes it fill the width.
A button with a caption is as wide as its container. False keeps it as wide as its caption. An icon-only button is small unless this is true.
A button with a caption, an icon, or both. Made with `tab = true` it is one of a row of tabs.
A caption with its value under it.
A category of the store by its row name, to lay it out or to add nodes to it. A name the store does not have raises an error that suggests the nearest one.

A category of your own. `game.Workshop:AddCategory` raises an error that says so. A node in one of the
game's categories does work: see "A node of your own" below.
A category's row name, such as "Workshop_Axes".
A category's row name, such as "Workshop_Axes".
A cell wide enough to fill the window gives you one column: a list.

A change can come while something is being made. A new time counts from the next moment. What is taken
and what comes out is read when the making ends. If the player cannot pay the new cost then, the making is dropped
without a message and nothing is lost. So change recipes when your mod loads.
A change that is refused raises an error that says so, and changes nothing.
A change that is refused raises an error that says so, and changes nothing.
A changed file is read again after your mod reloads.
A character appeared where there was none, or the one that was there is gone.
A character or a creature. game.Me when omitted.

A character that lives again and dies again is told again. When a character leaves the world, the handlers
you connected to that Instance are disconnected.
A character, a creature, a thing of a blueprint or a part. game.Me when omitted.
A class name, for every mount.
A class of the game that has a member of its own by one of these names keeps it.
A click anywhere else closes the panel.
A clip only moves a skeleton it was made for.
A collapsible card. It is a container for controls.
A colour and fill that many outlines share. Changing it changes all of them at once.
A colour behind the model, or `true` for the theme's card colour.
A colour behind the model, or true for the theme's card colour. See-through when left out.

A colour for a material or a mesh: a name ("Red", "Orange", "Yellow", "Green", "Cyan", "Blue", "Purple", "Magenta", "Pink", "White", "Grey", "Black"), "#rrggbb" or "#rrggbbaa", or a table of values from 0 to 1, written \{ R = 1, G = 0.5, B = 0 } or \{ 1, 0.5, 0 }, with A or a fourth value for the alpha (1 when omitted).
A colour for each vertex, for materials that read it. The values go on as given, without the change to linear values that a material's colours get.
A colour in the linear form the engine uses. Make one with `ui.Color`.
A colour in the linear form the engine uses. Make one with `ui.Color`.
A colour in the linear form the engine uses. Make one with `ui.Color`.
