A colour in the linear form the engine uses. Make one with `ui.Color`.
A colour in the linear form the engine uses. Make one with `ui.Color`.

A colour is a name from `game.Highlight.Colors`, a string such as `"#ff7a00"`, or a table such as
`{ R = 1, G = 0.5, B = 0 }` with values from 0 to 1.
A colour of your own. Make one with `ui.Color("#RRGGBB")`, or take one from `ui.Theme()`.
A colour selector. It opens a panel with a shade box, a hue bar and the colour as text that can be typed, pasted or copied.
A colour the user can change.

A colour the user can change. The row shows the colour and its code. A click opens a panel under it with a box
of shades, a bar of hues, and the code as text.
A command can wait. `task.wait(2) print("later")` works.
A command that makes the folder and the first files of a mod.
A commit that is waiting for review cannot be submitted a second time.
A connected function runs as a task, so it may call `task.wait`. With `FireDirect` it may not.
A console shows the list you give it. To add a line, keep the list, add to it and call `SetLines` again:
A container whose controls sit side by side.
A copy of every attribute, as a table of name and value.
A copy of every attribute, as name -> value.
A copy of Wax with `dev.txt` also does not update itself in the game. `Update Wax.cmd` still works.
A creature appeared. It fires for creatures that appear from now on.

A creature has fields of its own, so you can read one value without `Describe`. Each asks the game when you
read it.

A creature is a character too. It also has `Health`, `MaxHealth`, `Level`, `Alive`, `Position` and the other
fields listed on Your character, and stats and
modifiers.

A creature killed by a player's hit, so what `Killer` names then has not been looked at. Poison named the
animal itself.
A creature left the world. `info.Reason` is `"Destroyed"` or `"Unloaded"`.

A creature or any other skeletal mesh of the game, drawn in 3D. It turns slowly by itself until the player touches it. The model follows the mouse when dragged: to the right its near side goes right, and down it is seen more from above. The wheel moves the camera nearer and further while the mouse is over the view, and the page does not scroll then. Two presses in a row put the view back. Nothing is drawn while the view is not on screen.
A creature was killed. Its body stays for a few seconds.
A creature. Nearly all are an `IcarusNPCCharacter`. A few bosses are an `IcarusPawn`.
A currency's row name, such as "Credits".

A curve comes as a table with `First`, `Last`, `Values` and `Keys`. `Values` holds the curve's value at
`First`, `First + 1` and so on. For a creature's growth a step is a level:

A curve of the game (a `CurveFloat`) as plain numbers, the way a field that refers to one is read. For a creature's health or damage a step is a level: `curve.Values[level - curve.First + 1]` is the value at that level. A curve with no keys has First 0, Last -1 and empty Values and Keys.

A dropdown opens in place under its header. The chosen row is highlighted, and only one list is open at a time. The header is always one line: a choice too long for it ends in "..." there and is whole in the list.

A few bosses are built differently in the game: their class is `IcarusPawn`, which is not a character. On
those, `Epic`, `Behaviour`, `Action`, `Target`, `Stance` and `IsFrozen` read `nil`, and they have none of the
character fields.

A few creatures do not show well in this version. The bee draws nothing, some large ones are cut by the box
where the view starts, and a few are too dark or too bright. Pieces that sit on another skeleton, such as an
ice mammoth's armour, are left out.
A few muted words after the title, such as a version.

A few UE4SS functions are switched off inside Wax mods, because they break the game's Lua state. Calling
one raises an error that says why.

A field is `nil` when the character has no such value. `game.Me:DistanceTo(target)` gives the metres to an
Instance or a position.

A field is changed whole. `field` is a field of the row, such as `"Inputs"`, not a path into one. The
value has every part of it: a struct with each of its fields, a list with each of its entries.
A field that two mods changed in ways that do not both show, as Conflicts lists it.
A file of another type fails the check. Take it out of the repository.
A file or folder of the mod, as `mod.Utils` or `mod.extras.Utils` gives it. Pass it to require.
A file runs once. A second `require` of the same file gives back the same value.

A first load stops the game until it is done. An item picture took 0.2 to 1 ms and a mesh 5 ms. Load when
your mod starts or a window opens, not in the middle of a fight.
A fixed height. As tall as its controls when omitted.
A flag a node asks for.
A folder with an `init.lua` in it is loaded by the folder's name: `require(mod.extras)` loads `extras\init.lua`.
A function that runs at its own pace: the seconds between two runs, then the function, as in every = \{ 0.5, function(thing, dt) end }.
A function that runs when it has run to its end.
A function that runs when the panel is pressed where it has no control.
A function that says where the panel goes on a screen of a given size. See below.

A game someone else hosts. A change is made in the tables on your PC only. The store is paid from each
player's own account, so the other players are expected to keep their own store.

A global variable you set in one mod is not seen by other mods. Two mods can both use the name `settings`
without clashing.
A glowing ribbon behind an edge that moves: `from` and `to` are the ends of the edge, `seconds` how long the ribbon is in time, `life` how long it runs.
A grid for any number of items: only the cells in view exist, and they are reused as it scrolls. It follows its scrolling while the menu is open, so it belongs in a window, not in an overlay.
A grid needs two functions from you.

A grid only builds the cells you can see. When you scroll, it reuses those cells for other items. Ten
items and ten thousand items cost about the same.

A grid shows a long list in cells of the same size. It builds only the cells you can see, so a list of
thousands of items is fine. It has its own page: Grid.
A grid that fills the page, with a search box

A hand that follows a path while the rest stands still looks like a puppet. When a swing for the player's body
was first made here that way, it was plainly wrong. What made it read as a swing:
A hotkey reacts during play, while the menu is closed.

A hotkey with a name. It runs callback when its key is pressed, like `ui.Hotkey`, and it is listed on your mod's card of the Mods page, where the player can give it another key. The player's choice is remembered and used the next time, so `key` is only where it starts. When two mods act on one key both still run, and the Mods page says which keys clash. Use it for every key a player might want to change.
A key for a mod with an interface
A key is given by its name, as text.
A key shows and hides your mod's windows and frees the mouse. See The menu.
A key that runs a function when it is pressed, as `ui.Hotkey` returns it.

A key that somebody else already has is yours all the same. A notification says who else has it, and the
card shows the clash until one of the two is changed.

A key that the Wax panel, another mod's windows or another mod's hotkey already uses is given all the same.
A notification says who else has it, and the card shows the clash until one of the two is changed.
A key the user can change: after a click on it, the next key pressed becomes the key. Escape leaves it as it was.
A key with Ctrl, Shift or Alt
A kind is named the way the game names it. These all work:
A kind of thing, as `game.Blueprints:Define` gives it. It is a description in Lua, not an asset of the game.
A label that is not in a row wraps onto more lines, as before.
A line of help shown beside the mouse once it has rested on the button. Give one to every button that is only an icon. A table is `{ title = "...", lines = { "more" } }`.
A line of text that stays over a creature, a player or anything else in the world.
A line of text that stays over something in the world.
A line or two under the title. Longer text is cut short.

A list can be made longer or shorter only when it is a field of the row itself, has 4 entries or fewer
before and after, and its entries hold no strings, text or lists of their own. Any other list keeps its
length: its entries can be changed where they are.
A list of every live object of a class.
A list of the characters those players control right now.
A list of the Instances directly under this one.
A list opens with its arrow and shows what is in it. The places of a list are shown, not changed.
A list with one Instance per player in the session (their player state). It works for the host and for clients.

A listed mod was read by a person once. That is not a promise that it is safe. It is also not a promise
that it still works after the game is patched. ICARUS is patched often, and a patch can break a mod until
its author updates it.
A little below and to the right of the window before it.
A log: coloured lines the user can select across (drag, Ctrl+A) and copy (Ctrl+C).
A look is a colour and fill that many outlines share. Change the look and every outline that uses it changes.

A look is a table, and you can write one yourself for any skeletal mesh of the game: `mesh` is its path, and
`materials`, `parts`, `walk` and `idle` are optional. A mesh that is not a skeletal mesh fires `Failed`.
A look to give to many outlines, so one call changes them all.
A loop inside `task.spawn` with a `task.wait` in it. `task.wait()` with no number waits one frame.

A loop without a wait never lets the game run. Wax stops any Lua code that runs for more than five
seconds without pausing, and logs a `script timeout` error. The game still freezes for those five seconds.
A map is read whole. A path cannot go on into it.
A material does not outlive the map. Make it again after `game.MapChanged`.
A material for a part that the blueprint makes for itself from one of the game's. It is made once, shared by every thing of the blueprint, kept for your mod, and made again after a map change.
A material of your own from `game.Assets:Material` in place of the plain glowing one.

A material of your own in place of the plain glowing one, from `game.Assets:Material`. A thing held in first person is drawn bent toward the screen by its material, and a trail only lies on it when its material bends the same way.

A material of your own, made from one of the game's, with colours, numbers and textures set on it, kept for your mod. `parent` is a material from Load or its path. A material that Material itself made cannot be the parent: start from the one it was made from. Every call makes a new material (0.2 to 0.7 ms), so make it once and keep it. The options are read through before anything is made, so a mistake in them raises an error and leaves nothing behind: a parent or a texture the call itself loaded by path is let go again. A material does not outlive the map: it is let go when the map changes, so make it again after game.MapChanged.
A material that `Material` made cannot be the parent of another. Start from the one it was made from.
A middle nearer than this to the canvas's left or top has part of its node outside: 125.
A mistake in the shape raises an error that names the entry.
A mistake while the thing is put together raises an error and leaves nothing standing.
A mod can add a page to the Wax panel. Use it for tools you need while testing.

A mod can ask for a key. For a mod that asks for none, Wax picks the first of F6, F9, F10, F11, F5, F4, F3
and F2 that no window and no hotkey uses, and a notification tells you once which it is.

A mod can ask for a key. For a mod that asks for none, Wax picks the first of F6, F9, F10, F11, F5, F4, F3
and F2 that nobody uses, and a notification tells you once which it is.

A mod can bring **game content** of its own: meshes, textures, materials, sounds and blueprints made in the
Unreal editor. They travel in one file in the mod's folder, `content/<Id>.pak`. Wax checks that file, hands it to
the running game and your Lua then loads from it by name. The game is not restarted, and no file of the game is
replaced.

A mod can have more keys, each with a name (`ui.Bind`). They
are on the same card and are changed the same way.
A mod is a folder with one file in it, called `init.lua`. Wax runs that file inside the game.

A mod is a folder, and you can lay it out as you like. `init.lua` stays at the top. Other files go beside it or
in folders of their own.
A mod is a folder. The folder name is the mod's **id**.

A mod is code that runs in your game. Once it is switched on it can do what any program on your PC can do.
A mod is code says what is checked for you and what is not.

A mod is code that runs inside other people's games. So a person reads every version before players can add
it.

A mod is Lua that runs inside the game with your rights. It can read and write your files, start programs
and use the network, like any program you run. There is no sandbox.
A mod is made of plain text files, so any text editor works.
A mod is turned down when:
A mod that calls `ui.Window` or `ui.Panel` names a key in `mod.lua`.
A mod that makes a window names the key that shows it, and a mod that makes a panel or has other keys names those:
A mod that makes a window names the key that shows it, and a mod that makes a panel or has other keys names those:

A mod that needs another mod still loads after it. If you put it before that mod, the card goes back and a
notification says why.

A mod that needs one of them says so in its description, with the reason. Settings belong in
`storage`, which needs none of these.
A mod that passed the checks waits for review. It is listed after a person has looked at it.
A mod that uses it does two things. It lists the id under `dependencies`:

A mod that Wax has not seen before is listed switched off. Open the **Mods** page of the Wax menu and flip
its **Enabled** switch. This is so whether the folder was put there while the game ran or while it was
closed.

A mod Wax has not seen before is listed as **new** and switched off. Flip **Enabled** to load it. This is so
whether the mod was added while the game ran or while it was closed.

A mod whose code calls `ui.Window` or `ui.Panel` must name a default key in `mod.lua`: `key`, or at least one
line in `keys`. A mod with an interface and no key is refused, and the check says which file makes the window.
The reason is the player: the key is on the mod's card before they switch the mod on, they can change it there,
and Wax tells them when it is the same key as another mod's.

A mod whose whole layout depends on the screen can also load itself again. `mod.Reload()` does that at the
start of the next frame, the way saving a file does:
A mod with a window or a panel has `key` or `keys` in `mod.lua`.

A mod you already had keeps the state it had. The copy from before is kept, as described under
Manage your mods.

A mod you copy in by hand is checked by nobody. Take such a mod only from someone you trust, or read it
first. A mod is plain text: open the `.lua` files in its folder.
A mod you publish must name a key when it has a window or a panel.
A mod you switched on stays on. It loads by itself the next time the game starts.

A mod you wrote or copied into the mods folder yourself is never changed, even when the catalogue has a mod with
the same name. Wax only updates a folder that holds a `wax.origin` file, which **Add to game** writes.

A mod's **Auto Update** switch is about that mod only. Updates of Wax itself have a setting of their own:
Switching it off says how to change it.
A mod's key is on its card of the **Mods** page of the Wax panel, as **Show / hide**.

A model can have up to 65,000 vertices and the file up to 16 MB. A larger one belongs in a mod's
game content.

A model view can play your animation on a mesh in a window, where you can turn it and see it
from every side. `view:Play(animation, options)` takes the same options as `animation:Play`.
A modifier a mod put on stays for its time when the mod unloads.
A name for it in what Check says. "Place 3" when omitted.
A name for the key that stays the same between versions, such as "Open". One mod cannot have two of one name.
A name from game.Highlight.Colors, "#rrggbb", or values from 0 to 1. "Red" when omitted.

A name in `keys` is the name you give `ui.Bind`:
`ui.Bind("Show or hide the pins", nil, fn)` takes the key from `mod.lua`.

A name in `keys` is the name you give `ui.Bind`:
`ui.Bind("Show or hide the pins", nil, fn)` takes the key from `mod.lua`.
A name or a piece of text
A name that is no creature raises an error.
A name with a value at the right, for read-outs. The user cannot change it.
A name, a string and a text are Lua strings. Text is in the language the game is showing.
A named key of your mod, as `ui.Bind` returns it.
A named key. `name` stays the same between versions of your mod.

A new `Behaviour` counts from the next time the animal notices somebody. An animal that is already
attacking goes on attacking after `"Friendly"`.

A new category for the calling mod's store, to add nodes to. In this version of Wax it checks the names of its options and then raises "a new category is not switched on in this version of Wax": a category's name is text and its picture a reference to an asset, and game.Data does not write those yet.
A node can come after other nodes. With several, one of them bought is enough.

A node has two prices: `Research`, paid once, and `Replicate`, paid for each one made. A price is a table
from a currency to an amount, such as `{ Credits = 100 }`.
A node is a plain table. These are the fields you will use most:
A node of the store by its row name, to change it. Any node the store has can be named, whichever mod added it. A name the store does not have raises an error that suggests the nearest one.
A node that needs all of several nodes. The game only knows "one of".
A node, a list of nodes of which one is enough, or the long form. A node is named by its id in this store, or by the row name of one of the game's nodes.
A node's row name, such as "Workshop_Axe_Printed".
A node's row name, such as "Workshop_Axe_Printed".
A normal variable is lost every time your mod reloads. Wax gives you two ways to keep things.
A number from 0 to 1. It shows a progress line, and the notification stays until it is closed.
A number or a true/false value

A page has a signal called `NearEnd`. It fires when the user scrolls close to the bottom. Use it to add
more as the user scrolls.
A page in the page list
A page of a window that has navigation. It is a container for controls.
A page or group title: large text, an optional line under it, and a rule.

A pak is for what Lua cannot make from a file: a blueprint with logic of its own, a material built in the
editor, an animated or very large model, a sound set. Those are made in the Unreal editor, version 4.27, which is
a separate download of about 19 GB from Epic Games. ICARUS itself does not come with it: a game holds the part of
Unreal that plays content, not the editor that makes it.
A panel in the game lists your mods, shows the log and runs a line of Lua. See The Wax panel.
A panel made with a `place` function got another size. New in Wax 0.3.0.
A panel pinned to the screen that stays up during play and never takes the mouse.
A panel takes the options of an overlay, and these:
A panel that follows the screen
A panel that stays on screen while you play.
A part can show a shape made of numbers in place of a mesh of the game:
A particle effect that was started.

A path is written `"/Game/Folder/Name"` or `"/Game/Folder/Name.Name"`. The form the Unreal editor copies,
`Texture2D'/Game/Folder/Name.Name'`, works too. A blueprint's class is `"/Game/Folder/BP_Thing.BP_Thing_C"`.
Letter case does not matter.

A person reads the mod's code and its description, and looks at its pictures. This is done by hand, so there
is no fixed time for it.

A picture file as a texture, kept for your mod. The file is a .png or .jpg in your mod's folder, named from that folder ("logo.png", "pictures/logo.png"), or a whole path. Asked again, the same texture comes back and no file is read. A small picture took about half a millisecond. The first JPG of a session took 3.7 ms. It raises an error when the file is not there, is not a PNG or JPG picture, or leaves the mod's folder with "..", and for a bare file name while no mod is running. A file that changed on disk is read again once everything that asked for it has let it go, which reloading your mod does when no other mod uses the file.
A picture of the game by its path, such as an item's icon.
A picture only: no box, and the mouse passes over it.
A piece of text. It wraps to the width of its container. In a row it is one line: text too long for its share is cut short with "..." and shown whole as a tip while the mouse rests on it.
A place for a node: its middle. Neither number can be further than 1000000 from 0.

A plain key gives way to the same key with Ctrl, Shift or Alt. If `"Three"` and `"Ctrl+Three"` are both hotkeys,
pressing 3 while Ctrl is held runs only the second.
A player from `game.Players:GetPlayers()` or from `Joined` has three fields:
A player's character has six inventories:
A player's death. `game.Me.Died` has only run in tests outside the game.
A player's PC checks the signature before the mod is put in, and again before every update.
A position in the engine's units, or an actor or game.Me to go to.
A press that a hotkey of your mod takes is not also taken as the key of your windows.

A price: how many of each currency. A key is a currency's row name in D_MetaCurrency, as in `{ Credits = 100, Exotic1 = 25 }`. An amount is a whole number from 0 to 2147483647, the largest the game's field keeps.
A progress bar, with its caption and the value as a percentage on a line above it.
A reach on the arms seen in first person. On the body it was measured.
A reach that also turns the end of the limb.

A recipe is named by its row in the game's table `D_ProcessorRecipes`. It often has the name of the item
it makes, but not always, and some items have several recipes. `Making` finds them all.
A red message tells you what is wrong, and on which line.
A red notification shows the error.
A red notification shows the first line of the error.
A reference to an asset, such as an icon, is its path.

A registered picture is used by its name anywhere an icon name is taken. Use a PNG. Give the name a prefix of
your own so it does not clash with another mod's.

A removed mod is not erased. Its folder is renamed so that it starts with `.removed-`, and Wax leaves folders
with such names alone. To get the mod back, rename the folder to the mod's name again.
A request to draw the game's own menus smaller.
A resource cannot be added or taken away. How much of a resource a recipe takes can be changed.
A row handle cannot be pointed at another table than the one it names now.
A row handle: the two names many fields hold to point at a row of another table.
A row is a container too. `row.control` is the row itself, for `SetVisible`, `SetEnabled` and `Destroy`.
A row is a plain table, shaped like the game's own data files with every default filled in:

A row is shared by every mod that reads it. Writing into it changes nothing in the game and confuses the
others. To change the game, use `Set` or `Change`, below.
A row of the game is never removed.

A row with a small arrow has things inside it. Click the arrow to open the row. Click the row itself to pick
it.
A saddle as it fits one tamed animal: a row of the table D_Saddles.

A saddle goes into its saddle slot. That is what makes the game give a mount its seat. Without a saddle the
game does not offer to ride it.

A saddle the mount wears in the picture: the row of its item ("Saddle_Standard"), its tag ("Item.Mount.Saddle.Standard") or its own row in the game's saddle table ("Saddle_Horse_Standard"). The saddle is added to the model's parts as the game's table describes it for that mount: its mesh, its other material, the blueprint it follows the mount by and the socket it sits on. Where the game hides the mount's fur under that saddle, the fur gets the same mask. The second saddle the game shows under a cart is not added.
A scrolling list of cells for hundreds or thousands of items.
A search box uses `Typed`, so the list updates with every letter:
A second value from 0 to 1 makes it see-through. 0 is invisible and 1 is solid.
A section is a container. Add controls to the section, as you would to a window.

A shape made of numbers, as `game.Assets:Mesh` gives it. It is plain Lua and holds nothing of the game, so it can be kept for as long as you like and put on any number of parts. Its fields cannot be changed: make another mesh.

A shape made of numbers, checked through: a box, or your own vertices and triangles. Nothing is asked of the game until the mesh is put on a part with mesh:Apply. A mistake in the shape raises an error that names the entry.
A short line of that colour under the picture.
A short name for the kind of problem, such as "id-twice" or "off-screen".
A signal for one attribute, fired with (value, previous). Without a name it covers every attribute and fires with (name, value, previous).

A signal for one value of the object: a property of the game's that holds a number, true or false, text or an object, or a field Wax gives the class. It fires with (value, previous) when the value is found changed. The value is read ten times a second, and only while a handler is connected. An object arrives as an Instance, or nil when the property holds none. A table a field returns is compared by what it holds. `seconds` sets another time between reads, up to 3600. It is rounded to the nearest 0.05, and anything under 0.05 counts as 0.05. When one value is asked for at two paces, the faster is used. It works on an actor in the world and on a component that a property of its actor holds. Anything else raises an error that says why. When the object is gone, reading stops and every handler is disconnected. A task that waits on the signal is then not woken. A wrong name raises an error that suggests the right one.
A signal that fires when that attribute changes.
A signal that fires when the world changes.
A signal that fires with the new key of the Wax panel.
A signal that fires with the new key.
A signal that fires with the owner and the new key.
A signal that fires with the theme's name after it changes.

A signature says the mod is the one that was listed. It does not say the mod is harmless. A person read it
once, and that is not a promise.
A slider. The number beside it can be clicked and typed into.
A slot holds something else than a frame before.

A slot that holds something is never taken, nor any slot before it. The inventory then keeps as many slots
as it needs, and the second value says so: `"slot 31 holds something, so 31 slots stay"`.
A small icon in the upper left corner.
A small panel appears in the top left corner of the screen. That is the overlay.
A socket or a bone of the first mesh the part sits on, such as "RaptorSaddle". Left out, it sits on the mesh itself. A part on a socket is not counted when the model is fitted to its box.
A sound cannot be stopped once it plays.
A sound that comes from a thing.

A stack is a plain table: `Item`, `Count`, `Slot`, `Durability`, and `Properties` with every number the game
keeps for it. Changing the table changes nothing in the game.
A stack is the same table that inventories give.

A stack that only moves from one slot or inventory of your character to another is not added and not
removed. It is a change of both slots.

A store as a mod describes it. `game.Workshop:Check` says what is wrong with it, and `game.Workshop:Define` puts it into the game. A node added to one of the game's categories (`into`) shows there with its picture, price and line. When that happens while the player stands in the store, Wax has the game build its store again, so the node can be bought at once, and it goes again when the mod is switched off. What the account has researched is kept by the game under the node's row name, so it is still there after the mod was off for a while. A new category of a mod's own is not switched on in this version.
A struct is a table and an array is a list.

A struct or a list that you read with a map or a curve inside it cannot be handed to `Set` as it is.
Take that key out first.
A structure, such as a position

A switch can be given another caption later, and be set without its sliding animation. Both are for a row
that is reused to show something else:
A switch that is on or off, with a caption beside it.
A table by name, with or without the "D\_" in front. Letter case does not matter. A wrong name raises an error that suggests the right one.

A table is named as the game names it, with or without the `D_` in front: `"ProcessorRecipes"`,
`"ItemsStatic"`, `"Itemable"`. Letter case does not matter, and a wrong name raises an error that suggests
the right one. `game.Data:GetTables()` lists them all.
A table's meta table can be read, not changed.

A tag is a line of text that sits over something in the world and follows it. It shows while you play, not
only when the menu is open.
A tag must match the version in `mod.lua`. The tag `v1.2.0` goes with `version = "1.2.0"`.
A tag removes itself when the thing it is on leaves the world, and when your mod reloads.
A taming rule of the game: a row of the table D_Tames.
A theme colour for the icon and the value. The usual colours when omitted.
A theme colour the icon and the caption are drawn in while SetActive(true) holds.
A theme colour. The muted text colour when omitted.

A thing also has everything its actor has: `thing.Name`, `thing:IsA("Actor")`, and the actor's own
properties and functions.

A thing in the world: an actor that a blueprint spawned. It has the names below, and beyond them everything its actor's Instance has: thing.Name, thing:IsA("Actor"), thing:K2_GetActorLocation(), the class's own properties and functions. None of the names below is a member of any actor class of the game, so a thing hides nothing of its actor. A thing is not an Instance itself: where a function wants one, give thing.Actor. Once the thing is gone, everything but Data, Blueprint, Alive, IsValid and Destroy raises an error that says why.
A thing is made of **parts**. A part is a component of the game with what it shows and where it sits.
A thing of a blueprint, a part, a character or a creature.
A thing of a blueprint, or a part
A ticket for that one vote, then the vote
A tool comes new, with its full durability.

A tool outside the game, such as the play button of the VS Code extension, can only run Lua
in the game in developer mode. A normal install does not take Lua from outside.
The bridge and developer mode says how to switch it on and
what that allows.
A tool that wore is a change. A spoil timer that only counts down is not.
A track is a list of **keys**: a time in seconds, then what is added at that time.

A trail is laid on a curve through the places the edge was at, so a fast swing leaves an arc, not corners. It
keeps the edge's outer end (`to`) and closes in on it toward its old end, which gives a crescent.
A true-or-false member has a switch at the end of its row.

A turn is about the character's own directions, whichever way the bone points: `Yaw` about up (positive
turns right), `Pitch` about the character's right (negative leans forward), `Roll` about forward.
A value in colour is another object. Click it to go to that object.
A value that could not be read says so, and Wax leaves it alone.

A vector, a rotator or a colour opens when you click it, and each part is a row of its own that you change
like a number. Its arrow closes it again.
A version can be published once. You cannot replace `1.2.0` with other code.

A version is one commit of your repository. Mark it with a git tag: the letter `v` and the version from
`mod.lua`.
A version that needs a newer Wax than yours is left out until you update Wax.
A view made without a mesh shows nothing until you call `Show`.
A view that shows is drawn again every frame. One view 256 wide cost about half a millisecond a frame.
A wait is never shorter than one frame, even `task.wait(0)`.
A web address with more about the mod. The mod's page links to it.

A whole item is a row in several tables that point at each other: `ItemsStatic`, `Itemable`, `ItemTemplate`,
and the ones for what it does, such as `ToolDamage` and `Durable`. A recipe that makes it is a row of
`ProcessorRecipes` whose output names your `ItemTemplate` row.
A whole number of 1 or more.
A whole number of 1 or more.
A whole number of 1 or more.
A whole run takes about half an hour.

A window in the menu. Controls added to it go into its body, or into a first page called "Main" when it has pages. The player moves it by its title bar and resizes it by any edge or corner; the bottom right corner shows a grip. Resizing stops at the window's minimum size and at the edges of the screen. A mod's windows come up together, with that mod's key (see ui.Keys), and other mods' windows stay as they are.
A window is a box in the menu that holds your controls.
A window is removed when your mod reloads. `init.lua` then makes it again.
A window is shown or hidden.

A window of Wax opens on your PC. It shows the mod's name, version and author and asks whether to add it.
Nothing has been downloaded yet. If you say no, nothing happens.
A window rolled up to its title bar cannot be resized.
A word or two in a small pill at the right end.
A word or two shown in a small pill at the right end of the title, such as "New" or "Off".
A wrong name raises an error that suggests the right one.
A young animal beside its parent

Accepting a version signs it. The reviewer's tool fetches the zip that was checked, works out its checksum
itself and signs two things with Wax's key: the zip, and the list of the files in it. The key is on the
reviewer's PC and never on the server.
Account flags the player must have: row names of D_AccountFlags.
Add a theme of your own
Add this below the code above. It shows one warning each time your health drops under a quarter.

Adding a new recipe is not possible yet. `game.Recipes:Add` is there and raises an error that says it
is switched off.
Adds a bench to where each recipe of the list is made, as `Recipe:AddBench` does for one. The recipes that are made there already are left as they are.
Adds a bench to where the recipe is made. It does nothing when the recipe is made there already.
Adds a block of square cells for pictures, such as items. Give it looks with Set.
Adds a box that shows a creature or any other skeletal mesh of the game in 3D. Give it what `game.Creatures:GetModel` gives, or a mesh by its path.
Adds a button. on_click runs on each click. With an icon and no caption it is an icon button.
Adds a button. The function runs each time you click it.
Adds a caption with its value under it. Several in a Flow make a line of facts.
Adds a card to press: a title, a line of text, small counts and a badge, over a faded picture when it has one.
Adds a collapsible card and returns it as a container: section:Button(...), section:Toggle(...) and so on.
Adds a dropdown that opens in place. on_change(choice) runs when the user picks one. With nil for the caption the dropdown takes the whole width, or its whole share of a row.
Adds a grid for any number of items. It builds only the cells in view, with the `make` and `show` functions in `options`.
Adds a key the user can rebind by clicking it and pressing a key. on_change(key) gets the engine's key name.
Adds a name with a value beside it.
Adds a name with a value on the right, for read-outs.

Adds a node to the category, as a node of a described store. In this version of Wax it checks that it was given a table and then raises "adding rows to the game's tables is not switched on in this version of Wax".
Adds a page and gives it back.
Adds a page and returns it. Add controls to it as you would to a window.
Adds a page to a window made with nav = "side" or "top". The first page added is selected.
Adds a page to the debug panel for the calling mod. The page is removed when the mod reloads.
Adds a picture from a .png or .jpg file, in the shape the picture has. With nil for the file it shows nothing until Set is called.
Adds a place, or takes one away.
Adds a progress bar. value is 0..1.

Adds a recipe: a copy of the recipe `options.like` names, changed by the other options. `game.Recipes:Add("MyMod_Quick_Axe", { like = "Stone_Axe", inputs = { Stone = 1 }, seconds = 1 })`. The name begins with the mod's id and an underscore. It is switched off in this version of Wax and raises an error that says so: adding a row to the game's tables while the game runs has not been seen working yet.

Adds a row: a copy of the row `options.like` names, as that row is now, with `values` written over it as Set would. Returns the row's name. The name is letters, digits and underscores and begins with the mod's id and an underscore, such as "MyMod_Quick_Axe". A character of the id that is none of those counts as an underscore. The game's own index of the table is renewed, so the game knows the row at once. The row belongs to the mod that added it, and Add again for the same row uses the row that is there. When the mod unloads, what it wrote into the row is put back and the row stays in the table, because a row is not taken out while the game runs. A recipe is switched off then: bForceDisableRecipe is set and it is on no bench, which takes it off the game's lists. The game still makes it when something asks for it by name. A row of another table is left as it is. A row that could not be switched off like that in this version is refused as the row to start from, with an error that says why. A row of the game is never replaced or removed. While adding rows is switched off in a version of Wax, Add raises an error that says so.
Adds a row. Controls added to the returned container sit side by side and share the width.
Adds a scrolling list of text lines, such as a log.
Adds a slider with a read-out. on_change(value) runs while the user drags it.
Adds a status line along the bottom of the window, or returns the one the window already has. `text` sets its message.
Adds a switch. on_change(on) runs when the user flips it.
Adds a switch. The function runs each time you flip it. `on` is `true` or `false`.
Adds a text box. on_commit(text) runs when Enter is pressed or the box loses focus.
Adds a theme: a table with any of the colour settings (window, panel, raised, text, accent ...) as "#RRGGBB".
Adds a title for a page or a group of controls: large text, an optional explanation, and a rule under it.
Adds a word or two in a small pill, such as "New" or a tag.
Adds an area where controls keep their own size and wrap onto new lines. Add them to the returned container.
Adds an empty gap, as tall as the theme's spacing when no height is given.
Adds an icon from a PNG file. White on transparent works best, because the icon is tinted when drawn.
Adds an icon on its own, by name. The menu's Icons page lists the names.
Adds an icon with a number or a word beside it, such as a count of downloads.
Adds one line of a list or a tree: an arrow, an icon, a name, a note and a value. In a grid it makes a list of any length.

Adds text. It wraps to the container's width. In a row it does not wrap: each line of the text is one line in the label's share of the row, cut short with "..." when it is too long, and shown whole as a tip.
Adds two areas side by side. Add controls to its Left and Right.
Adds Wax's own settings (the key of its panel, theme, accent, animation, size) to a container, such as a "Settings" page.
After `Left`, the player's Instance can no longer be used. You can still compare it with one you kept.
After `Removed`, the creature can no longer be used. You can still compare it with one you kept.
After a dot, **Tab** lists what is there. Type `game.` and press **Tab**. The log lists the names you can use.

After a map change an Instance from before answers with an error. Call `Load` again, which costs little
because the asset is still kept.
After a reload your mod is in the same state as after a new start. Local variables start again too.

After an install or an update, `ue4ss\Mods\Wax` can be changed by the Windows account that ran the installer,
by administrators and by Windows itself. Other accounts can read it and no more. Your mods and settings are
inside it, so they are covered too.

After that it is an ordinary mount of the game: the game's own prompt to ride it works, it follows you, and it is
saved with the prospect.

After the signature is found good, the download itself is compared with the text: every file must have the
size and the checksum the text gives.
All `stepped` and `every` functions together get 2 ms of a frame. What is left over waits a frame.
All mods share them. Another mod can read a tag you set. Pick names that are your own, such as `mymod.seen`.

All of it was run on the host of a prospect: a sound, a shake, sparks and a light on the player's hand, a clip
of the game, an animation of keys on the arms and on the body with the clothing following, and a spawned cube
turning with a trail behind it. These have not been looked at yet:
All of them are whole numbers, except `IsAlive()`, which gives `true` or `false`.

All of this was seen on the host of a session, on a player's character: damage from a fall, and items given
and taken. A poisoned deer fired `Damaged` for each tick of the poison. These have not been seen:

All of this was tried on the host of a prospect, on the crafting tab. It has not been tried on a real bench,
as a guest, or after a fresh start of the game.
All the experience it has earned.

All three are `nil` when the character died with no hit that Wax heard. A creature killed with `Kill()` is
such a death. For `game.Creatures.Died`, `info` also has `Kind`, `Variant`, `ClassName` and `Name`, as
before.

All windows of your mod come up together, with one key, and go away with it. Other mods' windows and the Wax
panel stay as they are. Ask for the key with the `key` option of your first window. Without it Wax gives your
mod a free key and tells the player once.

Almost everything is inside the game folder, `...\steamapps\common\Icarus\Icarus\Binaries\Win64\`. Two
things are not: a registry key that is only made when you say yes, and a small log file of the
**Add to game** button.
Also reacts while a text box has the keyboard (for a key meant for the box, such as Tab).
Also reacts while the menu is open (off by default, so that typing in a box does not trigger it).
Also tints the whole model. True when omitted.

An **asset** is a file of the game: a mesh, a texture, a material, a blueprint's class. `game.Assets` loads
one by its path and keeps it in memory for your mod.
An **attribute** is a named value: a number, some text, `true` or `false`, or a table.

An **Instance** is one object of the game: your character, a tree, a component, the world itself.
`game.Character` gives you an Instance. So does `game.World`, and so does every entry of a list such as
`game.World:GetChildren()`.

An **overlay** is a panel pinned to the screen. It stays up while you play, and it never takes the mouse.
Clicks go through it. Use it for things you only read, such as your position or a health bar.

An actor is one thing placed in the world, such as a character or a tree. The children of `game.World` are
the actors. This counts them by class and prints the five most common ones.
An actor: a creature, a player's character, an item on the ground, a bench, a wall.
An animation of keys on a creature.
An animation written as keys, as `game.Animations:Define` gives it. It can play on any number of targets at once.
An animation written as keys, as `game.Animations:Define` gives it. It can play on any number of targets at once.
An asset by its name, such as `"T_Icon"` or `"Meshes/Rock"`, as game.Assets loads it

An asset the game still uses at that moment keeps its older look: a thing in the world that was spawned from a
blueprint, for example. `content.State` is then `"restart"` and `content.Reason` names those assets. Remove what
you spawned in `mod.OnUnload`, and the next reload takes the newer copy.
An effect came onto the character or left it.
An engine key name such as "A", "LeftShift" or "MiddleMouseButton".
An engine key name such as "F10" or "Ctrl+K".
An engine key name such as "F6", "K" or "MiddleMouseButton" (a Keybind control gives you these). It can be held with Ctrl, Shift or Alt: "Ctrl+Three", "Ctrl+Shift+K".
An engine key name such as "F6". It can be held with Ctrl, Shift or Alt: "Ctrl+K".

An engine object. Every class of the game (Actor, `Pawn`, `IcarusPlayerCharacter` ...) is an Instance: it has what is listed here, and adds the properties and functions of its own class and of the classes that one is built on. A member the editor does not know is still read from the object, so nothing here stops you using it.

An engine object. Every class of the game (Actor, `Pawn`, `IcarusPlayerCharacter` ...) is an Instance: it has what is listed here, and adds the properties and functions of its own class and of the classes that one is built on. A member the editor does not know is still read from the object, so nothing here stops you using it.

An error ends only the task it happens in. The error goes to the log and shows as a notification. Your other
tasks keep running.
An error in one function does not stop the others. It goes to the log.
An error is reported and the runs go on. After five errors in a row they stop.
An error means the store cannot be made as described.
An error that says there is no character.
An event that handlers connect to. `F` is the shape of a handler, as in `WaxSignal<fun(name: string)>`.
An icon by name, for a cell with no picture.
An icon of your choice, in place of the kind's own.
An icon shown before the caption.
An icon shown before the page's name.
An icon shown before the title.
An icon with a number or a word beside it.

An Instance does not outlive a map change, so connect again on the new object, as the example does with
`game.Me.Spawned`.

An Instance of a character has `Damaged` and `Died` too. The other signals in the table above belong to
`game.Me`. To follow another value of any object, see Watching a value.

An Instance you got before the map changed is gone afterwards. Using it raises an error that tells you to
get it again. Ask `game` for a new one each time you need it. Don't keep an old one for long.

An item is named by its row in the game's table `D_ItemsStatic`, such as `"Wood"` or `"Stone_Pickaxe"`.
Letter case, spaces, underscores and hyphens do not matter, so `"stone pickaxe"` is the same item. A name the
game does not have raises an error that suggests the nearest ones.
An object arrives as an Instance, or `nil` when the property holds none.
An open card folds to its name while you hold it, and opens again where you put it down.
An outline always shows through walls.
An output cannot be added or taken away. Each output can become another item and another count.

An overlay is a container, like a window. Add controls to it the same way. Nobody can click an overlay, so
use controls that show things: `Label`, `Heading`, `Field`, `Progress`, `Icon`, `Separator`.
And it loads the other mod with `@` in front of the id:

Another model to be seen beside, such as a young animal's adult. This one is then as much smaller in its box as it is smaller than that one in the game, by the two meshes' sizes and their scale. It never fills less than four tenths of the box, and a model larger than the other fills the box as it would alone. Only mesh and scale of the other are read.
Another page is chosen. Your function gets the page's name.
Another page of a window is chosen.
Any of it as a guest in someone else's game.

Any other bone goes by the name its skeleton gives it. `game.Animations:GetBones(target)` lists them, and a
name the skeleton does not have raises an error that suggests the nearest.

Anywhere else Wax looks at most four times a second. A new stack shows about a quarter of a second
later, and a change that leaves the weight as it was, such as durability, within two seconds.
Armour now, and the most it can be.
As for a character, for this inventory alone.
As tall as it is wide when left out.

Gives one field of a row a new value in the game. It is written before Set returns, so whatever the game reads from the row next is the new value. `field` is a whole field of the row, such as "Inputs", not a path into one. The value is whole: a struct with each of its fields, a list with each of its entries, as Change hands it to its function. Row gives the same, except that it leaves an enum inside a struct out until that enum's own path is named (`Row(name, { "SessionRequirement.DataTableName" })`). Set needs it and raises "SessionRequirement lacks DataTableName" without it. Two things may be left out of a struct: a typed row handle's DataTableName, which is filled in from the kind of handle, and text and references to assets, which stay as they are. A typed row handle only takes its own table: an `ItemsStaticRowHandle` names a row of ItemsStatic and nothing else, apart from the table and row the field holds already. A table name is taken with or without "D\_", in any letter case, and written as the game lists it. An enum takes its number. Once Wax has read a value of that field in this session (for a list: from a row where the list has an entry), the number has to be one the enum has or the one the field holds, and the enum's name as the game spells it is taken too. Until then a name raises an error that asks for the number. Everything is checked before anything is written: the row, the field, the kind of every value, and that a row handle or a row enum names a row its table has (a row the field already names may stay, as some of the game's own rows name rows that are not there). What is wrong raises an error that names the place, such as "Inputs\[2] lacks Count". After the write the field is read again. If the game did not take the value, the old one is put back and an error says what differed. The change belongs to the mod that makes it and is put back when the mod unloads. A mod that makes the same change again in the frame it reloads, or within 2 seconds of it, writes nothing. A change it no longer makes is put back when those 2 seconds are over. After a reload the row may still hold the mod's own earlier value, so a new value worked out from what the row holds belongs in Change. When two mods set one field, the mod that loads later is used, and Conflicts lists the field. With a table of fields in place of the field name, every value is checked before any is written. Two keys that mean the same field, such as Count and count, are an error. This version does not change text, references to assets, maps, sets, doubles or references to live objects. A list whose entries only the game can make (they hold one of those, a row enum or a multi row handle) keeps its length: its entries can be changed where they are, not added or removed. A kind of change that this version has switched off raises an error that says so. That can be a list that would get longer or shorter while it has more than 4 entries, while it is inside another value, or while its entries are strings or can hold strings or lists of their own. It can also be a row handle pointed at another table than the one it names now.

One crafting recipe: a row of D_ProcessorRecipes. `game.Recipes:Get("Stone_Axe")` gives one. Reading a field reads the game's table, so it is always what the table holds now. The lists it gives are yours to change: that changes nothing in the game. One exception keeps a mod steady while it is being reloaded: what the mod itself wrote before the reload is left out, so `if recipe.Work > 2000 then recipe:SetWork(2000) end` does the same thing each time. Every function that changes the recipe returns the recipe, so changes can follow one another: `game.Recipes:Get("Stone_Axe"):SetInputs({ Stone = 1 }):SetSeconds(1)`. A change is written before the function returns. It belongs to the mod that makes it and is put back when the mod unloads, as every change of game.Data is. What two mods do to one recipe is worked out in the order the mods load. SetInput, RemoveInput, the Scale functions, AddBench, RemoveBench and the output functions build on what an earlier mod did. SetInputs, SetBenches, MoveTo, SetWork, SetSeconds, SetRequirement, Hide and Show replace it, and `game.Data:Conflicts()` lists a field where that hides another mod's different value. What a change does to something that is being made or waiting in a queue, as it was seen on the host: a new time counts from the next moment, so what is half done by the old time may be nearly done, or done, by the new one. What is taken and what comes out is read from the recipe when the making ends, as the recipe is then. Nothing is taken before that. As soon as the player cannot pay what the recipe takes, the making is dropped without a message, and nothing is lost. So change recipes when the mod loads if a player should never see one change while it is being made. Names of items, benches, recipes and nodes are matched without regard to letter case. A name the game does not have raises an error that suggests the nearest ones. This version of Wax cannot make every list of a recipe longer or shorter. The outputs keep their number: each can become another item and another count. The resources keep their number too. The items, the tags and the benches of a recipe can be added to and taken from while the list has 4 entries or fewer, before and after. A change that is refused raises an error that says so, and changes nothing.

One of the game's data tables, such as ProcessorRecipes (every recipe) or Itemable (every item's name, icon and weight). A field path is a field's name, with a dot for each step into a struct or an array: "RequiredMillijoules", "Requirement.RowName", "Inputs.Element.RowName". Naming a struct or an array of structs asks for everything inside it. A wrong path raises an error that suggests the right one. Rows are read once and kept. A row is one table for as long as it is kept, and asking for more fields later adds them to that same table. Row names and field names are matched without regard to letter case. The keys of a row are spelled as the game spells them. Enum fields are read only when their own path is named, and they read as numbers. A map field is read only when its own path is named ("ArmourStats", "Creatures.WorldStatInjection"), and it is read whole: a path cannot go on into a map. It is a table from each key to its value. A key is a string or a number: a name, a string, the number of an enum, a whole number or a float, an asset's path, the row name of a row handle, and the one name inside a row enum or a tag, so a stat map reads `{ ["BaseMaximumHealth_+"] = 100 }`. An entry whose key is a reference to no asset is left out. A value is what a field of that kind is anywhere in a row: a number, true or false, a string, a struct as a table (a row handle among them, as its two names) without the enums, maps and curves inside it, an asset's path, or the numbers of a curve. A value that refers to nothing is false, so its key is still there. A map is refused when its keys are references to live objects, or structs other than a row handle and a struct with a single name or number in it, and when its values are lists, maps, sets or live objects other than curves. What a map holds is learned from the first entry read, so the error that says which of these it is comes when a row that has an entry in that map is read, and at once from then on. A map with more than 4,096 entries is not read: its row is nil and the log says why. A field that refers to a `CurveFloat` is read only when its own path is named, as a WaxDataCurve, or nil when it refers to nothing. A curve that several rows refer to is asked of the game once, and each row gets its own copy of the numbers. A field that refers to any other live object, such as a texture, raises an error when a row where it is set is read. Sets, delegates, doubles, weak references and lists of live objects are never read. Naming one raises an error that says what it is.

One of the game's function libraries ("KismetSystemLibrary", "GameplayStatics", "KismetMathLibrary"). A library has no objects in the world. Its functions are called on what this returns: `game:Library("KismetMathLibrary"):RandomFloat()`. A wrong name raises an error that suggests the right one.

Put the mod in a public repository on GitHub. The catalogue reads it from there.
Put the mods in another order
Put the settings in your own window

Puts a described store into the game: rows for its new categories, its nodes, what they sell and what they hand over, each named "\<ModId>\_\<id>" and added by the mod they are named after. The description is checked as Check does it, and an error of Check is raised as an error here, with how many more there are. In this version of Wax a store that passes then ends in one of three errors and nothing is added: a node that needs `all` of several is refused, a store with a new category raises "a new category is not switched on in this version of Wax", and any other store raises "adding rows to the game's tables is not switched on in this version of Wax". Research is saved in the player's account under a node's row name for good. So an id, and with it the mod's folder name, never changes once players have the mod: a node under a new name is a new node, and what was researched under the old name no longer counts.

Puts a line of text over an actor, over one part of an actor, or on a spot in the world. It follows what it is on, shows through walls, and tags that would cover each other pile up. The tag goes away by itself when the actor does.
Puts a modifier on for that many seconds. Gives back its `Id`, or `nil` when the game did not put it on.

Puts a modifier on the character. The modifier is named by its row of D_ModifierStates, such as "Health_Regen", in any letter case, and a name the game does not have raises an error that suggests the nearest ones. How long it stays has to be given: the game's table keeps no time of its own for a modifier. It is on at once, and GetModifiers and HasModifier say so in the same frame. It has been tried on a player's character. The game's table marks some modifiers as not for creatures.

Puts a new wild creature into the world with the game's own spawn. kind is a variant such as "Conifer_Wolf" or "Deer", or a kind that has one variant. A kind with several raises an error that lists them. place is a position, an actor or game.Me. When it is omitted the creature goes six metres in front of your character, and the options may stand in its place. Wax asks the game for ground a creature can walk on near the place, within 5 metres to the sides and at any height, and puts the creature a little above it. Where the game has none it raises an error and nothing is spawned. Inside a task Spawn waits until the game has given the creature its level, two seconds at most, and then answers the creature. Outside a task it answers at once, and Level and Health are right a few frames later. It answers nil and the reason when the creature left the world before it was finished. A tamed variant is refused in this version of Wax. The game's call took 3 to 4 ms when it was timed, and 18 ms once: a kind that is not in memory is loaded by the game inside the call. What is spawned stays when the mod unloads, unless the option keep is false.
Puts a node this mod hid back on its tree. Returns true when it was hidden. Switched off in this version of Wax, like Hide.
Puts a picture behind the card, faded and cut to the card's shape. Returns false and the reason when the file cannot be read.

Puts a shape from `game.Assets:Mesh` or `game.Assets:Model` on a socket or a bone of the model that shows: a tool in a hand, a hat on a head. The model has to be in the picture: wait for Loaded. It goes when another model is shown.
Puts a small cross at the right end of the box while it holds text. One press empties the box, fires Typed with "" and leaves the keyboard in the box. For a search box.

Puts a tamed animal into the world that is yours and can be ridden at once. kind is its set-up row such as "Mount_Moa" or "Mount_Horse", or a kind such as "Moa". It is made with the game's own spawn, named, given to you, and a saddle is put in its saddle slot, which is what makes the game give it a seat: after that the game's own "ride" works on it. place is a position or an actor. When it is omitted the mount comes a few metres in front of you, and the options may stand in its place. Where the game knows no ground to walk on under the place, as on a platform a mod built, the mount is made on the ground below and brought up. Inside a task it answers once the saddle is on, with the reason as a second value when the saddle did not go on. Outside a task it answers at once and finishes a moment later. The mount is saved with the prospect like any other.
Puts each recipe of the list back on the lists it was taken off with Hide, as `Recipe:Show` does for one.
Puts every theme setting back to the "Midnight" defaults.
Puts every theme setting back to the Midnight defaults.
Puts it on another team: `"Default"`, `"Friendly"`, `"Tame"`, `"HostileToPlayers"`, `"HostileToAll"`, or a team's own name.
Puts items into the backpack. Gives back how many went in, and why not all of them when fewer did.

Puts items into the inventory. They go onto the stacks of that item first, then into empty slots that the game says take that kind of item, a full stack to a slot. What does not fit is not given, and nothing is dropped on the ground. A tool comes as the game makes a new one, with its full durability. Count, Has and List follow in the same frame, the weight a moment later. It has been tried on a player's backpack.

Puts one in the world and gives the thing. `position` is \{ X = 0, Y = 0, Z = 0 } or \{ 0, 0, 0 }, also what a call such as K2_GetActorLocation gives. `rotation` is a turn in degrees, \{ Pitch = 0, Yaw = 90, Roll = 0 } or \{ 0, 90, 0 }, with what is left out being 0. `data` is a table of your own that the thing keeps as its Data. While there is no world it raises an error that says so. A mistake while the thing is put together raises an error and leaves nothing standing. Whether the other players of a session see a thing has not been tried. The game's own part of making a thing with two mesh parts took about half a millisecond.
Puts text on the clipboard, for pasting anywhere.
Puts the camera somewhere. What is left out stays as it is. The slow turn stops.
Puts the camera somewhere. What is left out stays. The slow turn stops.
Puts the recipe back on the lists it was taken off with Hide.

Puts the shape on a part as one of its sections, in place of what that section had. The part is an Instance of a `ProceduralMeshComponent` on an actor. When the mod that called this unloads, the section is cleared again if the part still exists. Every vertex is handed to the game one at a time. A box took 0.2 ms, with or without collision, and 3.7 ms the first time a shape with collision was put on in a session. So put a shape on once and keep it, not every frame. A character stands on a shape that has collision.
Puts the typing cursor in the box, so the user can type without clicking it.
Puts the view back where it started, and starts the slow turn again.
Puts the view back where it started, and starts the slow turn again.
Queues the table to be written under `name`. Only numbers, strings, booleans and tables of them are kept.
Raise `version` in `mod.lua`, for example from `1.2.0` to `1.2.1`.
Reaching: a hand or a foot goes somewhere
Read a property with a dot: `state.Health`.
Read and change the game's objects. Start at `game` and go to the world, the player and every other object. See The game tree.
read and change the game's tables: items, recipes, creatures, the store
read and change what is in the world: your character, its stats, its inventory, the time
Read any stat the game keeps for a character, see the effects that are on it, and put one on.

Read The bridge and developer mode first. With that file
in place, any program that runs as you can run code inside the game, and Wax no longer updates itself in the
game.
Read the game's clock, the weather on your character and the prospect you are in, and hear when a player joins or leaves.
Read your health, stamina, food, water and oxygen, and show them on the screen.
Read, change and call any object of the game.

Reading a field reads the game's table, so it is what the table holds now. The lists are yours: changing one
changes nothing in the game.

Reading takes time: about 20 whole recipes fit in a millisecond. Rows are read once and kept, so the second
time costs nothing.

Reads a 3D model from an .obj file in your mod's folder and gives it as a shape, the same kind `game.Assets:Mesh` gives: put it on a part with Apply, or name it as the mesh of a blueprint's part. No Unreal editor is needed. The file holds the shape only: give the part a material for its look. At most 65,000 vertices and 16 MB.
Reads a reflected property by name, including one whose name Wax also uses (Name, Parent ...).

Reads every slot again now. A whole backpack took the game between half a millisecond and a millisecond and a half when it was measured, so use it when something has to be exact at once, not every frame.

Reads many rows without holding the game up, and returns them by name. It only works inside a task. The task pauses whenever it has used its budget for the frame, and goes on in the next one. Rows that already hold the fields are not read again, so a second Load costs nothing and a Load that was stopped goes on where it left off.
Reads the name the game shows for every item, so that `Find` matches those too.

Reads the name the game shows for every item, so that Find matches those names too. It only works inside a task: it reads within a millisecond a frame and returns when all are read. Rows another mod has read already are not read again. When a mod changes the item tables, or the game makes them again, Find goes by item names alone until Load has run again.
Reads the whole store ahead of time, a little each frame. Only inside a task.

Reads the whole store ahead of time, a slice a frame, and returns how many nodes it has. It only works inside a task. Without it, the first GetNodes, also of one category, and the first Check of a store that gives something read every row of D_Talents and every node of the store in that one call, which holds the game up.

Recipes found together, in the order the game has them. `#list` is how many, `list[1]` the first, and it holds the recipes it was made with, whatever changes later. It has every function of a recipe that changes one, and does it to each recipe of the list: `game.Recipes:At("Fabricator"):ScaleTime(0.5)`. Each returns the list. A recipe the change does not apply to is left as it is where the function says so. When a change is refused for some recipes, the others are still changed, and then an error says how many were not and why the first was not. Inside a task, work on many recipes pauses when it has used a millisecond of a frame and goes on in the next. Anywhere else it is all done before the function returns, which for hundreds of recipes is a frame the player can notice.
Red. Shown with the **Errors** switch. Also pops up as a notification.
Refused in this version of Wax: the game has no such rule and nothing keeps it.
Releases older than 0.2.1 have no such list.
Remove a mod's folder to remove the mod. Wax unloads it the next time it looks.

Removes a page made with Page, with everything on it.
Removes everything your commands made, such as windows and signal connections.
Removes the mod, after asking. Its folder is renamed, not erased. Get mods says how to bring it back.
Removes the mod. Wax asks first.
Removes the overlay and everything on it.
Removes the overlay and everything on it.
Removes the window and everything on it.
Removes the window and everything on it.
Replaces the caption of a button that was made with one.
Replaces the caption. The button must have been made with one.
Replaces the text without firing Changed.
Replaces the title. Does nothing on a notification made without one.
Replaces the title. It does nothing on a notification made without a title.

Researches the node of a recipe, and first every node it still needs, with the player's own points. It does nothing unless the plan says `can`, and it stops at the first node the game does not research. It waits a few frames after each node, so call it inside a task.
Resizes it. A window does not go below its smallest size.
Resizes the window, no smaller than its minimum size.
Resizing stops at the window's smallest size and at the edges of the screen.
Returned by `game.Items:Get`. Used by `game.Items:Get`, `inventory:Count`, `inventory:Has`, `inventory:Where`, `inventory:Give`, `inventory:Take`, `playerItems:Count`, `playerItems:Has` and others.

Returned by `inventory:List`, `inventory:Slot`, `inventory:Where`, `playerItems:List`. Used by `game.Items:Get`, `inventory:Count`, `inventory:Has`, `inventory:Where`, `inventory:Give`, `inventory:Take`, `playerItems:Count`, `playerItems:Has` and others.
Returns a copy of `defaults` with whatever was saved under `name` laid over it.
Returns the value kept under `key`, storing `default` (or a new table) on first use. The value survives reloads of the mod.
Roll it up to its title bar
Rolls it up to its title bar. `false` rolls it back down.
Row names of nodes of which one bought is enough. An empty list takes every parent away.
Rows kept ready above and below the ones that show, so a fast scroll does not show empty space. Default: half of what shows, between 2 and 6.
Run a function when a key is pressed during play.
Run a function when something happens, such as a map change or a flipped switch. See Signals.
Run a function when something happens.
Run code alongside the game. See Tasks.
Run code over time. Wait, repeat and delay without freezing the game. See Tasks.

Run the installer from the Windows account you play on. Under another account Wax could not save its
settings.
Running Lua from outside the game
Runs `callback` when the key is pressed during play. The hotkey is removed when the mod reloads.
Runs `f` again and again, that many seconds apart. New in Wax 0.3.0: see Watching a value.
Runs `f` at the end of the current frame.
Runs `f` now, until it finishes or first pauses. Extra values are passed to `f`.
Runs `fn` on every fire. Gives back a connection.
Runs `fn` on the next fire only.

Runs `fn` once when the mod is about to unload, before anything of the mod is taken away: its windows, tasks, connections and table changes are all still there. `why` is "reload" when the mod loads again straight after, "off" when the player switched it off, "removed" when its folder went, "failed" when the mod raised an error while it loaded, and "shutdown" when Wax itself stops. Several run newest first, and one that raises an error is logged and stops none of the others. `fn` must return at once: it cannot wait. Use it for what Wax cannot undo for you, such as a change made to the world. It does not run when the game closes or the map changes. Returns a function that takes `fn` off again.
Runs every connected function with these values.

Runs every frame for each thing, with the seconds since it last ran for that thing. All stepped and every functions together get 2 ms a frame: what is left waits a frame and is then told the longer time. The time is real time, so it also runs while the game is paused.
Runs f(...) after `seconds`, never earlier than the next frame.

Runs f(...) again and again: the first time after `seconds`, then `seconds` after each run has ended. It never runs more than once a frame. An error in f is reported and the runs go on. After five errors in a row they stop. It stops when the mod unloads, and `task.cancel` stops it.
Runs f(...) at the end of the current frame's step (or of the next one, when called outside a step).
Runs f(...) now, until it returns or first pauses.
Runs functions as tasks: now, at the end of the frame, after a time, or again and again. A task can pause with `task.wait`, and the game goes on while it waits.
Runs once for each thing, when its actor has begun play and its parts are there. That is inside Spawn, or a frame later when the world itself had not begun.

Runs once, a frame after a thing has gone: "Destroyed" by Destroy or by the game, "MapChanged", or "Unloaded" with its part of the world. The actor is gone by then, so only Data, Blueprint and Alive can be read. It does not run when the blueprint is removed or your mod unloads.

Runs when an actor starts to overlap the thing. Wax asks the game what overlaps each such thing once in 6 frames, and tells of every actor that did not overlap at the look before. Only a part with collision = "touch" overlaps anything.
Runs when its arrow is pressed.
Runs when the animation has run to its end. Not when it is stopped.
Runs when the card is pressed.
Runs when the line is pressed.
Runs when the panel is pressed where it has no control.
Save a `.lua` file of your mod. A moment later, Wax reloads that mod. The game keeps running.
Save a file and your mod reloads in the running game.

Save a model as Wavefront `.obj` from any 3D program, put the file in your mod's folder, and `game.Assets:Model`
reads it. No Unreal editor and no pak are needed. It gives the same kind of shape as `game.Assets:Mesh`, so it
goes on a part the same way.
Save the file a few times. The number goes up each time.
Save the file a few times. The number goes up, because attributes live through a reload of your mod.
Saving a file reloads your mod. That is hot reload, and it works with any editor.
Saving any `.lua` file of the mod reloads the whole mod.
Search by a name, an author or a tag, pick a category or a tag, and sort by what is new, liked or downloaded most.
Search by the name players see
Seconds for open, close and expand animations. 0 turns animation off.
Seconds over which it dims at the end.
